10813-a-versailles-christmas-tide:
Mary Stuart Boyd published A Versailles Christmas-Tide in 1901, with fifty-three illustrations by A. S. Boyd, about an English family spending Christmas at Versailles. Chapters run from the unexpected happening and the town, through the Christmas tree and New Year's Day, to ice-bound days, a haunted chateau, Marie Antoinette, and prisoners released.

Boyd writes of French customs, shops, chestnuts in the avenue, and the pleasures of a foreign Christmas with warmth and humor. The illustrations add Parisian and Versailles scenes throughout. Readers get a delightful holiday travel book, full of the charm of France at Christmas.
1141-selected-poems-of-oscar-wilde:
Oscar Wilde's chosen lyrics gather here, from his lush Oxford verse to the stark Ballad of Reading Gaol, written after prison. Early poems praise art, Rome, and beauty in rich, musical lines, while later pieces turn sadder and sharper, with prison, shame, and pity in view.

The selection shows both Wildes: the young dandy who worshipped beauty and the older man who learned suffering. Poems like "The Harlot's House" and "The Sphinx" add a darker note. The book gives a compact path through Wilde's verse, and it pairs well with his plays and prose.
12524-the-englishing-of-french-words-the:
Brander Matthews's Society for Pure English tract, number five, printed at Oxford in 1921, treats French words in English, with a companion piece by Robert Bridges on dialect words in Blunden's poems. Matthews calls English an inn of strange meetings, where words of bluest blood mix with children of the gutter and strangers from all shores.

Seafaring terms, court words and everyday borrowings show how French entered English and settled, some tarrying briefly, some founding families equal to the oldest natives. Matthews writes with wit about adoption, spelling and use. The tract is a lively, learned note on language contact, and on how a living tongue takes in guests without losing itself.
12926-the-morris-book-part-1-a-history-o:
Cecil J. Sharp and Herbert C. Macilwaine wrote The Morris Book, part one of 1907, as a history of Morris dancing with eleven dances as performed by the Morris men of England. Issued with Morris Dance Tunes, it thanks Lady Isabel Margesson, Florence Warren, and Baring Gould, who lent the woodcut of Kemp dancing from London to Norwich. An introduction opens the work.

The authors define the Morris step and jump with care: the jump never varies, the step varies in height and vigour, but sturdiness never leaves it. Languor, they insist, is unknown to Morris men. The book preserves dances that might otherwise have faded from English villages.
1338-selected-prose-of-oscar-wilde:
Gathered from Wilde's essays, reviews, stories, and notebooks, this 1914 selection ranges across art, criticism, and society. Short pieces sit beside longer ones on Meredith, Browning, Newman, and Dante, and on themes such as the critic's craft, the limits of genius, and the art of the past.

Other pieces turn to Salome, to country houses, to London streets, and to the trials of the artist in a plain world. With a preface by Robert Ross, the book offers Wilde in many moods: witty, learned, and at times grave. It serves as a good first shelf of his prose outside the plays.
13441-the-sunny-side:
A. A. Milne gathers light essays and sketches from his nine happy years at the Punch office, dedicating the 1922 book to Owen Seaman. Chapters run from Oranges and Lemons and Men of Letters through Summer Days, War-Time, Home Notes, and A Few Guests. Simpson's letter to Myra, inviting friends round after dinner, sets the sociable tone.

Golf verses, a pianola grown out of and judged ugly, and talk of books, guests, and holidays fill the pages. Milne writes with gentle wit about ordinary pleasures, friendships, and the small absurdities of home life. The Sunny Side reads as a companion to his Punch work: clever, kind, and never in a hurry to make a grand point.
14089-homestead-on-the-hillside:
Mrs. Mary Jane Holmes's popular novel follows Lenora and her mother toward a hillside homestead after burial and hardship. Chapters trace a stepmother's rule, domestic life at the house, darkness, and retribution, ending in a finale that carries out dear Mr. Hamilton's plans. A second story, Rice Corner, follows with its own belle, cousin, and suitors.

Small domestic scenes carry large feeling. A feverish child creeps to a well at night for water, finds the pail empty, and drinks from a cup by moonlight before falling into final sleep. Later, Sally the servant reports on the Gilberts with comic grammar, counting carpets enough to cover every crack. Holmes knew her audience: tears, gossip, and moral order, served in plain prose. The book pleased thousands of readers who wanted home, loss, and justice in one volume.
14382-the-missing-bride:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth set this sensation novel at Luckenough, an old manor house in the forests of St. Mary's County, Maryland. Its founder, a Polish soldier of fortune, left a tangled inheritance behind him.

Edith, a young heiress, faces attacks, abductions, and family secrets as rival claimants circle the estate. Marian and other heroines endure snowbound journeys, midnight alarms, and courtroom reckonings before the missing bride of the title is found. Southworth piles incident on incident, and the novel rewards readers who enjoy Victorian melodrama at full stretch.
14992-the-life-of-froude:
Herbert Paul's 1905 life of James Anthony Froude, published by Pitman, opens by skipping genealogical details. To be born obscure and die famous, Paul notes, has been called the height of human luck. But it is a man himself, not his ancestors, whose life deserves writing, and Froude held that opinion too.

Few families hold more than one remarkable figure, Paul argues, and lineage fails scientific tests as evidence for or against a life. Nothing shows from what source, other than the ultimate source of every good gift, Froude drew his brilliant powers. He was a gentleman who did not care to find or make a pedigree for himself. Paul's biography follows Froude's own rule: the man, not the family tree.
15161-great-fortunes-and-how-they-were-m:
James McCabe's 1871 book tells how American self-made men built great fortunes, with portraits drawn from original designs. Fulton and his steamboat monster supply a striking front image, and a Carlyle motto sets the theme: not works, but the spirit in which men work, gives worth. The book runs to over a thousand pages in print.

Lives of merchants, makers, and traders show honest business as a public good, in McCabe's view, as well as a road to wealth. Struggles, risks, and triumphs fill each sketch. Readers interested in American enterprise will find the book a rich, if boosterish, gallery of nineteenth-century go-getters.
15627-verner-s-pride:
Mrs. Henry Wood published this long Victorian novel, Verner's Pride, illustrated by Harold Piffard, with Collins' Clear-Type Press in London and Glasgow. Thirty-seven chapters or more trace Rachel Frost, a willow pond, news brought home, a crowd in moonlight, and a tall gentleman in the lane. Dinah Roy's ghost, a revelation at an inquest, and Robin's vow follow.

Later chapters bring Mr. Verner's estrangement, Lady Verner, Lucy Tempest, an altered will, a disappearance, and a whispered suspicion. News from Australia, a packet in a shirt drawer, and Dr. West's sanctum deepen the mystery. Wood writes a sensation novel of family pride, inheritance, and secrets, in the full Victorian manner, where a will, a ghost, and a revelation can undo a household's standing.
1590-the-amazing-interlude:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's Amazing Interlude follows Sara Lee Kennedy, a Pennsylvania girl left alone at nineteen, knitting by the fire while the Great War gathers. Her life changes when she travels to France, where officers fight paper and pin battles at headquarters and soldiers crowd the roads behind the lines.

There Sara Lee finds work among the men at the front, and a love story grows out of her courage and humour. Rinehart writes with warmth about Americans abroad in wartime. The novel was a bestseller in 1918, and it remains a period romance of war, duty, and a girl's coming of age.
15928-the-nursery-number-164-a-monthly-m:
The Nursery, number one hundred and sixty-four, for August 1880, volume twenty-seven, a monthly magazine for youngest readers. The Nursery Publishing Company of Bromfield Street, Boston, issued it at one dollar and fifty cents a year, fifteen cents a copy. American News, New-England News, Central News, and Western News companies distributed it. The magazine entered Boston post office as second-class matter.

Short stories, verses, and pictures fill the number, sized for very young children. Reading aloud, learning letters, and gentle morals shape each page. The Nursery served mothers and teachers across America. The number gives a glimpse of 1880 childhood in print: simple, sweet, and made to be loved.
16433-the-gay-cockade:
Temple Bailey gathers fifteen short stories in this 1921 volume, most first printed in magazines like Harper's, Scribner's, and the Saturday Evening Post. Titles run from The Gay Cockade and The Hidden Land to White Birches, The Emperor's Ghost, Burned Toast, and Lady Crusoe. Each tale stands alone, with a fresh cast and a fresh setting.

Bailey's stories lean on warmth, humor, and a neat twist at the close. A rebellious grandmother, a canopy bed, and a wait for Prince Charming all get their turn. The book suits readers who like gentle, well-made magazine fiction of the early 1920s, told with a light hand and a kind eye.
1645-rhymes-a-la-mode:
Andrew Lang's Rhymes a la Mode, published by Kegan Paul in 1885, gathers verses that had appeared in periodicals. A harpsichord player on its cover and a ballade motto on its title page. Lang's light verse ranges over books, love, and London life, in ballades, rondeaux, and songs written for pleasure.

The rhymes are polished, witty, and deliberately old-fashioned, looking back to French forms and to the age of Villon. Lang's easy scholarship shows in every stanza. The volume is a pleasant shelf of Victorian light verse, for readers who enjoy form worn lightly.
16473-queen-hildegarde:
Laura E. Richards opens her Hildegarde-Margaret series with Queen Hildegarde, a girls' book of home, farm, and growing up. Chapters follow Hildegardis Graham through Dame and Farmer, The Prisoner of Despair, The New Hilda, The Blue Platter, Hartley's Glen, and The Warrior Queen, closing with The Tree-Party and a last word.

Richards writes warmly for girls, with humor, kindness, and a love of country life. Hildegarde's trials are real but gentle, and her spirit carries the book. Fans of Captain January and Richards's other stories will find the same sunny, wholesome charm here.
16897-the-tables-turned-or-nupkins-awake:
William Morris wrote this short socialist play, first played at the Socialist League hall on October 15, 1887, and issued by the Commonweal office in London the same year. The cast lists Mr. Justice Nupkins, counsel, sergeants, constables, Mary Pinch, a laborer's wife charged with theft, and Jack Freeman, a socialist charged with conspiracy, sedition, and blocking a highway.

Morris turns the tables on law itself: the judge and his court face the very charges they hand down. The play is brief, comic, and sharp, meant for a hall crowd, not a grand stage. Readers who like political farce will enjoy its swift justice and its socialist moral, delivered with laughs and bite.
1721-the-trees-of-pride:
Squire Vane has planted peacock trees on his Irish estate and made a wager about them. When a mystery gathers around the trees and a well, he strides off in a fury. When a mystery gathers around those trees and the well on his land, Vane storms off in a fury. His household is left to chase after the truth.

The story plays as a detective tale with a Chestertonian turn: the supernatural explanation is weighed against a plain human one. Pride — Vane's own — is the real subject. Told in four short chapters, it is a compact sample of Chesterton's method, in which a joke, a wager, and a landscape combine into an argument about belief.
17477-the-trail-horde:
Charles Alden Seltzer, author of The Ranchman and The Range Boss, wrote this western novel with a frontispiece. Chapters open with morals, driving a bargain, and a woman's eyes. Rebellion, a man's word, and an invisible power follow. A coalition, a woman's mercy, and the arm of power carry the story on.

Readers get a range novel of cattle, conflict, and codes of honour, in Seltzer's sturdy, popular style. The trail horde of the title suggests massed cattle and massed men moving across open country. The book suits readers of classic western fiction.
18060-the-good-comrade:
Una L. Silberrad wrote The Good Comrade in 1907, put out in New York by Doubleday, Page, with pictures by Anna Whelan Betts. Silberrad sets her tale among the Polkingtons, a family in debt, where a blue daffodil becomes a token of hope and pride.

Chapters run from the debt and the owner of the blue daffodil to an excursion, debtor and creditor, and how Julia did not get the flower. Pooferchjes and jealousy, a holiday, and a reprieve spice the plot. Silberrad writes with charm and moral warmth. It is a pleasant Edwardian novel of family, debt, and loyal friendship.
1817-a-question-of-latitude:
Richard Harding Davis follows Everett, a young writer of the muckraker school. He takes up a case of fever and filth in a place where chloride of lime, a canvas cot, and a tin chop-box mark the sickroom. Everett's skirmishes with corruption have made him a name, but this story tests whether exposure alone can change anything.

Davis, who knew the reporter's world, writes the tale as a study of conscience. A young man must decide how far to go, and what his writing costs the people he writes about. The title's latitude is both geography and morals, and the story's force lies in Everett's slow sense that truth-telling has a price.
18409-by-the-roadside:
Katherine M. Yates, author of Up the Sunbeams and Through the Woods, wrote this children's book, published by the Harmony Shop in Boston in 1908. By the Roadside opens with a little brown Dream telling Marjorie it is time to go to work. Marjorie, cross and snug in her pillow, says she is not ready, and the Dream sits on the footboard swinging his feet.

Marjorie soon finds that a true word, once said, stays with her and cannot be escaped by sleep. The Dream asks why she wants to escape a thing she knows is true, and the talk becomes a gentle lesson. Yates writes in dialogue, with a dream as teacher and a child as pupil. Young readers get a moral fancy: work, truth, and the small voice that will not let a child rest until she minds it.
18541-voyage-of-the-liberdade:
Captain Joshua Slocum published this sea memoir at Boston in 1890. It recounts his South American trading voyages, with hurricanes off the Cape Verde Islands, cholera in Argentina, mutiny aboard ship, and smallpox among his crew. After losing his bark Aquidneck, he built a small craft, the Liberdade, and sailed her north along the Brazilian coast.

Later chapters follow the Liberdade past Bahia and Pernambuco to Barbados, then through the Bahamas and the Gulf Stream to South Carolina and on to Washington. Slocum writes as a plain, salty sailor with an eye for ports, weather, and odd shipmates. The book is a stirring record of working sail in the late 1800s.
18573-abraham-lincoln-an-horatian-ode:
Richard Henry Stoddard published this ode at New York in 1865, weeks after Abraham Lincoln's murder. The title page notes Lincoln's birth on February 12, 1809, and his assassination on Good Friday, April 14, 1865. Stoddard frames the poem with lines from Macbeth on murder and treason, setting the tone of shock.

The ode says the nation's grief is wider than that for a captain fallen in battle or a statesman worn out by care. Lincoln fell not in war's tide but after it, when his work seemed done. Stoddard calls him a man without precedent, sent to do his work and perish. The poem stands as an early, moving tribute.
18617-on-the-blockade:
Oliver Optic wrote this 1890 boys' novel as part of his Blue and Gray Afloat series on the Civil War at sea. It follows the crew of the United States steamer Bronx on blockade duty, with a dinner for the Confederacy, a deaf-and-dumb puzzle, sealed orders, and a captured steamer renamed in mid-voyage. Later chapters bring a Gulf expedition, a shore battery visit, and a fight with a privateer.

Optic keeps the pace brisk and the talk plain, with seamanship and duty at the fore. Young readers learn how a blockade worked while following one ship's cruise. The book stands as a lively sample of late-1800s adventure fiction for boys.
18682-a-declaration-of-the-causes-which-:
Printed at London in 1589 by the deputies of Christopher Barker, printer to the Queen, this short tract defends the English fleet's seizure of Hanse ships. The ships were bound for Lisbon with corn and war stores for the King of Spain. They were stopped at the mouth of the Tagus on June 30, 1589, during the English voyage to Portugal. Hanse merchants of the Sound in Denmark cried foul, citing old treaties and their claimed neutral rights.

The declaration answers that aiding Spain in wartime breaks neutrality, and that old pacts do not cover such cargoes. Its spelling keeps the flavor of the age, with forms such as nauie and maiestie. The tract is a rare, vivid voice from Elizabethan sea war and trade law.
18884-ducks-at-a-distance-a-waterfowl-id:
Bob Hines wrote this waterfowl identification guide for the United States Fish and Wildlife Service, published in Washington in 1978. It teaches birdwatchers to name ducks, geese, and swans seen far off, on water or in flight, where color and fine markings cannot be trusted. Identification by shape, flight, and behavior is the book's method.

The guide covers puddle ducks such as mallard, pintail, and wood duck, diving ducks such as canvasback and goldeneye, and mergansers, scoters, and whistling ducks. Notes on eclipse plumage warn readers when drakes look plainest. Readers get a practical field aid, illustrated in the original, that still serves anyone learning ducks on a lake or marsh.
18902-flood-tide:
Sara Ware Bassett's novel, published by A. L. Burt in March 1921 by arrangement with Little, Brown, opens with Willie Spence, a trial and a treasure of Wilton. Neighbors love the little old man with short-sighted blue eyes and an appealing smile, though he owns uncommon little common sense.

Willie lives in a silver-gray cottage on the Harbor Road, where his housekeeper Celestina Morton worships him even as she scolds his dreamy disregard for dinner, chowder cooling and popovers shriveling. Chapters name a weaver's fancies, a green-eyed monster, apparitions, the Galbraith household, and Delight's decision. Fame at last comes to the dreamer of dreams, in a tale of village kindliness.
19979-a-righte-merrie-christmasse-the-st:
John Ashton compiled A Righte Merrie Christmasse as the story of Christ-tide. He begins with a scholar's puzzle about dates. The day of Christ's death is plainly distinguishable, he notes. The day of his birth is open to much question. December 25 must be taken as purely conjectural, Ashton concludes. From that honesty he builds a history of Christmas customs. Merriment, in his title's old spelling, is the theme.

Ashton was a tireless antiquarian of English social life. His Christmas book gathers carols, feasts, mummings, and church ales. Old prints and copperplates illustrate the customs he describes. The work helped Victorians reinvent Christmas as heritage. Much of our traditional Christmas imagery passes through such books. Ashton's is among the merriest sources.
20004-tancred-or-the-new-crusade:
Disraeli published Tancred, or The New Crusade, in 1847. Its hero, young Lord Tancred, seeks faith in the Holy Land. The opening finds English aristocrats abroad, betting on the Derby even there. Goodwood and play hold their interest more than shrines, at first. Polite nations' language conveys their worldliness, Disraeli notes dryly. Tancred's pilgrimage cuts against his whole class's grain. The novel completes his Young England trilogy.

With Coningsby and Sybil, Tancred argues England needs spiritual renewal. Its new crusade is one of ideas, not swords. Disraeli's Eastern journey of 1830 feeds its scenes. Jews, Arabs, and churchmen debate destiny in its pages. The book baffled and fascinated Victorian readers equally. It remains the strangest of his major novels.
20383-marriage-a-la-mode:
Marriage à la Mode opens on a steamer that has left Washington about an hour before, bound for Mount Vernon. A young man sits down beside his uncle in the deck saloon. Through the open doorway they see a wide stretch of river flowing between banks of spring green.

From that calm start, the story turns to courtship and marriage in fashionable life. The river trip gives the pair time to talk, and talk drives the plot. Readers meet the manners, money concerns, and family pressures that shape a smart match in the world the tale describes.
20435-the-world-in-chains-some-aspects-o:
The World in Chains studies how war and trade bind the modern world together. Written while great wars shook Europe, it asks what war means for nations tied by commerce. The author treats the question as one for moral philosophy first of all.

An anthropologist, the book grants, may see war as a gallant survival. War keeps an impressive ritual and a code of honour strangely cut off from social life. But the book presses past that romance to war's costs in trade, trust, and daily work. It suits readers who want ideas, not battle stories.
2051-dickory-cronke-the-dumb-philosopher:
This curious eighteenth-century pamphlet tells of Dickory Cronke, a Cornish tinner's son born dumb who kept silence for fifty-eight years, then found speech a few days before his death. His life, faith, and meditations follow. The pamphlet first appeared in the eighteenth century, when wonder tales of dumb prophets sold well.

Cronke's prophetical notes on Europe and Britain from 1720 to 1729, an elegy, and an epitaph close the volume. The piece mixes wonder tale, religious reflection, and political prophecy, and it reads as a strange relic of its age. Cronke's meditations show a man who, denied speech, turned to writing and to prayer instead.
210-an-international-episode:
Two young Englishmen land in New York in the summer of 1874 and find America strange and vivid. Henry James's International Episode follows Lord Lambeth and Percy Beaumont through Broadway heat, hotels, and Newport society. An American girl, Bessie Alden, tests their manners.

James reverses his usual direction: here Europeans abroad must learn American ways. Flirtation, misunderstanding, and a near-engagement carry the comedy. The tale's second half returns the Americans to London for a cool reckoning. It remains a neat study of national character. The episode pairs neatly with Daisy Miller as a study of Americans abroad.
21695-life-in-the-red-brigade-london-fir:
R. M. Ballantyne follows a London fireman home in Life in the Red Brigade. Wet, worn, and weary, with water squeaking in his boots, the man walks smartly through the streets. Charcoal and water streak his face past his own mother's knowing.

His blue coat, sailor's cap, hatchet, and brass helmet mark him a fireman of London. Ballantyne calls such men dare-anything characters who live in smoke as a native element. They carry their lives in their hands, night and day, facing flames for strangers. The book opens the station house, the tressel bed, and the call at midnight to young readers.
21816-the-confidence-man-his-masquerade:
A mute stranger boards a Mississippi steamboat at the start of Herman Melville's The Confidence-Man, published at New York in 1857. It was Melville's last novel, and his strangest. Aboard the boat, a shifting figure moves among the passengers in many guises. He appears as a man with a weed, an herb-doctor, a soldier of fortune, and a man in a traveling cap.

Each scene tests charity, trust, and the ease with which men part with money. Chapter heads promise business transacted, injuries forgiven, and misers persuaded to invest. Melville turns the riverboat into a floating market of American faith and fraud. The book puzzled its first readers and still teases ours. It is a masquerade where the mask may be the only true face.
22513-sense-from-thought-divide:
Sense From Thought Divide is a science fiction story with a hard-boiled edge. Its narrator faces a tight-lipped officer in a tense interview. Lieutenant Murphy answers shortly, the narrator reports of the man.

Murphy manages to open his teeth a bare quarter inch for words. Pentagon, he says, naming the power behind the meeting. His light gray eyes pierce the narrator for effect. He watches to see if the narrator is impressed by it. Such clipped scenes give the story its interrogation-room pressure. Thought and sense divided, the title warns, is the tale's problem. Readers get period science fiction with a detective's voice and pace.
22626-an-ode:
An Ode is a patriotic poem honoring the first settlers who carried their faith to an unknown shore. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its speaker calls on the spirits of the departed dead, who scorned the bigot's yoke, to gather round the sacred place and shed their influence there.

The poem recalls how those daring hands unfurled the flag of faith, to float through future time as a beacon-banner of another world. Such odes were written for anniversaries and monuments, when towns honored founding fathers in verse. The diction is lofty and the feeling sincere. Readers of early American verse will find a fair sample of the ceremonial poetry that once marked public memory.
22661-clarimonde:
Clarimonde is Théophile Gautier's famous tale of a young priest haunted by a beautiful dead woman. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Told in the first person, the story opens with the narrator's confession that from earliest childhood he felt a calling to the priesthood.

All his studies bent toward that end, and his life to age twenty-four was one long preparation. His superiors judged him worthy, despite his youth, and his ordination was set for Easter week. Then Clarimonde enters, and the vowed life splits in two. Gautier's tale of sacred vows against undead desire became a classic of the fantastic. It is short, strange, and told with jeweler's care.
23397-at-the-seaside:
Mrs. Grey wrote this seaside picture book, with verses by Mrs. Warner-Sleigh, for young children. Georgie and Maudie come home from school with prizes for hard work and good conduct, and their mother rewards them with a month by the sea.

Nurse packs their toys, new clothes are bought for all weathers, and the family takes the train to Margate, then a fly to their lodgings. Bright mornings, beach play, and small seaside joys follow, each scene in verse and picture. The book suits reading aloud to small children, with its easy rhymes, its praise for effort, and its sunny view of a holiday earned by being good.
23852-canadian-postal-guide:
John Dewé, post office inspector, compiled the Canadian Postal Guide at Toronto in 1863, priced at twenty-five cents and published with the Postmaster General's permission. Its principal object is the spread of information about the Canadian postal service, for the public and for the post office alike.

Inside are the chief regulations of the post office, the rates of postage, and every information in regard to money orders. A short sketch of the post office's progress in Canada, drawn from authentic sources, runs over one hundred years of improvement in a country then purely agricultural. Postal historians and stamp collectors still use it as a record of how early Canadian mail worked.
23860-the-young-man-s-guide:
William A. Alcott published The Young Man's Guide in Boston, in a twelfth edition dated 1838. He began intending a mere compilation from the best books for young men, but found less in them wholly in accord with his sentiments than he expected. The project of compiling was given up, and the work became chiefly original.

Quotations from Burgh, Cobbett, Chesterfield, and Hawes remain, but most of the book is Alcott's own, rewritten and modified from his sources. Its object, he writes in December 1833, is to elevate and reform. For modern readers it is a window onto what antebellum America told its young men about character, work, and conduct.
23921-barometer-and-weather-guide:
Rear-Admiral FitzRoy compiled the Barometer and Weather Guide for the Board of Trade, in a third edition dated 1859 and sold for one shilling. Its preface records a practical proposal: placing barometers at exposed fishing villages, so that fishermen could read coming weather before putting to sea.

The guide teaches its rules in short, memorable lines. Long foretold, long last; short notice, soon past. First rise after low foretells a stronger blow. Tables adjust readings for height above the sea, a tenth for each hundred feet. For sailors and weather watchers, it is FitzRoy's plain, humane attempt to save lives with an instrument and a rhyme.
24044-myths-and-legends-of-christmastide:
Bertha F. Herrick published Myths and Legends of Christmastide in San Francisco in 1901, reprinting an article from a Christmas edition of the San Francisco Chronicle. Herrick sets foreign rites, ceremonies, and quaint beliefs beside matter-of-fact American ones, in a season the Puritans once deemed idolatrous.

Many odd customs now live only as tradition, but singular superstitions still survive among credulous classes, even in the twentieth century. In parts of England, the peasantry once said oxen kneel in stalls at midnight, the hour said to be Christ's birth. Bees sang in their hives and subterranean bells rang a merry peal. Old British legend says cocks crowed lustily through the night of December 24 against witches and evil spirits. In Bavaria, other old beliefs held on.
24402-catalogue-of-economic-plants-in-th:
William Saunders, superintendent of gardens and grounds, wrote this catalogue of economic plants in the United States Department of Agriculture collection. It was published by authority of the Secretary of Agriculture in Washington in 1891. Saunders writes to Secretary J. M. Rusk on June 5, 1891, that he has prepared, by direction, a list of the important economic plants in the department's collection. It meets the wants of visitors and others interested in the department's work.

The catalogue opens with Abelmoschus moschatus, a native of Bengal, whose seeds once mixed with hair powder still perfume pomatum. Arabs mix them with coffee berries, and in the West Indies the crushed seeds, steeped in rum, cure snake bites externally and internally. Next comes Abrus precatorius, wild liquorice, a twining plant of the East, now found in the West Indies and tropical regions, remarkable for its small seeds. Readers get useful plants, catalogued.
24539-kinston-whitehall-and-goldsboro-no:
General J. G. Foster led an expedition to Kinston, Whitehall, and Goldsboro in North Carolina in December 1862. The letterpress of this volume comes from the New York Herald of 20 to 25 December 1862, with permission, and from the New York Times. Portraits and views are reproduced from Harper's History of the Rebellion.

Contents follow the march, the battles of Kinston, Whitehall, and Goldsboro, and the losses in all three. Later pages record the death of Colonel C. O. Gray, and the death and obsequies of General Foster himself. The volume gives a contemporary newspaper record of a hard winter campaign, preserved for readers of a later age.
2461-the-lady-of-lyons-or-love-and-pride:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's Lady of Lyons, or Love and Pride, is a melodrama. A proud beauty rejects a humble suitor, who then returns in disguise as a prince to win her. The play's plot turns on deception, pride, and a marriage that must be remade by truth. Lytton's verse and sentiment made it a stage favorite for generations.

The drama's famous speeches and its romantic reversals still play well in reading. Its view of love and class is earnest and theatrical. Theater lovers will enjoy a classic Victorian melodrama. The play stayed in the repertory for decades after its first success.
24857-journeys-through-bookland-vol-10-t:
Charles H. Sylvester published volume ten of Journeys Through Bookland in Chicago in 1922, as the guide to his reading plan for children. The series aimed to lead young readers through the world's best literature, and this volume speaks straight to parents, teachers, and adults who want to renew old friendships with books.

Sylvester urges talk over preaching: a parent should chat with children about what a story teaches, asking questions with light comments, rather than hammering home a lesson. Portraits of Holmes, Hawthorne, Longfellow, Irving, Whittier, Lowell, and Bryant head the book. The guide still offers sound counsel on raising readers.
24955-man-made:
Albert R. Teichner's story asks what a soul is and where it resides, and offers a new answer through Treb Hawley, a man who has lived more than two hundred years. From the age of ten he specialized in astronautics, joined the Ninth Jupiter Expedition at twenty-four, married at thirty, and fathered Robert and Neil. His long life runs on advanced techniques and good will, yet joy in the future stays uncertain.

On Planet 12 of the Centauri system, when he was fifty, a six-limbed primate mangled his left side. Surgeons removed his left leg and arm, fitting prosthetics that left him with constant phantom pain. Dr. Erics promised the trouble would prove a blessing, and later Treb seeks Stabilizine from another doctor as the pain brushes past him again. The story turns on what remains of a person when the body is replaced piece by piece.
25082-the-yellow-horde:
Hal G. Evarts's Yellow Horde, published in Toronto in 1921, is a wilderness novel whose hero is Breed, a yellow wolf learning to hunt with a pack in the foothills. Evarts, a writer of outdoor fiction, follows the animals through the seasons rather than keeping people at the center of the story.

As the elk migrate and deer leave the valleys, Breed's pack must range farther for food, and a renegade coyote named Flatear turns killer, striking silently by night. The novel's strength lies in its close observation of animal behavior, tracking, and the harsh balance of hunger and survival in the high country.
25342-the-incomparable-29th-and-the-rive:
Major George Davidson's Incomparable 29th and the River Clyde, published in Aberdeen, is a Gallipoli diary kept by a Royal Army Medical Corps officer. Davidson jotted notes for his wife at odd times and odd places, then published them on friends' advice, dedicating the book to the stretcher-bearers of the 89th Field Ambulance.

Entries record howitzer fire, Asiatic Annie's shells, and a casualty clearing station hit without harm. Trenches taken after hard fighting are lost again, church parade is cancelled because firing is too hot, and walking wounded straggle in singly. The diary gives the medical side of the 29th Division's ordeal.
25455-the-song-of-the-flag-a-national-od:
Eric Mackay's 1893 ode raises England's flag as a pledge of honour. The flag waves through shine and shower, peace and battle-time, as a token of a truth sublime. Mackay praises the throne where chivalry sat, the happy isles where men are free, and the million-mouthed sea that fought for England of yore. Winds toss the banner and brag of English renown.

Later stanzas denounce traitors high and low, warning readers to trust neither their word nor their love. The ode speaks for sovereign and country in high Victorian verse. Lamley and Company published it in London, from an author already known for Love Letters of a Violinist.
25506-the-adventures-of-bobby-orde:
Stewart Edward White follows Bobby Orde through boyhood in a novel built around outdoor life and a father's code of conduct. A motto printed at the front sets the standard. A true sportsman, honest in ways no one else can judge, is both rare and fine. Bobby must learn to live up to that standard.

Small home scenes open the tale. Bobby fetches cap and coat from his proper place under the stairs. Wider lessons follow in fair play, courage, and self-command. The tale moves at a boy's pace. Games, chores, and talk with his father shape character step by step.
25629-postmark-ganymede:
Robert Silverberg writes this space mail tale, opening with a poor mailman of the future facing sleet, snow, dead of night, sub zero void, meteors, and planets that will not stay put. Six cents an ounce may not seem worth it.

Preston, removed from Space Patrol Service and transferred to postal delivery, growls that he is washed up and that they made a postman out of him. He crumples his assignment memo and hurls it at his own bristly image in a bar mirror, unshaven for three days. A patrolman in trim grey then lays a hand on his shoulder.
25867-the-tragic-bride:
Francis Brett Young tells of Gabrielle Hewish, a baronet's only child whose marriage drained the color from her name as surely as a nun's vow. The narrator never met her, and knew her tale only through Arthur Payne and a slow Devon coroner's jury. When Sir Jocelyn died early in his daughter's married life, the Hewish line, long down to one thin branch, withered away, and Gabrielle vanished from Debrett and from common talk.

Printed in 1920, the novel turns back to Arthur Payne's youth at Overton, deep in green country, where his love of wild things ruled him. As a child he spent hours with the keeper, learning birds by call, habit, and haunt, and in the woods he moved with a wild grace of his own. That tender bond with nature throws dark light on the marriage that undid Gabrielle.
25879-an-historical-account-of-the-settl:
J. P. MacLean tells how Scotch Highlanders settled in America before the peace of 1783, with notes on Highland regiments and short lives of settlers. Printed in 1900 at Cleveland and Glasgow, the book opens with the Highlanders of Scotland, the Scotch Irish in America, and the causes that drove folk to leave home. Battle pictures, such as Culloden, front the tale.

One sailing stands out in detail: the Hector, mastered by John Spears, took families aboard at Greenock and Lochbroom in 1773. Some two hundred souls, with thirty three families and twenty five single men, sailed on July 1 for a land they knew naught of. A piper named John McKay came aboard just as the ship started, and the emigrants bade farewell to friends, home, and country.
25932-short-history-of-the-london-rifle-:
Compiled regimentally and printed at Aldershot in 1916, this short history links the London Rifle Brigade in peace to its war service. Part one sketches the pre war years as a connecting link, owning that it cannot show the hard work done under strain by all ranks. The note credits Lieut. Colonel Lord Bingham, later the Earl of Lucan, whose cheerful optimism in dark days before the Territorial Force kept the regiment alive.

War pages follow the battalions to France, with rest at Tatinghem in perfect weather after the line, and later work on lines of communication. Handing over guns and transport proved a bitter blow, since transport men and animals had won high praise. Profits from the pamphlet went to regimental funds. The book is a plain, proud record of a London unit at war.
26778-the-ocean-wireless-boys-and-the-na:
Captain Wilbur Lawton published this boys' adventure with Hurst and Company at New York in 1915, illustrated by Charles L. Wrenn. Lawton also wrote the Boy Aviators' series and the Dreadnought Boys' series. Its opening chapter, Vacation Days, finds Jack Ready, Billy Raynor, and Noddy Nipper sailing the speedy sloop Curlew on Alexandria Bay, above the Thousand Islands.

Noddy, a red-headed former Bowery waif, jerks the tiller over and spins the Curlew round just as jagged rocks loom ahead. Jack forgives even Noddy's awful pun on that skillful bit of boat-handling. Later chapters bring Captain Simms of the Thespis, secret service, night signals, and the naval code. A monkey interlude, a ghostess abroad, a strange wreck, castaways with a python, capture by radio, and Thurman's plot follow. The wireless makes good in the end.
28051-caesar-rodney-s-ride:
Henry Fisk Carlton's Caesar Rodney's Ride is a short radio play about a dramatic night in the American Revolution. Caesar Rodney, a Delaware delegate, rides through the night to Philadelphia to cast a vote for independence. Claire T. Zyve edited the volume for school use, and Teachers College at Columbia University published it.

The book first teaches young actors how to perform for radio: no costumes or scenery, just clear voices around a microphone. Then the play itself lets a class live through Rodney's ride by sound alone. It offers a lively way to teach history through speaking and listening.
28328-americanism-contrasted-with-foreig:
William G. Brownlow wrote Americanism Contrasted with Foreignism, Romanism, and Bogus Democracy, Nashville, 1856, as a Know-Nothing polemic. Brownlow, editor of Brownlow's Knoxville Whig, dedicates the book to young men of America, charged with preserving civil and religious liberty. Campbell's lines on bloody rites open the volume.

Brownlow argues that native and legal voters must watch with sleepless vigilance over blood-bought liberties, against foreign influence, Romanism, and demagogues in Tennessee and elsewhere. His tone is fierce and partisan. The book offers a primary record of nativist feeling before the Civil War.
28607-the-road-and-the-roadside:
Burton Willis Potter's The Road and the Roadside, published by Little, Brown and Company of Boston in 1886, began as lectures. Potter read the road-law chapters at the Massachusetts Board of Agriculture's country meeting in Framingham in December 1885. He states Massachusetts law on public and private ways, while noting that common-law principles travel to other states.

Good roads and love of rural life, Potter argues, serve true happiness and lasting prosperity. Chapters trace roads as symbols of progress, from Babylon to Memphis, Carthaginian makers, Roman construction, Chinese highways, and Peruvian roads. Location, the survival of the fittest among routes, and modern improvement follow. Readers get law, history, and a plea for country roads.
28704-free-ships-the-restoration-of-the-:
John Codman wrote this 1878 argument for restoring America's carrying trade, the business of shipping goods in American vessels. Codman opens by mocking a House committee of 1869 that set out to study the decline of American commerce and instead became, in his view, a charity for shipbuilders. Its report, he says, fell dead on the House floor and was ridiculed in the Senate.

The book argues that the Civil War did not destroy shipbuilding in the way the committee claimed, and that free ships, rather than subsidies, would revive American shipping. Codman writes as a sharp-tongued reformer, naming names and quoting debates. Readers interested in trade policy get a lively period polemic, and a window into how Americans argued about protection and free trade after the war.
29313-war-from-the-inside:
Frederick L. Hitchcock, late adjutant and major of the 132nd Pennsylvania Volunteer Infantry, published this regimental history in 1903, covering 1862 to 1863. Pennsylvania erected a monument to the 132nd on the Antietam battlefield. It was dedicated September 17, 1904, and stands some two hundred yards ahead of the battle line, near the famous Sunken Road, or Bloody Lane.

Chapters move from first lessons and the regiment's organization through marching, South Mountain, and Antietam. Later chapters cover Harper's Ferry, Fredericksburg, why Fredericksburg was lost, lost colors recovered, and the winter at Falmouth. Readers get a soldier's inside view of a Pennsylvania regiment's war, detailed and personal, from a man who served in it.
29432-the-man-the-martians-made:
Frank Belknap Long's suspenseful tale opens in a desert camp where death has come in the night. No mortal has ever seen the Martians, the narrator says, but their whisperings have been heard, hiding a terrible secret. Waking with a prickling scalp and cold sweat, he disciplines himself, crosses his arms, and waits for day to flood the desert with light. There was death in the camp, and it waits with them.

Long builds dread from whispers, hardship, and privation as the daily lot on Mars, rather than from monsters shown outright. The tale's power lies in what is heard, not seen. Fans of classic science fiction will enjoy a tense, atmospheric story by a writer his editors ranked high among the field's deans.
29545-the-spanish-jade:
Maurice Hewlett's novel, printed in 1908 by Cassell and Company of London, Paris, New York, Toronto, and Melbourne, takes its reader to Castile. Full-page colored pictures by William Hyde show the table lands, Valladolid, the towers of Segovia, and Madrid by night. The tale opens on a pleasant errand into the plain beyond Burgos, in the sunless glare before dawn.

Hewlett writes of Spain with a painter's eye for light, dress, and town. The Spanish jade of the title stands at the heart of a story of love, honor, and travel. Readers who love romantic tales of old Spain will find a rich, sunlit novel, vivid in place and strong in feeling.
29656-the-mountain-divide:
Frank H. Spearman, author of Whispering Smith and Robert Kimberly, wrote The Mountain Divide, printed in 1912 by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York with pictures by Armand Both. It opens in a large, roughly framed public waiting-room, lit by hanging kerosene lamps, where a door leads to the agent's office. A picture shows Buck watching as a second Indian strikes a club down.

Spearman writes a railroad and mountain novel of the West, where the divide itself tests men and loyalties. The story, inscribed without love, is nonetheless lovingly told, as its dedication says. Readers of railroad and western fiction will find a strong, atmospheric novel from Spearman's prime.
3043-the-quaker-colonies-a-chronicle-of-:
Sydney Fisher wrote The Quaker Colonies, volume eight of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. Chapters follow the birth of Pennsylvania, Penn's sailing for the Delaware, and life in Philadelphia. Types of population, the troubles of Penn and his sons, the French and Indian War, the decline of Quaker government, and the beginnings of New Jersey follow. The proprietors of the Delaware form the thread.

Fisher credits Penn with retaining political control and family wealth down to the Revolution, despite ruling a wild country whose civil and religious convictions opposed anything feudal. The narrative balances praise with the troubles that followed. The book gives a compact history of Pennsylvania and New Jersey under Quaker proprietors.
31328-the-early-negro-convention-movemen:
John W. Cromwell's 1904 paper, number nine in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, traces the early Negro convention movement. After the second war with Britain, he argues, the nation moved to fix the free man of color in an inferior social and political status, resisted at every step. Church protests at St. James and Bethel in Philadelphia and Zion in New York led to independent denominations founded in 1816 and 1820.

Later landmarks crowd the story: the Colonization Society of 1816, the Missouri Compromise of 1820, the martyrs of 1822, Freedom's Journal in 1827, and Nat Turner's insurrection in 1831. Then Ohio mobs drove free Black people to marshal their moral forces in convention. The paper remains a concise history of Black organized protest before the Civil War.
31924-eden-an-episode:
Edgar Saltus's 1888 novel Eden, an episode published by Belford, Clarke and Company, opens only when Miss Menemon's engagement to John Usselex is made public. The world she moves in shows interest in her future husband. Rumors circulate at once: his real name is Tchurchenthaler, and his boyhood was passed tending geese in a remote Bavarian village.

Other reports make him Baron Varvedsen of Denmark, fled not from military service but from the death penalty for striking a prince of the blood. He may instead be the outlawed nephew of a Flemish money-lender. Readers get a decadent society novel of identity, rumor, and love, with a Tasso epigraph that all time not spent in love is lost.
31955-niagara-an-aboriginal-center-of-tr:
Peter A. Porter's 1906 study Niagara, An Aboriginal Center of Trade argues that Niagara was a trading hub long before printed history begins. Porter observes that Niagara's printed story reaches back just three centuries, with mentions in its first three decades sparse and scattered.

Three facts, he says, seem proven before that printed story. Its portage had long been in use, and it was then, and long had been, a center of trade among native peoples. Readers get a short, focused history of the Falls as an aboriginal meeting place, with the portage route at its center.
31961-joy-ride:
Mark Meadows's short story Joy Ride was printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in December 1954 and illustrated by Dick Francis. It opens with a tagline asking whether men or machines had to give, and answering that perhaps both must. Its historian's note says the statements that follow are extracted from depositions taken by the Commission of Formal Inquiry. That commission was appointed by the Peloric Rehabilitation Council, a body formed as a provisional government in the third month of the Calamity.

Andrews, third assistant vice president in charge of maintenance for Cybernetic Publishers, testifies that all the world's periodical publications were put out by Cybernetics. Other houses' names gave an impression of variety. Readers get a satirical science-fiction tale of a publishing monopoly run by machines.
31982-dressed-game-and-poultry-a-la-mode:
Mrs. de Salis's Dressed Game and Poultry à la Mode is one of her little series of cookbooks. The series also includes d Savouries à la Mode and Entrées à la Mode. It was offered at the sporting season of the year. Its preface, signed H. A. de Salis from Hampton Lea, Sutton, Surrey, in 1888, says many recipes are well known, but all were collected from culinary preserves and tested by personal experience.

Its first recipe, Blackbird Pie, stuffs the birds with French roll crumb soaked in milk, butter, shallot, parsley, pepper, salt, nutmeg, and egg yolks. The dish is lined with fried collops of rump steak. Readers get a Victorian game cookbook, practical and confident, for cooks who dressed what the season brought home.
31991-some-of-my-war-stories-a-paper-rea:
Allen Ripley Foote read this paper before the Ohio Commandery of the Loyal Legion at Cincinnati on October 1, 1913. Foote was nineteen in 1861, when he rushed to enlist after President Lincoln called for volunteers. He served as a private in Company B of the 3rd Michigan Infantry. He later became a second lieutenant in Company B of the 21st Michigan Infantry. He tells his war years in his own voice, as a veteran speaking to fellow veterans.

His stories cover enlistment, the train ride through Ohio towns, and camp at the Maryland end of Chain Bridge. Along the way, women tossed flower bouquets into the cars. The march toward the first battle of Bull Run follows. The value lies in small detail: grey uniforms, old muskets changed from flint locks, and cheering crowds. It reads as memory, not as a formal history.
32225-elsie-at-viamede:
Martha Finley's Elsie at Viamede belongs to the long Elsie series. It runs from Elsie Dinsmore and Elsie's Holidays at Roselands through Elsie's Girlhood, Womanhood, Motherhood, and Children. It continues to Elsie at Nantucket, The Two Elsies, and Elsie at Ion, and returns to the family at Viamede. The series follows Elsie through a lifetime of family, faith, and travel, and this volume sets her in Louisiana.

Its first chapter opens on a beautiful evening at Viamede. The sun nears its setting, shadows sleep on a velvety, flower-bespangled lawn, and bayou waters beyond mirror the sunset clouds' rosy hues. Tea is over. The family gathers on the veranda overlooking the bayou. Rosie asks Mamma, or grandpa, or the captain, to tell the tale of Jackson defending New Orleans, now that they are in the neighbourhood. Readers get a gentle family novel, where evening talk turns to history.
32311-a-soldier-s-trial-an-episode-of-th:
General Charles King's A Soldier's Trial, an episode of the canteen crusade, published in New York by the Hobart Company in 1905, is a novel of the army's temperance fight. King, author of A Daughter of the Sioux, Comrades in Arms, and The Medal of Honor, fronts the book with Brigadier-General Frederick D. Grant's complaint: it is distressing that the prosperity of keepers of vile resorts is due to good and worthy though misguided citizens, who succeeded in abolishing the canteen in the army.

Its first chapter is Two Announcements, and the novel that follows tests the canteen crusade's consequences for soldiers. Readers get a military novel with a reform argument, where abolishing the army canteen, meant to protect soldiers, drives them instead to the vile resorts outside camp. King's soldier's trial is both a courtroom matter and a moral one, set in the army of his day.
32325-the-adventures-of-huckleberry-finn:
Mark Twain's The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Tom Sawyer's Comrade, comes in a new edition from new plates by Harper and Brothers in New York and London. Its scene is the Mississippi Valley. Its time is forty to fifty years ago. Its narrator is Huck himself, who tells readers they may not know about him unless they have read The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that it does not matter.

That book, Huck says, was made by Mr. Mark Twain, who told the truth mainly. There were things he stretched, though. Aunt Polly, Tom's Aunt Polly, and Mary, and the Widow Douglas all appear in that book, which is mostly true, with some stretchers. Readers get the great American river novel in Huck's own voice, where a boy's story follows Tom Sawyer's and outgrows it.
32412-the-black-tide:
Arthur G. Stangland's tale, printed in IF Worlds of Science Fiction in March 1953, opens with a nightmare of a vast black meteor twirling through space like a massive black diamond. Bill Staker, a passenger rocket captain for Interplanetary Lines, wakes in his New York hotel room savouring weight, gravity, and relief, muttering thanks that it was only a dream. Cold sweat on his hands tells another story.

Stangland's framing note warns that space in its far dark reaches can shatter dreams and fill a man with fear and hate, yet can also cure him if he is strong enough. From a hotel-room awakening, the story follows a spaceman whose inner tide of dread must be faced rather than outrun. It pairs space adventure with a study of fear, nerve, and recovery.
32463-the-justice-and-necessity-of-taxin:
The Justice and Necessity of Taxing the American Colonies, printed in London in 1766 for one shilling, defends Parliament's authority to tax the colonies. Its opening argues that since the revolution, no question has mattered more to the legislature than settling quarrels with the Americans. Britain's riches and power, it says, rest mainly on trade, and trade on her colonies, so her standing as the first commercial nation turns on this hinge.

The pamphlet invites a clash of opinions, saying truth is struck out as fire is struck by flint, and offers light to legislators groping through a dark, intricate labyrinth. No past case, it admits, gives a precedent to guide them. The tract remains a key primary source for the Stamp Act crisis and for British arguments on empire, trade, and tax.
32611-the-falling-flag-evacuation-of-ric:
Edward M. Boykin's The Falling Flag, published in New York in 1874, gives a lieutenant colonel's account of the end of the Army of Northern Virginia. Boykin, of the Seventh South Carolina Cavalry, writes only what fell within his own observation, largely what happened to his own brigade.

The narrative opens on April 1, 1865, with orders sending dismounted men forward, and follows the weary march from Richmond to Appomattox. Boykin dedicates the short account to the officers and men of his regiment, calling his comradeship with them the proudest recollection of his life.
32886-the-battleship-boys-first-step-upw:
Frank Gee Patchin sends the Battleship Boys toward petty officer grades, published by the Saalfield Publishing Company in 1911. Dan and red-haired Sam Hickey serve aboard the battleship Long Island, and the book follows them from lookout duty to torpedo practice and a board examination.

The first chapter opens in a sixty-mile gale, with seas sweeping the bridge forty feet above the sea. Sam, on lookout by the number one searchlight, reports a green light off the starboard bow. The watch officer sees nothing, but Sam insists: it looked like a shooting star, and it shot right up from the sea. Later chapters bring whaleboats to the rescue, big guns, a lost tompion, the battle of the dinghies, and an act of heroism.
32942-the-red-city-a-novel-of-the-second:
S. Weir Mitchell's novel The Red City is set in Philadelphia during the second administration of President Washington. It opens on May 23, 1792, as the brig Morning Star of Bristol runs into Delaware Bay with a topgallant breeze. Her captain praises his salt-powdered ship while a young fellow laughs in the lower rigging. The red city itself, the national capital of the young republic, waits at the end of that voyage.

Mitchell, a physician and novelist known for Hugh Wynne, uses the capital's drawing rooms, streets, and politics as the ground for a story. The story is one of love, honor, and intrigue in the 1790s. Illustrations by Arthur I. Keller picture its scenes. The novel gives readers the early republic in its working clothes. Philadelphia was the seat of government and the future of the country was still being argued face to face.
3315-down-the-mother-lode:
Vivia Hemphill gathers pioneer tales of California in this 1922 volume. A foreword explains the question behind the book: so many readers asked exactly where and what the Mother Lode is. The geologist and the historian agree on its location and composition, Hemphill notes, but old miners and sojourners of the vanished golden era give strangely different versions of it.

Some of those versions are set down here, for enlightenment and for entertainment both. The tales follow the gold country down its spine, from camp to camp, with miners, merchants, and wanderers telling their own stories. The miners' own versions keep the gold rush human, before legend hardens their stories into one tale.
33291-pitching-in-a-pinch-or-baseball-fr:
Christy Mathewson's book gives baseball from the inside, by one of the game's great pitchers. Copyrighted in 1912, its chapters take up the most dangerous batters he met. Calls to take a pitcher out, pitching in a pinch, big league pitchers and their quirks, play from the bench, coaching good and bad, and honest and dishonest play follow. An introduction by John N. Wheeler frames the star's own account.

Mathewson writes in a plain, knowing voice, sharing how a pitcher reads batters, fields, and pressure. The book suits both fans of the dead-ball era and modern readers who want the game's early craft. Its lessons on nerve, control, and fair play still ring true, making it a classic of baseball writing from inside the game.
33355-oahu-traveler-s-guide:
Bill and Diana Gleasner's Oahu Traveler's Guide leads visitors round the Hawaiian island, from the bus and Hawaiian words and phrases to Honolulu highlights and Waikiki. Its contents move to Oahu's east end, with Koko Head and Sea Life Park, to the windward coast, the north shore, and central Oahu, with Schofield Barracks and Wahiawa. The guide quotes Mark Twain on Hawaii as the loveliest fleet of islands in any ocean.

The guide suits travelers who want a plain, practical tour, with stops, sights, and local words in one handy book. Its tone is friendly and direct, aimed at first-time visitors. For those planning a trip to Oahu, it remains a clear, old-fashioned companion to the island's main draws.
33727-creative-intelligence-essays-in-th:
John Dewey, Addison W. Moore, Harold Chapman Brown, George H. Mead, and Boyd H. Bode present essays in the pragmatic attitude. So do Henry Walgrave Stuart, James Hayden Tufts, and Horace M. Kallen, in this 1917 Henry Holt volume. The prefatory note stresses intellectual cooperation without unanimity. These include no platform of planks, no imposed agreement, but a unity in attitude rather than uniformity in results, with each writer responsible only for his own essay.

Contributions apply the common attitude to philosophy itself, then to logic, mathematics, physical science, psychology, ethics, and economics, and again to philosophy with aesthetics and religion. Points of agreement concern the genuineness of the future and intelligence as the organ for determining its quality. The volume is a landmark of American pragmatism, showing a school of thought working together while thinking independently.
34065-the-sentimental-adventures-of-jimm:
Marie Van Vorst wrote this set of adventures, published in New York in March 1908 with pictures by Alonzo Kimball. Jimmy Bulstrode's eight adventures run from buying a Christmas tree and trying to buy a portrait to finding that some things cannot be bought. He makes three people happy, then nobody happy at all.

Later adventures have him discard a knave and save a queen, gain a piece of property, and come into his own. Van Vorst writes with warmth and humor about money, kindness, and luck. The book offers a light, sentimental tale of a good-hearted man.
34891-sketch-of-the-first-kentucky-briga:
Sketch of the First Kentucky Brigade is a unit history by Hodge, the brigade's adjutant general, printed at Frankfort, Kentucky, in 1874. Hodge dedicates it to General John Breckinridge, the brigade's commander, and to its dead. The opening argues that so small a force will earn only a brief note in large histories, yet its place was odd and its own.

It had risen against both state and federal power, and its men left home, wealth, kin, and friends, and gave up all that makes life sweet, save honour. Kentucky, he says, will hold the band in sad and fond thought, for its deeds spoke for most Kentuckians and for their sense of right. It is a fond memorial by one who was there, warm in tone throughout.
35368-friends-i-have-made:
Friends I Have Made is a book of anecdotes that came out in London in 1883 under the name of George Manville Fenn. The narrator, a woman of forty-eight, looks in her mirror and frankly describes her thin, careworn face before telling of her life. The chapters are a chain of almost separate tales about people she has known.

Readers should know this hosted copy is not whole: two sets of pages were missing from the scans, so chapters ten, eleven, and sixteen are absent, and two more are short. What remains is still warm and lively, full of small portraits drawn from a busy life. The book shows the Victorian taste for true-seeming tales told by a friendly voice at the fireside.
3546-the-eureka-stockade:
Raffaello Carboni, an Italian immigrant on the Australian goldfields, writes an eyewitness account of the Eureka Stockade rebellion at Ballarat in 1854. Gold miners, angered by license fees, police hunts, and lack of political rights, built a wooden stockade and raised a flag of their own. Troops stormed it before dawn, killing miners and soldiers alike.

Carboni, who took part in the rising, writes with the heat of a participant and the detail of a man who knew the diggings. His book became a key source for the event that Australians later called a birthplace of democracy. Readers interested in gold rush history, protest, and colonial politics will find a vivid, partisan, first hand narrative.
35771-when-the-ku-klux-rode:
When the Ku Klux Rode, by Eyre Damer, was published in 1912. The Neale Publishing Company issued it at New York. Twenty one chapters carry Alabama's story. Provisional, native, and military governments open the book. The Freedmen's Bureau and the Union League follow. Carpetbag government and ruinous misgovernment are the middle verdicts. The whites aroused and the Ku Klux Klan come at chapters eleven and twelve. Riots in Marengo and Greene fill the late pages. A final chapter is named for the restoration of white supremacy. Chapter one begins with the peace proclamations of 1865. The president declared the war at an end on May 10. Lee's surrender on April 9 was taken as the true close.

Property seized was restored in May, slaves excepted. Alabama, Damer writes, expected quick readmission to her old place.
35811-matelda-and-the-cloister-of-hellfd:
Matelda and the Cloister of Hellfde holds extracts from the book of Matilda of Magdeburg, chosen and translated by Frances Bevan. Nisbet published it in London in 1896. Bevan had written Three Friends of God, sketches of medieval mystics, as the head's list of her books shows.

A history of the cloister opens the volume. Count Burkhardt of Mansfeldt founded the convent in 1219, the text says. Cistercian nuns served God there, among them the blessed maidens Mechthild and Gertrude. Matilda's own writings tell of her visions and her love of God in rich, bold speech. Readers get a window on the fervent inner life of medieval nuns.
35956-a-northern-countryside:
A Northern Countryside is a record of a Maine year by Rosalind Richards, printed at New York in 1916. Wentworth took the photographs. Henry Holt published it. Sixteen chapters run from the river to early winter, with harvest and a town chapter between.

Richards places her county in a northern state, in a region of innumerable lakes. It is wooded, hilly, irregular country, bold in outline but not mountainous. Chapters bear names like By the Acushticook, The Eastman Hill Cross-Road, and Tresumpscott Pond. Photographs show the woods jutting round ledges, corn among golden pumpkins, and ice-cutting on the river. The book is a quiet portrait of a place.
3619-cousin-maude:
Mary Jane Holmes writes a domestic novel set among the Northern Hills, dedicated to Morris Smith of New Orleans. The chapters follow Dr Kennedy, a journey, a new home, a child called Little Louis, Mrs Janet Blodgett, a mother, and the past and present of a family. Later chapters introduce James, the milkman's heiress, an engagement real and prospective, and Maud Glendower herself.

Holmes, a popular American novelist of the nineteenth century, writes about love, money, and family duty with warmth and moral clarity. Her heroines face hard choices between comfort and conscience. The book suits readers who enjoy old fashioned domestic fiction, where a new home and a new cousin can change a family's fate.
36391-the-meadow-brook-girls-across-coun:
The Meadow-Brook Girls Across Country, or the young pathfinders on a summer hike, by Janet Aldridge, was copyrighted in 1913 and published by Henry Altemus Company of Philadelphia. Aldridge wrote a line of Meadow-Brook Girls books, under canvas, afloat, and across country. The party is a group of schoolgirls hiking with their guardian, Miss Elting. Harriet Burrell carries the map and keeps her head.

The first chapter is a night of excitement: the girls are lost in the woods, and Crazy Jane has not come. A red eye in the dark and midnight prowlers follow, then speckled trout to catch. The girls are caught in a morass and rescued by the Tramp Club, and Harriet plans to outwit that club in return. A race for life, a gypsy trail, and a harmonica serenade fill the twenty four chapters.
36423-the-pony-rider-boys-in-the-alkali-:
Frank Gee Patchin wrote The Pony Rider Boys in the Alkali, also titled Finding a Key to the Desert Maze. The Saalfield Publishing Company held the copyright from nineteen hundred ten. Patchin wrote many Pony Rider Boys books, set from the Rockies to Texas. Tom Parry guides the boys in this one.

Stacy Brown, nicknamed Chunky, grumbles that he likes hills more than sand. Parry tells him the true Nevada desert still lies ahead. Alkali flats bake on both sides of the Diamond Range. Tad Butler and Ned Rector ride with the group. Professor Zepplin keeps the boys in line. Chapters promise a twister, a wild horse hunt, and men lost in the maze of sand.
36591-marital-power-exemplified-in-mrs-p:
Marital Power is Elizabeth Packard's account of her own trial and her defence against a charge of insanity. Clarke and Company published it at Chicago in 1870. Its longer title tells the story: three years' imprisonment for religious belief, by the arbitrary will of a husband. A picture shows the house in Manteno, Illinois, from which she was kidnapped.

Packard's husband, a minister, had her confined in the Illinois state asylum as insane. Freed at last, she was imprisoned again in her own house, then released on a writ and tried before a jury, who found her sane. Her book appeals to the government to change the laws and give married women legal protection. It became a landmark of women's rights.
36778-twenty-five-years-in-the-rifle-bri:
Twenty Five Years in the Rifle Brigade is a war life tale by William Surtees. Surtees served as stores chief of that corps in his army years. A Blackwood house and a Cadell house share the print of eighteen thirty three. His brother John gave the book to the corps chief and its rank men. Surtees joined the army as a youth in seventeen ninety five.

First foe sight came in Holland with the Duke of York host in his youth. In eighteen two he joined the Rifle Brigade as a rank man for good. Rise by rank steps brought him to the stores chief post in time. His post kept him from the fight line, yet he watched each field near. Faith true print from his own hand is the front word claim.
36881-the-sea-bride:
Ben Ames Williams wrote The Sea Bride, a novel printed in New York with rights held in 1919. All the Brothers Were Valiant stands by his name. They were to be married before the open fire, the tale begins, in the big living-room of the old house on the hill. Upstairs, Bess Holt is helping Faith dress.

Faith sits quiet and happy at the old dressing table, scarce hearing Bess's chatter. Her soft eyes rest on her own image like one who dreams dreams. The low room, the canopy bed with its split frame, holds her whole girlhood. She is to wed a sea captain, and the sea will claim its bride. Fans get a strong tale of love and the whaling age.
3696-the-prince-and-the-page-a-story-of-:
Charlotte Yonge, writing as the author of The Heir of Redclyffe, sets this tale for young readers in the age of Edward the First and the last crusade. Its hero is a page caught between two great names of the time, Simon de Montfort and the young Prince Edward, whose households, wars, and shifting loyalties shape the boy's fate. The preface owns frankly that its proofs lie in household books and older histories, not in deep archives.

Loyalty drives the plot, as the page must choose whom to serve when old friends turn foes and a familiar face appears under a lowered visor. Battles, castles, and court scenes alternate with quiet tests of honor. Readers who like historical tales of duty and daring will find a brisk story that keeps its history in the foreground without turning into a lesson.
37056-baseball-joe-of-the-silver-stars-o:
Baseball Joe of the Silver Stars is a boys' baseball novel by Lester Chadwick, published by Cupples and Leon of New York in 1912. Joe Matson, the young hero, pitches for the Silver Stars under manager Darrell Blackney. Sam Morton is listed as the club's pitcher too, and the rival club is the Resolutes of Rocky Ford.

Chapter titles promise the season's shape: Joe's tryout, his first game, and a mean protest. Plotters work against the club and get foiled. The season builds toward the winning throw. The story runs on clean sport, loyalty, and last-inning pressure. Books of this series gave boy readers a hero who wins by skill and nerve rather than luck. It stands as a period piece of early baseball fiction.
37166-mr-punch-at-the-seaside:
Punch at the Seaside is a book of jest from the great jest sheet of London. Hammerton saw the set through the press. It stands in a set of jest books, each whole in its self. That set aims to give the cream of the jest of the land. Its stuff was drawn from the great sheet from its birth in eighteen forty one to the day of the set. Two mint plates stand in this book.

The draw men of the plates are named on the title leaf. Keene, Leech, and du Maurier stand first in that roll. May, Raven-Hill, Partridge, Browne, and Reed stand past them. The set list at the front names five and twenty books. Life in the great town, life in the wilds, and life in the high lands of the north stand in it.
37627-lady-barbarina-the-siege-of-london:
Henry James gathered six tales in this volume, issued by Macmillan at London in 1922. Lady Barbarina gives the book its name. The Siege of London and An International Episode stand beside it.

Lady Barbarina opens in Hyde Park on a fine June afternoon. Two quiet, elderly watchers sit in iron chairs under the great trees. The Drive's slow line passes behind them. The Row's bright stir faces them. They rank with the spectators, not the spectacle. They are husband and wife, growing old together, and fond of it. They are native aliens in London, at home and not at home. James builds the tale on such watchers.
37910-homes-of-american-statesmen-with-a:
Homes of American Statesmen, issued at Hartford in 1856, gathers sketches by various writers of the dwellings of eminent Americans. Wood engravings from drawings and daguerreotypes picture the houses, and facsimiles of autograph letters add a personal touch. The publishers present it as a companion to Homes of American Authors, meant to save private memories fast passing away.

The contents march in order of fame: Washington, by Mrs C M Kirkland, then Franklin, Jefferson, Hancock, John Adams, and Patrick Henry. Madison, Jay, Hamilton, and Marshall follow. Plates show the birthplace of Henry Clay and Marshfield, the home of Daniel Webster.
3796-rilla-of-ingleside:
Lucy Maud Montgomery follows Rilla, the youngest daughter of Anne of Ingleside, through the years of the Great War. The book opens on a golden afternoon at Ingleside, where Susan Baker keeps house with grim satisfaction, and soon the pipes call Rilla's brothers away, Jem, Walter, and Shirley among them. Rilla, once a frivolous girl, takes up war work, a war baby, and a concert for starving Belgian children.

Dog Monday waits at the station for a master who may never return, while Rilla argues with a scoffer who doubts the Belgians starve at all. Chapters of waiting, black Sundays, and word from the front lead to victory and a lover's return. Readers who know Anne's world will find Rilla's growth from girl to woman the most moving book of the series.
3811-the-star-of-gettysburg-a-story-of-s:
Joseph Altsheler centers this Civil War romance on Harry Kenton, a young Southerner fighting with the Invincibles under Colonel Leonidas Talbot. The book is the fifth in a series that began at Bull Run and ran through Shiloh, Stonewall, and Antietam. It follows Harry and his Northern cousin Dick Mason toward the high tide at Gettysburg. Colonel Talbot's severity, softened by a twinkle, keeps the lads in awe and affection.

A new officer from South Carolina, tall and dark, joins the regiment in a place left vacant by death, and Harry feels he has seen the man's eager gesture before. Altsheler writes for young readers, with battles, marches, and friendships in full color. Those who like historical adventure will find a stirring chapter of the war, told from the Southern side of the lines.
38251-oscar-wilde:
Leonard Cresswell Ingleby wrote a study of Oscar Wilde, published in London in 1907. The first part treats Wilde the man. Later parts take up the modern playwright, with chapters on Lady Windermere's Fan and A Woman of No Importance. The Ideal Husband and The Importance of Being Earnest are treated in turn.

Romantic dramas come next, from Salomé to Vera and The Florentine Tragedy. Separate parts cover the fairy stories, the poems, and the fiction. A part on the philosophy of beauty follows. The book closes with De Profundis and an index. Ingleby aims at a full survey of Wilde's work soon after his death.
38999-mellifont-abbey-co-louth-its-ruins:
Mellifont Abbey in County Louth is the subject of a guide and popular history of its ruins and associations. A front photograph gives a general view of the abbey, taken by a Dublin photographer. Verses at the head call it a house of prayer once set apart for God's service, now desolate. A ruin stands where a shrine once shone, the lines say.

The guide serves visitors who come to walk the remains and learn their story. Its title promises both uses at once: a handbook for the ground and a history in plain form. The abbey's associations, the people and events tied to the place, share the title with the stones themselves. Such local guides of the period mixed devotion, history, and touring in one small book. This one opens with that mix in view.
39296-the-story-of-francis-cludde:
The Story of Francis Cludde is a past age tale by Stanley Weyman, first out in eighteen ninety one. Weyman wrote famed France set tales of the same kind in those years. A Longmans print of eighteen ninety eight is the form shown in this text. The tale is told in the voice of Francis himself, in memoir cast. Its first part names a cry heard on the Ridgeway road of old.

That road splits the shires of Warwick and Worcester on their bound line. Parts run through a bishop room, a cry down with tax men, and a ship ride. A face in a porch, a foul blow, and a witch warn thick the mid parts. Queen rise and last mass parts set the faith strife of the age. A port at last names the end part of the long road.
39297-the-red-cockade:
The Red Cockade is a historical novel by Stanley Weyman, published in London in 1895. Weyman was known for A Gentleman of France and Under the Red Robe. The tale is set in France as the old order cracks and crowds take to the streets.

Its first chapters bring in the Marquis de St Alais and a sharp talk on gardens and the people. Later heads name the Assembly, a duel, the tricolour, and the two camps. Nimes and its troubles fill much of the later action. Readers get a brisk story of nobles and mobs at the start of the French Revolution, told with Weyman's usual pace.
39358-a-winter-nosegay-being-tales-for-c:
A Winter Nosegay, being tales for children at Christmastide, is a children's story book issued at London in 1881. Its contents name three pieces. The man in the moon, and how he got there, comes first. Cat and dog stories follow, and a fortune in an empty wallet closes the short list. The first tale opens in the once upon a time manner.

Long before people could learn what they wanted from printed books, it begins, and long before children had pretty pictures to tell them tales, there lived an old student with his pupil. Together they spent all day poring over musty old books and papers. They tried to find out why the sun was hot. At night they might always be seen gazing at the sky, counting how many stars there were. They were very curious men, the tale goes on.
