39471-zoological-illustrations-volume-1-:
William Swainson, a fellow of the Royal Society, began Zoological Illustrations as a series of plates with text. Volume one came out in London in 1820 and 1821. Its full title promises figures and accounts of new, rare, or choice animals. Birds, insects, and shells form the chief classes shown.

Swainson says he had two aims in view. He wanted to spread fresh facts that serve science and please general readers. He also wanted to drive out poor copied figures that spread error. Each plate was drawn from nature or fine specimens, on the system of Cuvier and other modern men. The volume set a pattern for the fine natural history part-works of its day.
39472-zoological-illustrations-volume-2-:
Volume two of Zoological Illustrations is a work of natural history by William Swainson, printed at London in 1821 and 1822. Its full title promises original figures and descriptions of new, rare, or interesting animals. Birds, insects, and shells supply most of the subjects. The arrangement follows Cuvier and other modern zoologists. Swainson dedicates both volumes to James Edward Smith. Smith had founded and presided over the Linnaean Society of London.

Plate sixty seven shows a kingfisher, the Cinnamon Crabeater. Its Latin character is given first, then the same in English. Blue green above and pale cinnamon below, the bird wears a slender black collar. Swainson believes it quite new and hitherto undescribed. The specimen belonged to Leadbeater, a dealer of Brewer Street. It had reached him from New Zealand, and he let Swainson publish it.
39477-zoological-illustrations-volume-3-:
Zoological Illustrations, volume three, is a work of natural history by William Swainson, printed at London in 1822 and 1823. The catalog title is a row of stars, but the title page gives the real name. Swainson offers figures and accounts of new, rare, or striking animals. He sorts them by the methods of Cuvier and other modern men of science.

Birds, insects, and shells form the chief classes here. In his preface, Swainson defends books that range over the whole animal kingdom. He notes that grand, costly works sit locked in rich libraries, out of reach. His own plates aimed to spread new finds more widely. Naturalists still value the book as an early record of species then new to science.
39500-beauties-and-antiquities-of-irelan:
Beauties and Antiquities of Ireland, by Russell, was published in London and St Louis in 1897. Its subtitle joins two aims in one volume. It serves as a tourist's guide to fine scenery. It also serves as a handbook for the student of ruins. Cong Abbey forms the frontispiece. Killarney opens the contents, with fame said to be world wide. Macaulay is quoted in its praise. Autumn is named the best time to see it, for softness and colour.

Tara follows, called the most historic spot in these islands. Dr Petrie's great work on Tara is praised, with his map. The Lia Fail, or Stone of Destiny, gets its notice. Roads that centred on Tara are traced. The guide mixes travel pleasure with close respect for old Ireland.
40092-guernsey-pictorial-directory-and-s:
Guernsey Pictorial Directory and Stranger's Guide is a guidebook by Thomas Bellamy, printed on Guernsey in 1843 with numerous wood-cuts. Bellamy says in his preface that the guides offered to the public so far have fallen short. They fail to give the stranger a just notion of the island and its interior beauty, for want of pictures and of leisure for natural observation.

His own pages aim at simplicity of arrangement and usefulness of matter. A few tail-pieces picture native scenery. He asks the candour of strangers for a work meant for their information and the welfare of others. The transcriber's note lists the author's quaint spellings, left as printed, such as goal for gaol. The guide is an early picture of the island for visitors. It belongs to the first age of Channel Islands tourism, when the stranger needed a directory as much as a map.
40220-how-women-should-ride:
How Women Should Ride, written under the byline De Hurst, was printed by Harper and Brothers in New York in 1892. The writer thanks a friend in the dedication for the experience behind the book.

A word to parents opens the guide, warning of the dangers of early riding. Girls on horseback get hints on the right horse, dress, and first lessons. Later chapters treat mounting, the stirrup, hands, and seat. Emergencies fill a full chapter: shy horses, stumblers, rearers, and runaways. Choosing a mount and the right riding dress close the book. Women and girls of the horse age got plain, full counsel on riding well and safely.
40519-the-captain-of-the-janizaries-a-st:
James Ludlow's The Captain of the Janizaries was a story of the times of Scanderbeg and the fall of Constantinople, and it reached its eleventh edition with Harper and Brothers. Ludlow's preface says the story grew from the fascination of its times, not from a wish to write a book. His hero is George Castriot, called Scanderbeg by the Turks, who with unequal arms resisted the Ottoman Empire for twenty-three years.

Gibbon, Ludlow complains, gives Scanderbeg only a few pages, and Creasy less than a page in his history of the Turks. The romance is more than founded on fact, he insists: its details come from the chronicles of the monk Barletius, from later Byzantine annals, and from travel in the East. The tale, first copyrighted in 1886, opens at Brousa in Asia Minor in the middle of the fifteenth century.
40862-the-flower-girl-of-the-cha-teau-d-:
The Flower Girl of the Château d'Eau, in its second volume, is a novel by Paul de Kock. The Jefferson Press issued it in Boston and New York in 1904. It forms the sixteenth volume of a collected set of de Kock's novels. A frontispiece shows a daughter at the moment of her father's death.

A husband is telling how his marriage went wrong from the start. He had fallen madly in love with Lucienne Courtenay and won her hand. The first year of union was happy, he confesses to his listener. Then he found his wife a coquette to the very core. Dress was her one real occupation, and homage her daily need. Amiable among admirers, she yawned when the two were alone.
40961-luna-escapade:
H B Fyfe wrote Luna Escapade, a short science fiction tale printed in Orbit, volume one, number two, in nineteen hundred fifty three. Pete Dudley flies a rocket freighter toward the Moon. He has an hour of flight left before he must brake. His ship points tail first for the drop.

Dudley checks his ship and eyes the crater Ericsson on his screen. Then a girl’s voice speaks behind him in the sealed cabin. Freight ships fly with one pilot, and no guest should be aboard. Perfume hangs in the stale cabin air. She grips a machine to keep her feet on the deck. Her thick lipstick and false fair hair make her look like a kid in grown dress.
41288-beginners-book-in-language-a-book-:
Beginners' Book in Language, a book for the third grade by Jeschke, joint author of Oral and Written English, was published by Ginn and Company in 1918. The course runs to some fifty short sections. It opens with the study of a picture story in four parts, about a boy named Tom, and moves on to story-telling and making stories better.

Poems and fables are studied between the drills: Thomas Hood's Queen Mab, Aesop's Ants and the Grasshoppers, and fairy tales retold by the class. Correct usage lessons take up saw and seen, have, did and done, rang, sang, and drank, and may and can. Letter writing gets three sections, then letter improving, and the children end by making a little book of their own. The plan joins speech, reading, and writing in one daily round of small tasks.
41289-the-magazine-style-code:
The Magazine Style-Code is a manual for all who write, by Leigh H. Irvine. Its title states its users: authors, reporters, typewriters, ministers, lawyers, proofreaders, compositors, and publishers. It was put out in San Francisco in 1906 by the Crown Publishing Company. The printing came from the Mysell-Rollins Bank Note Company.

The code was drawn in large part from the system of Theodore Low De Vinne, from the Century Magazine and its books, and from the treatises of F. Horace Teall, as the title page states. The use of capital letters, abbreviations, and compound words is fully shown and made plain. Irvine was the author of The New California and The Writer's Blue Book, as the page adds. The book is a style rule book of the American magazine age.
41299-the-flower-girl-of-the-cha-teau-d-:
Volume one of The Flower Girl of the Chateau d'Eau is volume fifteen of the novels of Paul de Kock, printed at Boston and New York by the Jefferson Press. A frontispiece shows Violette resisting Jericourt, digging her nails into his face until the blood flows and he lets go. The novel opens in May 1853, at a flower market on Boulevard Saint-Martin, in front of the Chateau d'Eau in Paris. A chapter called Papa's Birthday starts the plot.

De Kock wrote comic Paris novels of clerks, flower girls, and shopkeepers, read all over Europe. This one follows a flower seller in the market world he knew best.
41549-god-wills-it-a-tale-of-the-first-c:
William Stearns Davis wrote a tale of the First Crusade, drawn by Louis Betts, by the author of A Friend of Caesar. A picture caption shows Richard at the head of a raging brute in a twinkling. A scripture motto heads the title: who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, and stopped the mouths of lions. God wills it was the crusaders' cry at Clermont in 1095.

Davis was a historian at the University of Minnesota who wrote novels from his scholarship. His crusade tale follows knights to the Holy Land. Betts illustrated many historical novels of the period. The book joined a shelf of crusade romance for young and old readers.
41864-life-of-kit-carson-the-great-weste:
Charles Burdett wrote a life of Kit Carson, the great western hunter and guide, copyrighted in 1869 and published at Philadelphia by Porter and Coates. The title promises wild and romantic exploits as a hunter and trapper in the Rocky Mountains. Thrilling adventures and hairbreadth escapes among Indians and Mexicans follow. Carson's services as a guide to scouting parties are stressed.

An account of government expeditions to the far west is included. The preface offers a revised and complete history of the most remarkable of American frontiersmen. Carson guided Frémont's expeditions and fought in the Mexican and Civil wars. He died in 1868, a year before this life. Burdett writes the legend while witnesses lived.
41894-christmas-tide:
Elizabeth Harrison wrote a book of Christmas lore for those who teach the young. Harrison was co-chief of the Chicago Kindergarten College. Her book came out in Chicago in 1902. A small tale at its front tells of a boy and a great plate. He had heard the Christ Child tale in her school room.

In Europe, the boy chose a Christ Child plate for his teacher. It looked as he felt the Child must have looked, he said. Harrison holds that great thoughts do leave marks on young minds. Murillo's canvas and a child's heart prove the same point. Tales, songs, and feast plans fill her book in turn. Teachers get a warm store for the feast days.
41901-the-victorious-attitude:
The Victorious Attitude is a work of self help by Orison Swett Marden, author of Pushing to the Front, with copyright in 1916. It had reached its sixteenth thousand, and Marden gave it to his friend Charles Schwab. Its motto runs: to think you can, creates the force that can.

Marden argues that bearing is the first step to success: walk, talk, and act as a winner, and others will take you at your own price. Chapters treat doubt as a traitor, dreams made true, and the mind at work in sleep. Others warn against drawing the poorhouse near by fearful thought. The book is New Thought counsel in a brisk, hearty voice.
42154-miss-leslie-s-lady-s-new-receipt-b:
Miss Leslie's Lady's New Receipt-Book, third edition enlarged, was published at Philadelphia by A Hart in 1850. The book is a guide for large or small families. It is a sequel to her Complete Cookery, under its other name, Directions for Cookery in All its Branches. This edition adds one hundred twenty receipts, for farina, Indian meal, fancy tea cake, and marmalades among them.

The contents span the whole house: soups, fish, meats, vegetables, poultry, oysters, and game. Puddings, pies, tarts, custards, ice creams, cakes, jellies, syrups, and cordials follow. Candies and even perfumery close the list. In her preface Miss Leslie says the new items were noted down as fresh knowledge came to her. Her motto promises that receipts fairly tried will seldom disappoint.
43867-farm-engines-and-how-to-run-them-t:
James H Stephenson and other expert engineers wrote Farm Engines and How to Run Them, also called The Young Engineer's Guide. Frederick J Drake and Company of Chicago copyrighted the handbook in 1903. It speaks to experts and amateurs alike. Every part of an engine and boiler is described, the title page says, with directions for safe and low-cost running.

The first chapter warns buyers that one good engine may still be the wrong engine for their farm. Later parts answer hundreds of questions asked in license examinations. Special chapters treat traction engines and gasoline farm engines. A final chapter covers the science of successful threshing. Pictures show nearly every make of traction engine then sold.
44076-autumn-impressions-of-the-gironde:
Sieveking wrote this travel book, Autumn Impressions of the Gironde, published at London; the head gives her initial only. The volume opens with praise quoted from The Times for another book, Russia of To-Day, bound in as an advertisement. Sieveking's own frontispiece shows an ancient headdress in Airvault. She begins with a meditation: once or twice in every life comes the chance of a glimpse through the magic gates of idealism.

Those who have seen, she says, carry an unforgettable longing ever after. Her journey runs through the Bordeaux country in autumn: vineyards, old towns, and French provincial life. She had earlier written a turning point of the Indian Mutiny and a memoir of Francis Newman. This is her gentler book, a season's impressions gathered like vintage grapes.
44090-catalogue-of-special-technical-wor:
Catalogue of Special Technical Works is a publisher's catalogue dated May 1904. It lists books for manufacturers, students, and technical schools. All the works offered are by expert writers, it says. An index to subjects opens the catalogue. Agricultural chemistry, alum, and ammonia head that index. Aniline colours and animal fats follow close behind. Bleaching, bone products, and bookbinding each have their pages. Brick making, carpet yarn printing, and ceramics are listed too.

Dyeing in its many branches fills a large share of the subject list. Cotton dyeing, woollen dyeing, and dyers' materials are separate heads. Enamels, essential oils, and evaporating apparatus come in turn. Dental metallurgy and a dictionary of paint materials also appear. The catalogue is a shelf list of industrial knowledge for sale. It shows what a technical reader could buy in 1904.
44409-a-thousand-years-of-jewish-history:
A Thousand Years of Jewish History runs from Alexander the Great to the Moslem conquest of Spain. The Rev Maurice H Harris wrote the textbook. Bloch Publishing Company issued this sixth edition, revised and enlarged, in New York in 1914. Harris had also written a history of the medieval Jews. Maps and illustrations support the text, and themes for discussion are listed.

Book one treats Judea as a vassal state. Persian sway and the Bible canon open the story. Greek and Jew meet under Alexander, and Judea passes to Greco-Egypt. The Maccabean chapters follow: persecution, Judas Maccabeus, and the feast of Hanukkah. The Apocrypha gets a chapter of summaries. The Diaspora chapter covers Egypt, the Septuagint, and Onias's temple. Book two turns to independent Judea. Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes divide its politics. A royal house returns under Aristobulus and Alexander Janneus.
44780-bessie-at-the-sea-side:
Joanna Mathews wrote Bessie at the Sea-Side, one of the six Bessie Books listed in the front matter with their prices. The set, sold in a box for seven dollars and a half, follows Bessie at the seaside, in the city, among friends, in the mountains, at school, and on her travels. Mathews wrote many such series for children.

Her other lists fill the page: the Flowerets, stories on the commandments, the Little Sunbeams, and the Kitty and Lulu books. Bessie at the sea shore gives the heroine salt air, sand, and the small moral trials of a holiday. Mathews wrote in the Sunday school tradition, where every pleasure carries a lesson. The Bessie books were steady sellers for two generations of girls.
46110-pattie-s-personal-narrative-1824-1:
Volume eighteen of the Early Western Travels series reprints three rare accounts of the early West. Reuben Gold Thwaites edited them with notes, and they were published at Cleveland in 1905. The chief piece is the personal narrative of Pattie. It covers an expedition from St Louis through the vast regions between that place and the Pacific Ocean. The party then came back through Mexico, in the years 1824 to 1830.

The volume also gives Willard's account of inland trade with New Mexico in 1825 and the downfall of the Fredonian Republic, plus Malte-Brun's account of Mexico. Thwaites's series preserved scarce travel books for students. This volume shows the fur trade era through the eyes of men who lived it.
46497-the-legend-of-sir-lancelot-du-lac-:
Jessie Weston wrote The Legend of Sir Lancelot du Lac, a study of how the famed knight grew in old tales. David Nutt put it out in London in 1901, as number twelve in the Grimm Library. Weston tracks where Lancelot came from, how his tale grew, and where he stands in the Arthurian cycle. She notes that he was no part of the first Arthur tales. The first clear note of him comes with Chretien de Troyes, and fame came fast.

Later parts weigh the Lanzelet of Ulrich von Zatzikhoven line by line. Weston tests views on the name Lancelot from scholars such as Gaston Paris and Rhys. She finds the claimed Celtic root weak and maps how the poem may have grown. Arthur fans get a close, calm guide to one knight and the books that made him.
46827-the-book-of-jade:
The Book of Jade is a book of poems printed by Doxey's, at the Sign of the Lark, in New York in 1901. The poet gives the book to the memory of Charles Baudelaire, and the French master's shadow lies over every page. A prelude opens in Ispahan, where the speaker reclines on a deep divan, tired of all mortal things.

Poems bear names like Ashtoreth, Opium, Ennui, Litany, and Poppy Song. Sonnets, rondeaus, and songs of golden youth fill the first part. The second part darkens: Mad Sonnet, Sonnet of the Instruments of Death, The Grave, Mummy, and Corpse. Love, weariness, and death trade lines through the whole, in the lush mode of the French decadents.
47509-an-essay-to-the-restoring-of-our-d:
Joseph Trevers wrote An Essay to the Restoring of our Decayed Trade in sixteen seventy eight. Giles Widdowes and two more London men sold the sharp plea. Smugglers, lawyers, and officers’ frauds stand named on its title. No nation holds such trade gifts as England, its first head boasts.

Wool and fuller’s earth slip out in secret, draining the realm. Banned foreign goods slip in by the same dark back roads. The common folk know no law, and no prize stirs informers up. Silk and ribbon weavers starve while the clothing trade decays. Clothing is the chiefest thing in the nation, Trevers insists. Millions a year in customs bleed from king and kingdom, he counts. Dutch craft undercuts English cloth in market after market abroad. Queries by way of remedy close his twelve part plea.
48174-little-visits-with-great-americans:
Orison Swett Marden edited this first volume of Little Visits with Great Americans. Its full title adds the point: Success Ideals and How to Attain Them. The book was copyrighted in 1903 and issued by the Success Company of New York. Marden founded Success magazine and wrote Pushing to the Front. His portrait stands at the front of the book. The catalog title is the copyright line.

The visits are sorted by calling. Invention opens the book, with Thomas Edison's hard work named the secret of his genius, and Hiram Maxim, the gun maker, after him. Each visit tells how a great man rose, in talk meant to fire young readers. The book is the gospel of success in its classic American form.
48175-little-visits-with-great-americans:
Little Visits with Great Americans, volume two, is a set of short lives edited by Orison Swett Marden, author of Pushing to the Front. The full title adds a promise: success ideals and how to attain them. The set was printed at New York by the Success Company in 1905, with copyrights of 1903 and 1904, and a picture called Joys of Home stands at the front.

The part of the volume shown here opens at chapter thirty-four, on the caricaturist Opper. Once a printer's devil, he won fame for the Dinkelspiel stories drawn for Hobart in the New York Morning Journal. Marden calls his life an example of determination, and visits him at his house in Bensonhurst to draw out the tale.
48577-colin-campbell-lord-clyde:
Archibald Forbes wrote this life of Colin Campbell, Lord Clyde, published at London in 1895 in the English Men of Action series. A portrait after Francis Grant fronts the book. The contents run from early life and the Peninsula, through colonial and home service, to China and India. The Crimea takes a chapter, and the Indian Mutiny three: the relief of Lucknow, the storming of the city, and the campaigns after.

The opening marvels at contrasts: three veterans sailed for the East in 1854 who had all first faced fire under Wellington in 1807 and 1808. Campbell was the greatest of them, a Scots ranker's son who rose to command in chief. Forbes, a famous war correspondent, writes his life as a soldier's epic. The pacification of Oude closes the story.
49137-cassell-s-book-of-in-door-amusemen:
Cassell's Book of In-Door Amusements, Card Games, and Fireside Fun is a household entertainment manual published by Cassell, Petter, Galpin in London, Paris, and New York, here in its third edition. Its illustrated frontispiece names the fare: Blind Man's Buff, Nine Pins, Fireside Fun, Whist, and Parlour Magic. The preface calls it a companion volume to Cassell's Book of Sports and Pastimes.

That companion deals largely with games played out-of-doors. The present book is almost exclusively devoted to indoor games of various kinds, and forms a fitting supplement. The writers aimed, the preface says, to convey their information in plain, accurate, direct fashion. Cross references let readers use the two books together without difficulty. A note preserved in the copy adds a rule for the magic section. In Parlour Magic no trick is described that involves apparatus in any degree elaborate.
49173-patty-bride:
Carolyn Wells, the prolific American writer of light verse and girls' books, brings her heroine Patty to the altar in this volume, copyrighted in 1918. She gives the book to one of the dearest little girls in the world, Barbara Buehler. Patty had grown up through a long shelf of earlier tales.

The contents open with Philip's Chance, and Philip is the man Patty will marry. Bumble arrives, Captain Bill blusters in, and the boys in khaki remind readers that a world war is on. A sleigh ride, a valentine, and an important document carry Patty toward her wedding day. Readers get a beloved series at its happiest turn.
49261-the-glebe-1913-11-vol-1-no-2-diary:
Diary of a Suicide is the second number of The Glebe, a little magazine of 1913. Albert and Charles Boni published it at New York. Alfred Kreymborg edited the magazine. Its sole policy was absolute freedom of expression. Each issue was devoted to one writer alone. Wallace Baker is the writer presented here. A foreword prints a letter dated September 27, 1913.

The letter's sender mails in the record of a young man about to kill himself. His only object is that publication may ease the way for some who come after. The letter went to an editor at The International magazine. The diary form lets the doomed man speak for himself across its pages. The Glebe promised twelve to twenty such books a year. Merit alone, not popular demand, chose them.
49955-bohemia-from-the-earliest-times-to:
Bohemia, in The Story of the Nations series, tells the history of the Czech lands from the earliest times to the fall of national independence. The series offered short national histories by named scholars, running from Rome and the Jews to Germany, Carthage, Egypt, Hungary, and Ireland. Each volume promised a whole people's story in a single readable book for general readers.

This volume traces Bohemia's kings, wars, faith struggles, and loss of self-rule. For English readers of the late nineteenth century, such books were the common path into the history of smaller European nations. The Czech story, with its mix of empire and resistance, suited the series well.
50107-julius-levallon-an-episode:
Julius LeVallon, an episode, is a novel by Algernon Blackwood, first published in 1916. Blackwood had written The Centaur and John Silence, as the title page notes. Four books divide it: schooldays, Edinburgh, the chalet in the Jura mountains, and the attempted restitution.

Verses from a mystic poet head the first book. A quote on death as part of life's rhythm opens chapter one. The narrator waits at Basle for letters after a climbing holiday in the nineties. Memory carries him back to a school friend of strange gifts. LeVallon's soul, the tale argues, had lived before. Readers get Blackwood's novel of rebirth and old souls meeting again.
50243-the-subtropical-garden-or-beauty-o:
The Subtropical Garden, or Beauty of Form in the Flower Garden, is a gardening book by Robinson, author of The Wild Garden and Alpine Flowers for English Gardens. Murray published it at London in 1871, with illustrations. In his preface Robinson says the book is written to assist a newly awakened interest in fine foliage plants. Its guiding aim, he adds, is the choice of really suitable subjects.

He rejects many plants that had been recommended and tried for subtropical planting in English gardens. This point matters more than it first appears, he argues, for most writing on the subject names plants entirely unsuitable to the purpose. His own lists rest on trial. The subtropical style set great leaved plants like palms, bananas, and castor oil plants in summer beds for a lush, foreign effect. Robinson led the revolt against stiff carpet bedding.
50255-fishpingle-a-romance-of-the-countr:
Horace Vachell wrote Fishpingle, a romance of the countryside, in 1917. Doran at New York put out the book that year. Vachell was the author of Quinneys', the title page notes. The book is dedicated to the country gentlemen of England. Fishpingle's room at Pomfret Court challenges visitors' interest at its opening.

The room was part of the old Pomfret House. Fire destroyed that house long ago, it says. Its walls are of stone quarried on the estate. A master-builder revelled in his craft there. The effect is that of a crypt, it owns. A south window was cut into the wall in 1830. A Cromwellian table faces the wide open fireplace in the room. Cavaliers cut their initials into that table. The room was the steward's in an earlier time. Vachell gives an old house its steward for a hero.
50483-reminiscences-of-a-soldier-of-the-:
L D Young wrote Reminiscences of a Soldier of the Orphan Brigade, issued at Paris, Kentucky, and given to those who wore the gray and to their children. The Richard Hawes Chapter of the Daughters of the Confederacy commends the booklet warmly. It calls it a worthy addition to the literature of the South. A poem on the Orphan Brigade by Professor N S Shaler heads the work.

Shaler served in the Federal Army, the note stresses. His verse marches the host of 1861 forth in hope's array, five thousand strong. Shiloh's field and the years 1862 and 1863 are sung in turn. The chapter calls Young a splendid Christian gentleman and a gallant Confederate soldier. His own tale gives personal experiences and much valuable historic information, it says. Kentucky troops in the western war are the theme throughout.
507-adam-bede:
George Eliot sets this novel in a Midland farming village, where carpenter Adam Bede loves Hetty Sorrel, a pretty dairymaid. Hetty, vain and restless, falls for squire Arthur Donnithorne, while preacher Dinah Morris offers Adam a steadier love. A trial, a prison visit, and a harvest close the long arc.

Eliot writes with rich, patient detail, from workshops to dairy to church. Her moral eye is stern yet kind, weighing pride, lust, and forgiveness. The novel stands as her first great portrait of English country life, where plain folk face grave choices and learn, slowly, to live with them.
50907-the-anatomy-of-suicide:
The Anatomy of Suicide is a medical treatise by Forbes Winslow, a member of the Royal College of Surgeons, published in London in 1840 and dedicated to the physician James Johnson. Winslow argues that the wish to end one's own life often grows out of bodily and mental illness, and so can be met with the same care used for other diseases. The work grew from a paper he read before the Westminster Medical Society, where it drew a lively debate among leading doctors of the day.

The chapters trace the history and forms of self-destruction, its signs and causes, and the ways doctors and families might step in before an act. Winslow writes for fellow medical men, but his plea reaches wider: that despair be treated as sickness rather than crime or sin. The treatise stands as an early landmark in the medical study of suicide.
50927-scientific-american-architects-and:
The Scientific American issued this architects and builders edition, number 26, dated December 1887. Munn and Company of 361 Broadway, New York, published it at twenty-five cents a copy or two dollars fifty a year. Two supplements came with it: two plates in colour and one large sheet of details, the sheet now lost, as a note admits. Ads open the number.

The first ads push economic gas engines, called best in principle, workmanship, and materials. A plumbers' gas engine pumps two hundred and fifty gallons fifty feet high in an hour. Larger sizes serve flats, hotels, and private houses. A saw blade that cuts iron nearly as fast as wood gets its puff below. The edition served builders with plans, products, and prices.
51009-picture-bride:
William Morrison wrote this science fiction story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in June 1955. The narrator's brother Perry is a born experimenter who nearly blew up the house as a boy. Now Perry shows him a picture of a strange girl in odd clothes and says he is in love with her. She is brainy looking, and not a blonde, which puzzles his brother all the more.

The tag line gives the twist away in part: she is as pretty as a picture because a picture is all she is, or all she will one day be. Morrison builds the tale on that hook, a love across time or art. It is a neat, wry piece of 1950s magazine science fiction.
51337-the-man-outside:
A science fiction story by Evelyn E Smith. Galaxy Science Fiction printed it in August 1957. Dillon illustrated the piece. The headnote poses the puzzle plainly. Kin should guard a man's life, it says. But what of kin who have not been born yet? Martin, the boy at the centre, lives that puzzle.

Martin's mother has disappeared, as mothers do in his ruined district. A woman named Ninian arrives to care for him. She claims to be his great-great-granddaughter, come from the future. Martin must call her Aunt Ninian anyway. A cousin named Conrad is travelling back to kill the boy. Killing him serves a plan to change the social order. Smith mixes slum realism with time travel paradox.
51940-a-garden-of-peace-a-medley-in-quie:
Frankfort Moore, an Irish novelist who wrote The Jessamy Bride, published A Garden of Peace with Doran in New York in 1920. Its subtitle calls it a medley in quietude. Chapter the first opens with Dorothy frowning at the title: it has a catchpenny click, she thinks, trading on the Peace everyone was talking about after the war.

Moore answers her at length, in the book's teasing manner, comparing such titles to backing a horse after the race is secretly won. The medley form lets him wander a literal garden and the peace of 1919 together, essay by essay. Dorothy stands in for the reader who doubts the whole enterprise, and the author charms the doubt chapter by chapter.
51951-the-jessamy-bride:
The Jessamy Bride is a historical novel by Frank Frankfort Moore, published by Duffield at New York in 1906. Color pictures by Allan Gilbert illustrate it. The story opens at a dinner table of wits. Johnson chides the company, Goldsmith answers that his own self-satisfaction is proof against any lesser mind, and Burke laughs at the twinkle in his eye.

Sir Joshua Reynolds turns his ear-trumpet toward Johnson with a smile. Boswell and Garrick sit solemn-faced, Garrick in mimicry of Boswell. The scene sets the book's world: the London circle of Johnson and Goldsmith, where talk was an art and pride a daily comedy. Moore builds his romance among these famed talkers.
52072-life-of-joseph-brant-thayendanegea:
Volume one of Life of Joseph Brant, called Thayendanegea, is a biography by William L. Stone, printed at New York in 1838. The full work runs to two volumes. Brant was a Mohawk leader tied to both the United States and Great Britain. Stone also takes in the border wars of the American Revolution.

The first chapter sorts out Brant's birth and parentage. It draws on the journals of Sir William Johnson, a key British hand in Indian affairs. Readers follow the young Brant to school at Lebanon and into the wars against Pontiac. His work as an interpreter and his part in translating Scripture also appear. The book preserves a full early life of a famed Native leader.
52839-texas-rocks-and-minerals-an-amateu:
Texas Rocks and Minerals, an amateur guide, is a work by Roselle Girard, issued at Austin in 1964. It is guidebook six of the Bureau of Economic Geology of the University of Texas. Harris drew the sketches for the guide in its pages. Printings run from 1964 to a fourth printing of May 1979 in the edition note.

Contents open with the earth outer crust, geologists, and time and rock units for the beginner. A geologic map and the question what are rocks and minerals follow in the list. Igneous rocks, extrusive and intrusive, and sedimentary rocks fill the shown heads of the guide. Girard writes for the rockhound: where in Texas to find agate, quartz, and petrified wood, and how to name what he finds. State guidebooks of this kind put a science into the glove box of the family car for a generation of collectors.
53015-a-guest-of-ganymede:
MacApp wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Worlds of Tomorrow in June 1963. Its blurb promises great treasure on Jupiter's moons for a daring man, and death waiting beside it. The hero is Gil Murdoch, a hired hand on a secret run.

His employer paid hugely to disguise a small ship as a chunk of asteroid rock. Murdoch slipped it past the quarantine around Ganymede and melted it into the ice. Now he eases the ship forward while a blind man named Waverill demands to know what he is doing. Readers get a cold, tense tale of smuggling at the edge of the solar system.
53089-the-creature-inside:
Jack Sharkey wrote The Creature Inside, a science fiction story printed in Worlds of Tomorrow in December 1963, with pictures by Wood. The opening line sets the odd stage: the room was small, but it held a whole universe, and Norcriss had no place in it.

Doctor Alan Burgess briefs Lieutenant Jerry Norcriss on an urgent fix the service is in. About a year earlier, Burgess explains, he stumbled on a way to reverse an electro-encephalograph, the machine that reads the brain's waves. Played backward, the device plays recordings back into a mind. Burgess puffs nervously at a cigarette as he talks. Sharkey builds the tale on that one invention and the creature it lets inside.
53786-the-dolls-on-dress-parade:
Effa Preston wrote The Dolls on Dress Parade, a children's entertainment published by the Paine Publishing Company of Dayton, Ohio. The piece, priced at twenty-five cents, was copyrighted in 1922. It is a short play meant for school and home programs, where children perform as dolls.

The stage shows the inside of a doll shop. A shop woman, guests, and a soldier doll are present as the curtain rises. Dolls enter as they are announced, walking stiffly, except the rag dolls. The front pages list song novelties the same firm sold for school entertainments: welcome songs, closing songs, and other pieces in sheet music form. Such booklets helped teachers stage a full evening's program with little cost.
5399-an-essay-on-the-american-contributi:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, argues in this short essay that Americans are idealists at heart, not merely money-makers. He cites Emerson and William James as interpreters of that character. He also quotes a French observer who noted how poorly nations judge one another, France for its chefs and America as a land of dollar-chasers. Churchill insists the caricature misses the point.

The essay then connects that idealism to democracy itself, presenting the American contribution as a belief in self-government and human dignity. Written in the aftermath of war, it reads as a defense of democratic values against cynicism. Readers get a brief, earnest statement of what Churchill thought America stood for.
54134-the-senator-s-bride:
Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller wrote The Senator Bride, issued in New York by Street and Smith as Number Twenty in the Eagle Library at ten cents. The weekly number is dated July twelfth, eighteen ninety seven. The tale itself was entered for copyright in eighteen eighty seven. Chapter one is The Fall of a Meteor. A long chapter list shows a Washington romance.

Too Late, Sweetheart Good By, and Renunciation follow the opening fall. What the Winner Hand Threw By and Lulu deepen the feud. But as for Her, She Staid at Home shows the heroine temper. At the Capitol brings the Senate scene. On the Ocean, A New Year Gift, and Wedding Cards fill the close. Rue and later chapters end the tale. Dime novel readers get love, pride, and politics in a famed Miller romance.
54487-waterfowl-identification-guide:
The Waterfowl Identification Guide, published by the Central Flyway Council for its ten member states from Montana to Texas. It teaches hunters and watchers to name the ducks, geese, and other water birds of the flyway. The council thanks the Atlantic Flyway Council for illustrations and most of the text, and Alan Munro for the art. A page on the parts of a duck opens the teaching.

Species accounts follow in order: the whistling swan, the geese, the dabbling ducks from mallard to wood duck, the diving ducks and mergansers. Last come the cormorant, loon, grebes, coot, rails, and snipe. A waterfowler's code closes the booklet. The foreword tells the hard story behind it: nesting grounds drained by the million acres, wintering grounds lost to farms and cities, and the coming of scientific management. Spring shooting and market hunting were abolished.
54638-julia-and-the-pet-lamb-or-good-tem:
Julia and the Pet-Lamb, or Good Temper and Compassion Rewarded is a tale for children, printed at London in 1813 by Darton, Harvey, and Darton, a house known for children's books. The front picture shows a lamb crying as if in pain. The tale opens with little Julia showing her mother a pocket handkerchief she has just hemmed, and asking if it is well done.

Her mother praises the neat work, and the story runs from that small goodness to the lamb of the title. Compassion to a hurt animal is the lesson, rewarded in the manner of the subtitle. Such tales taught the youngest readers of the Regency to join kindness with duty. The book is a neat relic of the moral nursery shelf.
54704-marriage-as-a-trade:
Marriage as a Trade is a feminist essay by Cicely Hamilton, the author of the play Diana of Dobson's. Moffat, Yard and Company published it in New York in 1909. Hamilton argues that marriage, for most women of her day, was not a romance but a trade, the only one open to them.

She begins with habit. Curiosity, she writes, wakes only for the unfamiliar, and custom has made us accept without inquiry the illogical and unsatisfactory position of women. Her book, she says, is nothing more than the attempt of an unscientific woman to explain honestly the disadvantages under which she and her sisters exist. She defines her terms at once. A woman, for her, is an individual human being whose life is her own concern. Her worth is in no way raised or lowered by the accident of marriage. The book became a classic of the suffrage years.
54910-the-rising-tide:
Margaret Deland wrote The Rising Tide, a novel first published in 1915 and issued again in 1916 with pictures by F Walter Taylor. Deland had written The Iron Woman and the Old Chester tales. The frontispiece shows Frederica, the young woman at the center of the book, and a quote from Job about people sure that wisdom will die with them hangs over the story.

The novel opens on Payton Street, once grand, now given over to lodgers and small shops as trolleys crowd the rest of the town. Frederica has a project of her own, which her man of business must put into plain words for her. Howard and Laura appear in the scenes the pictures name. Deland writes about money, work, and a young woman pushing against the limits her world sets.
55145-the-orchid-album-volume-1-comprisi:
The Orchid Album, volume 1, is a partwork of coloured figures and descriptions of new, rare, and beautiful orchidaceous plants, published in London in 1882. B S Williams issued it at the Victoria and Paradise Nurseries. Robert Warner and Benjamin Samuel Williams conducted it, Thomas Moore wrote the botanical descriptions, and John Nugent Fitch drew the coloured figures.

The volume is dedicated, by special permission, to Her Royal Highness the Princess of Wales. Its preface says recent advances in introducing and growing exotic orchids called for a monthly publication showing the best forms and the methods that succeed with them. Growers were expected to use the plates to direct purchases and to learn points of masterly management for these aristocratic plants.
55636-orlo-ff-and-his-wife-tales-of-the-:
Orlóff and His Wife: Tales of the Barefoot Brigade is a book of stories by Maxim Gorky, translated from Russian by Isabel Hapgood and printed in New York in 1901. Gorky wrote of the poor and the drifting men of Russia, whom he knew from his own hard youth. The eight tales here date from 1896 and 1897.

The title story opens on a Saturday night in a cellar flat, where a drunken fight between a shoemaker and his wife draws the whole court-yard to listen. Other tales, such as Konováloff, Men with Pasts, and Comrades, follow tramps, exiles, and workers. Gorky's style is rough, warm, and close to speech. The book helped make his name in the English-speaking world.
56576-legends-of-fire-island-beach-and-t:
Edward Richard Shaw collects shore tales in Legends of Fire Island Beach and the South Side, copyrighted in 1895. His preface, written at Bellport, Long Island, says the stories hold only a small part of the folklore of the Great South Bay. They were told by a class of men now gone, in taverns, by cabin fires, and aboard small craft crossing the bay.

Fact, imagination, and superstition each had a share, he owns. The tales are The Pot of Gold, The Bogy of the Beach, The Mower's Phantom, Enchanted Treasure, The Money Ship, and Widow Molly. Photographs by R Eickemeyer illustrate the coast.
56949-the-humour-of-america-selected-wit:
James Barr selected The Humour of America, published in London in 1909 in a Humour Series that already held volumes for France, Germany, Italy, and other nations. Illustrations are by C E Brock, and an introduction and an index of American humorists frame the collection. The first piece is My Dog, by Bill Nye.

James Whitcomb Riley's Knee-Deep in June follows, then Eugene Field on baked beans and culture. George Washington Cable, John G Saxe, and Robert Jones Burdette all appear. Mark Twain's speech on the babies is here, as is more of Bill Nye, this time on cyclones. Harriet Beecher Stowe's The Minister's Wooing is excerpted further on. Barr aimed to show British readers that American humour was more than dialect and brag: a national literature in its own right.
57010-alexandria-a-history-and-a-guide:
Alexandria: A History and a Guide, by E M Forster, was published in 1922 after Forster's wartime years in Egypt. The book has two parts. The history marches like a pageant through twenty-two centuries and a half: Alexander the Great, the Ptolemies, Cleopatra, and the literature and science of the Greek Egyptian city. Then come the Christian and later periods, each given its own color. The guide half turns the past into walks a visitor can take.

Forster wrote Howards End and The Longest Journey before Alexandria, and the same humane eye is at work on stones and streets. Quotations from Ibn Dukmak and Plotinus stand at the door. The book remains the classic English portrait of the city, part scholarship and part love letter, by a novelist who learned Alexandria on foot.
57098-british-museum-natural-history-gen:
A guide to the museum of the past of life in London fills this book, printed in 1913 by the word of its board. It is the thirteenth shape of the guide. The house stands on Cromwell Road. Plans and views of the house go with the text, and fifty-eight cuts fill it. A photo at its front shows the west front of the house as its first plans had it.

The word at the front, by L. Fletcher, the head of the house, states the aim of the guide. It is for the use of guests who wish just to get a broad sense of the plan and the goods of the house. Guides of a close kind have been made for guests who wish to study the goods in depth. A list of those guides is given at the back of this book.
57161-notes-of-a-gold-digger-and-gold-di:
James Bonwick wrote Notes of a Gold Digger, and Gold Diggers' Guide in Melbourne in 1852, at the height of the rush to the gold fields of Victoria. Bonwick had dug there himself and wrote from what he saw. The book speaks straight to new men who dream of quick wealth.

Bonwick warns readers not to load up with gear in town, where prices tempt and needs are unclear. He maps the road to the diggings and tells what stores at the mines charge. His notes mix praise for the rich ground with plain talk on cost and toil. New diggers get hints on what to buy, what to skip, and how to start. The guide is a close look at rush life in its first wild year.
57288-indians-of-the-mesa-verde:
Indians of the Mesa Verde, by Don Watson, was printed by the Mesa Verde Museum Association at the national park in Colorado in 1953. A photo of Cliff Palace, the greatest known cliff dwelling, stands at the front. The book was lithoprinted at Ann Arbor, Michigan.

Part one treats the people of the Mesa Verde, from echoes of the past and the finding of the ruins to life in ancient times. Chapters walk through spring, summer, autumn, and winter in the cliff towns, then the end of the story. Part two gives the background, on the origin of the American Indian and the digging of the Mesa Verde. Plates show black on white pottery, jars, and busy cliff scenes. Park visitors get a clear guide to a lost town world.
58329-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the works of Oscar Wilde held by Project Gutenberg. It is a finding list, not a work by Wilde himself, though Wilde's name stands as the subject. The contents run through the plays, tales, poems, and essays that Gutenberg offers, from The Picture of Dorian Gray in both its shorter and longer forms to The Ballad of Reading Gaol.

For each volume the index prints its table of contents, so a reader can see what a file holds before opening it. Listings cover Lady Windermere's Fan, The Importance of Being Earnest, De Profundis, The Happy Prince, and the poems. As Gutenberg added texts, such guides helped readers sort a large and growing set of files by one author. It serves librarians and Wilde readers who want the whole shelf at a glance.
58436-multitude-and-solitude:
Multitude and Solitude is a novel by John Masefield, published by Macmillan in New York in 1916. Masefield was already known for The Everlasting Mercy and Captain Margaret. The hero is Roger Naldrett, a writer watching his own tragedy fail on its first night.

The opening puts Naldrett in a box, far back so his friend John O'Neill can see the stage. The first act has gone cold, the cast is nervous, and the house has begun to fidget. Naldrett watches with strange calm, since his excitement burned itself out before the production. Actors drop lines and cover for one another, and he admires their nerve. A pause in the action, a cough, and one half-hearted clap strike him as worse than a hiss. He longs for the end, so that he may be decently damned and allowed to go.
59011-the-last-crusade:
George Smith wrote The Last Crusade, a tale first printed in Worlds of If in February 1955. A picture in part of a building that was once the Louvre holds a name for Whitey, lost in his memory. In the mud of ruined Paris, Sergeant Marty Coleman tells his armoured men how Caesar named the place Lutetia, the mud town.

Ward and Joe White listen over the company circuit, in mecho-armour, while the other side raises hell near by. The city of light has little light left. A crusade of the far future fights over its ruins. Fans get a grim, funny tale of soldiers who are walking tanks in a dead Paris.
59109-the-orchid-album-volume-2-comprisi:
The Orchid Album, volume two, was published in London in 1883. Robert Warner and Benjamin Samuel Williams conducted the work, and Thomas Moore of the Chelsea Botanic Gardens wrote the plant descriptions. John Nugent Fitch drew the coloured figures. The volume was dedicated, by special permission, to the Princess of Wales.

Each plate shows a new, rare, or beautiful orchid, with notes on its form and care. Cattleyas, cypripediums, dendrobiums, and masdevallias fill the index. Growers of the day prized such albums for both beauty and use. The book joins art and garden science: fine colour plates on one side, plain facts for the orchid house on the other.
59411-the-orchid-album-volume-3-comprisi:
The Orchid Album printed coloured figures and accounts of new, rare, and fine orchids for the growers of Victorian England. Robert Warner and Benjamin Samuel Williams conducted the work, Thomas Moore of the Chelsea Botanic Gardens wrote the plant accounts, and John Nugent Fitch drew the coloured plates. Volume three came out in London in 1884, from Williams's Victoria and Paradise Nurseries.

The volume is dedicated, by leave, to the Princess of Wales. Its index lists plate after plate: cattleyas, dendrobiums, cypripediums, and laelias, each with the scholar's name who first named it. Orchid growing was a costly passion of the age, and albums like this one were its record and its catalogue, part science and part show.
60010-the-up-grade:
Wilder Goodwin wrote a novel of mining life, issued at Boston in 1910 with pictures by Charles Grunwald. Stephen Loring sits drunk and broke on a sidewalk in Phoenix, too spent to care where he rests. A brisk man named McKay finds him there and offers work.

McKay rounds up men for the Quentin Mining Company in the hills, and Loring makes the forty-first hand. The boss had bet McKay would get only forty, and that half would slip away on the road. A girl named Jean, a man named Hankins, and a fight by a body in later pictures hint at the hard road Loring must climb.
6017-the-silver-horde:
Rex Beach sets a northern adventure on the trail to Kalvik, down from the mountains over tundra and tide flats, out upon salt ice and across to the village. A spiritless man and a rogue appear first, break bread with a lonely woman, and meet Cherry Malotte, who displays a temper and gives heart to a hopeless man.

A compact is formed, Boreas and Neptune take a hand, Boyd Emerson admits failure and gains a year of grace, and Big George meets his enemy. Doors of vaults swing shut, new enemies appear, and Miss Wayland wavers between minds. Beach writes of salmon, silver, and hard bargains in Alaska's cold country.
60331-the-man-on-the-other-side:
The Man on the Other Side is a novel by Ada Barnett, printed at New York in 1922. Barnett gives the book simply to him, and sets a verse by Stella Benson at the front about besieging the golden coasts of space to see the million ghosts come home. Twelve chapters tell the tale.

The story opens in 1919, the year of the Great Peace, with Ruth Courthope Seer standing on her own doorstep in delight. Past forty, with no kin and no home of her own till now, she has at last bought Thorpe Farm. Fields, a trout stream, and five Shorthorns bought at Uckfield market are all hers. The love of the land sweeps through her like a clean wind.
60567-the-epistle-of-othea-to-hector-or-:
The Epistle of Othea to Hector, or The Boke of Knyghthode, is Christine de Pisan's work in English dress. Stephen Scrope translated it from the French, with a dedication to Sir John Fastolf. Warner edited this printing from a manuscript in the library of the Marquis of Bath. Nichols printed it at London in 1904 for the Roxburghe Club.

A picture from a Harley manuscript shows Othea delivering her epistle to Hector. The club's list of members fills the front pages, dukes and earls among them. The editor's note says this English version is printed here for the first time. It comes from a manuscript believed unique, or very near the original. The book gives a goddess's counsel to a knight.
61133-the-happy-homicide:
The Happy Homicide is a science fiction tale by Frank Banta, first printed in Worlds of If in March 1962. Its blurb gives the hook at once: it is not so bad to be on trial for murder, save for one thing. The chief witness is the corpse. The scene is a courtroom of the year 1986. Attendants wheel in the body of Fannie Bork on a cot, her red-painted toenails out of the sheet. Her husband John, forty years old, hears the charge read.

The proof is a machine as tall as a man, with forty-three meters on its face. The prosecutor says it will stir the dead woman's brain. She will then tell the court herself who killed her, and how and why. The jury hears the claim in shocked silence. The tale is a courtroom twist on the tools of a future age.
61397-the-faces-outside:
The Faces Outside, a science fiction story by Bruce McAllister, was printed in Worlds of If in July 1963. Its headnote says its pair were all that was left of humanity, if they were still human. The narrator wanted to call his mate Soft Breast, for she is soft when he holds her. But the Voice told him to call her Diane.

The Voice orders their mating each day when the water is brightest, at noon, when the sun stands over the tank. The tank is a vast watery world with four corners and a cave where they sleep. Faces watch them from outside, as they sometimes watch the porpoises. It took long to grow used to being watched so, the narrator says. McAllister tells the tale from inside the tank, in simple words. The result is a strange, sad story of captivity and love.
61564-attitude:
Hal Clement wrote Attitude, a short tale first printed in Astounding Science-Fiction in September 1943. The head note tells of captors with a strange way: they let captives build the gear to flee, and urge them on. Only at the last moment do the captors always stop them, for a hidden cause.

Little wakes with a start as if he had stepped off a cliff, to find a copper-hued ceiling a few feet up. He is used to weightless sleep in space and scorns his own jumpy start. Then he sees he should not be awake here at all. Fans get a taut puzzle of minds in space.
62439-scripture-histories-from-the-creat:
Scripture Histories tells Bible tales from Creation to the death of Jesus Christ. F Houlston and Son printed the penny book at Wellington, with cuts throughout. A verse at the front praises God's wisdom shown in his book. A short account of St Paul's Church in London ends the work.

Adam in Eden, Eve from his rib, and the serpent's trick open the tale. Noah and Seth carry the line through flood and sin. Short, plain parts suit children and new readers of the time. Church teachers gain a cheap, clear path through the whole Bible story.
62839-badger-house-community-trail-guide:
The Badger House Community Trail Guide is a visitor's booklet for a group of ruins covering nearly seven acres on Wetherill Mesa at Mesa Verde. The trail leads past Basketmaker pithouses, a pueblo village, and Two Raven House. Stops at the Badger House itself serve the little train that carried visitors through the site. The walk covers six hundred years of prehistory in less than a mile.

The booklet explains how archaeologists read the past from buildings, tools, and village plans. It admits freely that they do not always agree. It then introduces the Anasazi, ancestors of the Pueblo peoples, who farmed corn across the northern Southwest. Sold for a small donation at the trailhead, the guide teaches while it directs. It preserves the National Park Service's way of presenting Mesa Verde.
6285-you-never-know-your-luck-being-the-:
On a late August day at Askatoon, a prairie town on the way to the Rockies, a young voice sings into the morning over a field of cloth of gold. The singer is twenty-two, brushing a coat, with wheat stretching for scores of miles, and she seems in tone with the scene itself. Her hair, cheeks, eyes, skin, laugh, and voice are all gold, so golden that a watcher might suspect the gold was made, not born.

This first volume holds a proem, pioneers, closing doors, the Logan trial, strength promised, and a story to be told. Shiel Crozier, lean and angular like a figure in an old Spanish painting, stands at its centre, a man whose very name seems to fit him. Parker opens a tale of a matrimonial deserter on the prairie, where singing, wheat, and a trial set the terms of a life.
6286-you-never-know-your-luck-being-the-:
Stillness on a summer day in Prairie Land has the character of music, Parker says, a divine quiet of the senses and a suspension of motion. Sleepy notes sprinkle that stillness: pine sough at the door, insect murmur, a steam thresher's low beat out of sight, and a cat purring in Kitty Tynan's arms. With fascinated eyes she listens to Shiel Crozier tell a life as distant from hers as Eve's, awed more than curious.

This second volume ends a first lesson and finds a woman's way to knowledge. An unopened letter, night shade and morning glory, a call for help, and a camp of the deserter follow. Parker writes prairie listening as an act, where a story told in stillness can change a hearer. Kitty, once only a listener, begins to know, and the deserter's past moves closer to her present.
6287-you-never-know-your-luck-being-the-:
Kitty laughs in a big rocking chair, swinging back and forth and gazing at a distant sky, while her mother Mrs. Tynan scolds her for cackling like a young hen with her first egg. A close observer would see that Kitty's laughter is not joy, but bitterness with the smart of a nettle in it. Her mother's question only makes her laugh more, until Mrs. Tynan, worn by housework and worry, says she could shake her.

This third volume runs from the receipt of custom through Kitty speaking her mind again. Awaiting a verdict, a chapter on male and female created, and a pleasure turned to duty lead to an epilogue. Parker closes his deserter's tale with a household under strain, where a daughter's laugh hides trouble and a mother's hands tremble. The verdict, when it comes, settles more than one life.
6288-you-never-know-your-luck-being-the-:
Askatoon, a prairie town on the road to the Rockies, opens with a girl of twenty-two singing over golden wheat, a symphony in gold from hair to voice. Shiel Crozier, lean and angular, tells his story in prairie stillness to Kitty Tynan, who listens with a cat in her arms. Trials, unopened letters, and a deserter's camp follow, until Kitty speaks her mind and a verdict waits.

Read whole, the novel follows a matrimonial deserter across three volumes, from pioneers and closing doors to night shade, morning glory, and an epilogue. Parker writes the prairie as a place of music and silence, where a man's past arrives by story before it arrives in person. It is a tale of luck that cannot be counted on, and of a woman learning to judge a man by his telling.
62925-your-1952-champion-owner-s-guide:
The Studebaker Corporation issued this owner's guide for buyers of its 1952 Champion. It tells them what they had in the car, how to operate it, and what care it should receive to serve them best. Early pages name every instrument and control, from the ammeter and oil pressure gauge to the overdrive control and the parking brake handle.

Later sections cover the run-in period for a new engine, driving, lubrication, and how to change a tire, followed by upkeep, service and adjustments, and technical reference data. Seasonal services, a wiring diagram, and an index close the book. The guide also explains the Dealer Service Policy, under which the selling dealer owed the owner two thorough free check-ups during the warranty period. Any dealer could also replace faulty parts without charge for material or labor.
63223-the-man-inside:
Natalie Sumner Lincoln published The Man Inside in New York in 1914, after earlier mystery novels such as The Trevor Case. Chapter heads promise a ball, a sad event, a broken meeting, and proof built from small clues. One head names the State Department, which hints at a Washington setting and public stakes.

A piece of silk from the East, a theft, and talk over tea cups all feed the puzzle as it grows. Lincoln keeps the pace quick, with short chapters and a new turn in most of them. The dedication honors a senior army officer whose advice helped her. Readers get a period mystery of crime, clues, and high social life in the capital.
63422-roentgen-rays-and-phenomena-of-the:
Roentgen Rays and Phenomena of the Anode and Cathode is a technical book by Edward Thompson, copyrighted in 1896 and published by Van Nostrand. William Anthony, formerly of Cornell, wrote the concluding chapter. Sixty diagrams and forty-five half-tones illustrate the text, and the frontispiece shows Roentgen himself.

The preface says the book sets out the facts and principles of what happens around charged electrodes in gases at various pressures. Its real subject is the radiant energy made inside a discharge tube, then the only source of X-rays. Thompson follows the German plan of numbered paragraphs with cross-references, so that likeness, contrast, and suggestion can be weighed. Each experiment is given by its object, its apparatus, its result, and the inferences drawn. He writes for students and readers as well as for electricians, expecting years to pass before the discharge gives up all its secrets.
63426-will-bradley-his-chap-book-an-acco:
The Typophiles of New York published an account of the printer and designer Will Bradley in 1955. Bennett held the rights in the added matter. Bradley tells his own tale in his own words, as the title page sets out. He was a boy printer in Ishpeming, then an art student in Chicago.

From there he went on to found the Wayside Press as designer, printer, and publisher. Years as an art director in magazine work came after. Stage work, films, and writing fill the gaps between. An opening essay weighs what Bradley did to his age. It sets him beside Morris and Beardsley across the sea. In the 1890s, it says, Bradley woke the American public from its sleep. He found a spring in old American colonial type, bold and free, and built a fresh, home grown art of design on it.
6350-via-crucis-a-romance-of-the-second-:
F. Marion Crawford sets his romance on the fifth day of May, 1145, at sunset in a garden at Stoke Regis Manor. A lady walks a narrow path between high rose bushes on the masonry and a low flower bed of squares planted with flowers and sweet herbs, bordered with budding violets. Beyond the moat's deep green water lie close cropped sward, great oaks in spring leaf, and corn and meadow land in long green waves.

The sun reddens her golden hair and fires her clear blue eyes as she walks. The illustrations promise her first meeting with a queen, a cry for crosses, and the knighting of Gilbert. Gilbert Warde, Norman fighter, stands against Arnold the dreamer, theory against action, in a tale of the Second Crusade. Crawford writes the way of the cross as love, war, and faith braided together.
63824-the-man-the-sun-gods-made:
Gardner Fox's story, from Planet Stories in the winter of 1946, tells of Tyr, a man worshipped as a god on the planet Lyallar. Tyr neither eats nor breathes: he draws all he needs from the sun, drinking its energy through his skin. From his ruby throne he gives gifts to the beautiful Fay, and even likes the rat-face of Otho at worship time.

Yet grief bows him, for he knows he is human. Wandering in a moment of sun-fed clarity, he finds a lone stone tower on the silver sand, full of glass and metal instruments and strange books. His opened mind understands the books, and the discovery changes everything.
63889-the-luminous-blonde:
Hayden Howard wrote "The Luminous Blonde," a science fiction story printed in Planet Stories in November 1952. The magazine's blurb calls its heroine the gorgeous wife of a playboy commissioner. She has, it says, all the gifts needed to cut a modern spaceship, and a marriage, in two with one sweep of a clock hand.

The tale opens aboard a rocket, where the newly appointed Commissioner for Economics for Mars, Edwin Elbert, rides in luxury. A pretty attendant helps him out of his safety corset while his wife is out of the room, and he makes the most of the moment. Howard plays the scene for leering comedy, then turns the flight toward the trouble the blurb promises.
63942-the-man-the-tech-men-made:
Man the Tech Men Made is a science fiction tale by Fox Holden of Kane. The story ran in Planet Stories for March nineteen fifty four. Kane was a man of a hundred planets, the blurb tells readers first. They drew him from the blackness of space to save a tech galaxy.

Kane is a warrior mechanic and memory king of knowledgeless worlds there. Millions call him savior, but the ruling few call him maniac and heretic. A dragnet over the stars is thrown to stop his dangerous work. Twin suns boil the thin air of the Desert of One Thousand Mirages. Kane rides a silver skinned beast not bred for men across it.
64141-slay-ride:
Winston Marks wrote this science fiction tale for Planet Stories, where it ran in November 1953. Frane Lewis is a hired killer and space pirate who has stowed away on a small freighter. The ship's warm air, he thinks with pleasure, still smells of death.

Lewis has already shot three crewmen at their posts. He tricks the captain with a call about lunch and kills him as the door opens. The navigator is still in the room, so Lewis must fight him hand to hand. He binds the man with strips of his own uniform. The blurb promises a comic twist: the killer will end as the sweating victim of a piece of spaceman's underwear.
64330-where-the-gods-decide:
James McKimmey, junior, wrote this short story, printed in Planet Stories in July 1953. High over the wet plains and muggy jungles of Venus rests a temple of an ancient order. Green-faced Venusian men in gray capes and hoods walk its maze with webbed fingers hid in long sleeves. They circle a silver orb set in gold walls, pacing without a sound.

The orb is the Screece gem, held in their hands while a dozen minds probe Venus for cores of evil and purity. Some call the gem a fabulous diamond, some an emerald, some a ruby. Caine, the Earth man of the tale, guesses it is death itself. A giant black cat's scream breaks the rite.
64546-moonglade:
Moonglade is a novel by the anonymous author of The Martyrdom of an Empress, published by Harper and Brothers of New York and London in 1915. The writer, an officer of the French order of public instruction, published a shelf of court romances. A Doffed Coronet, Emerald and Ermine, and The Tribulations of a Princess stand in the same list.

The book opens with verses of its own: moonglade lying white upon the waters. Wind shouts from the western verge and herds the flying cloud rack. Glory breaks again through the rift, in the poem's stormy image. A dedication of three words, to A, with everlasting thoughts, guards the author's privacy. The novel belongs to the romantic school of courts and princesses that flourished before the Great War scattered its world. Harper issued it in February 1915, into a Europe already at war.
64548-by-scarlet-torch-and-blade:
Anthony Euwer wrote By Scarlet Torch and Blade, a book of verse put out by Putnam in 1923, with pictures drawn by Euwer himself. He gave the book to the memory of his sister Marian. Euwer had won readers with Rhymes of Our Valley and his cricket tales.

The title poem sings of a forest fire, a four-league stretch of woods in flame. One part roams the open spaces of Oregon: snow, rivers, caves, and high tops. A pageant of trees praises the sequoia, the Douglas fir, and the yellow pine. Light rhymes on cats, flies, and Mondays sit beside war rhymes of France. Euwer's verse is warm, plain, and fond of the wild Northwest he knew well.
65119-homecoming-horde:
Homecoming Horde, a science fiction tale by Robert Silverberg, ran in Imagination magazine in August 1958. Haverford knows from his radio contacts that he is the last man alive on Earth. His death is certain, for the enemy numbers trillions, the head note warns. The tale opens in a room sealed as tightly as he can make it.

He has checked the room for cracks and caulked the windows with care. Now he keeps constant guard against the alien invaders breaking through. The aliens came six days before the tale opens in his count. He picked up their ultimatum on his ham radio set at the time. Earthmen, the Lanthaii are coming, beware, was all that warning said to him. Last man dread and a siege of one fill this short tale.
65587-wild-nat-the-trooper-or-the-cedar-:
William Eyster wrote Wild Nat the Trooper, for Beadle and Adams. Its second title names the Cedar Swamp Brigade, from 1875. Contents open with Catherine Vale and the Tory spy. Going out to shear and returning shorn follows in the heads. The wolf and the lamb and Cedar Swamp itself come next.

The stoutest hearts once despaired, chapter one opens. The defeat of Gates and the overrunning of the Carolinas darkened it. Arnold's treachery weighed on the cause then. That darkest hour is the tale's chosen period. Two women sat by a fireside, it begins. Catherine Vale's face is moulded fine in the description that follows. Hot work ahead and an assault on a barn stand in contents. Captor, captive, and a happy end close it. Eyster gives the revolution a swamp brigade of its own.
65768-trouble-on-sun-side:
Tenneshaw wrote the short tale Trouble on Sun-Side for Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy, where it ran in October 1956. Mercury's burning edge sets the scene.

Jansen steps off his ship into the twilight zone, sweating at once under the huge sun. He came to Mercury to find one man, and the hunt looked easy. Back at the barracks he finds his luggage has been searched on the ship. That means trouble, and it means haste. As a hunter he is also the hunted. Bogs on the sun-side, a rating of twelve, and a laid-back work force fill out the strange post. The tale runs on heat and suspicion.
66029-two-slatterns-and-a-king-a-moral-i:
Edna St Vincent Millay wrote a short moral play first staged at Vassar College, printed at Cincinnati in 1921. The play belongs to the Stewart Kidd Modern Plays series, edited by Frank Shay for readers and small theatres. Millay was already known for Aria da Capo when this piece appeared.

The cast is small and pointed, with a king, Chance as the Vice, and two slatterns. Tidy is the false slattern and Slut the true one, a pairing that sets the play's game in motion. A prologue opens the action in the old interlude manner. Readers get a sharp, witty fable in verse and prose about seeming and being, small enough for a college stage and pointed enough to hold a modern reader.
66109-young-engineer-s-guide:
Young Engineer's Guide, a practical manual by J V Rohan of Racine, Wisconsin, was copyrighted in 1894. It sold at one dollar in cloth and a dollar and a quarter in leather. The book teaches the care and running of steam engines and boilers, above all the traction engines of farm and road. A long index and many rules and tables support the text.

Questions with answers on boilers open the instruction, and more sets prepare men for the engineer's licence. The parts of the engine are taken in order: cylinder, crosshead, crank, eccentrics, governor, injector, and valves. Firing with coal, wood, and straw is treated in turn. Banking fires, laying up an engine, crossing bridges, and the dangers of foaming and low water all get their pages. Hints to purchasers stand near the front.
66196-the-enchanted-crusade:
Reynard wrote this fantasy story, printed in Imagination magazine in April 1953. The blurb sets its stakes. Saracen blades held no fear for Godwin, but now he faces the sorcery of Mufaddal. The fate of the beautiful Ramizail, and of England, rests on the fight. The tale opens at daybreak in the desert. A dying man hears horses' hooves on sand and croaks for help in God's name.

The riders who find him joke over his state. One of them suffers from a breakfast of three pounds of figs. A woman's honeyed voice teases Godwin, the party's leader. Reynard mixes crusader adventure, magic, and pulp humor. The enchanted crusade of the title is a war fought with spells as much as swords.
66227-delaware-tom-or-the-traitor-guide:
Harry Hazard wrote Delaware Tom, or The Traitor Guide, a pocket novel issued by Beadle and Adams in New York. The book was entered for copyright in eighteen seventy two by Frank Starr and Company. Hazard had written The Heart Eater, The White Outlaw, Arkansas Jack, and Rattling Dick in the same line. Twelve chapters fill the tale. A wagon train of emigrants opens the action.

Chapter one, An Altercation, opens on a hot, sultry afternoon in the year fifty four. Wagons, driven stock, women, and children mark the train as emigrants. Horses and mules hang their heads, damp with sweat and fine sand, and scarce heed lash or cry. Later chapters bring a wild race, a forlorn hope, and Delaware Tom himself. Tom Maxwell turns Indian, a tangled trail follows, and a man is bound to the stake. Dime novel readers got fast frontier peril.
66351-slaves-to-the-metal-horde:
Slaves to the Metal Horde is a science fiction story by Milton Lesser, printed in Imagination in June 1954. Johnny Hope knew the robot armies were made to serve man, the head note says. War and plague destroyed civilization, and left humans their slaves.

Johnny backs toward a dry creek bed, unarmed, as men close in a half circle. He begs leave to bury some dead and then go in peace. Mayor DeReggio brandishes a club made from a rifle stock. The faces around Johnny are stamped with hostility from one mold. His plea to bury the dead meets a hard refusal. Readers get a post ruin tale of men under their own machines.
66432-and-all-the-girls-were-nude:
And All the Girls Were Nude, a short tale by Richard Magruder, ran in Imagination in December 1954. Nathanial Evergood, a bookkeeper, is so dull and reserved that no coworker has ever shared a drink or lunch with him. None has seen inside his rooms. The blurb gives the hook: the old man has a secret passion for pretty girls and invents a camera lens for special effects.

The narrator warns that looks deceive and things are not as they seem. Evergood's dull front hides a sly, hidden life that he guards with care. Magruder builds a dark comic tale on the gap between a tame public face and a wild private urge, with the lens as the tool that may bare both.
66592-the-last-duchess-of-belgarde:
Molly Seawell's The Last Duchess of Belgarde was published by Appleton in 1908 and given to the dear memory of Henrietta. A cast list heads the book: Trimousette, the Countess and Count Victor of Floramour, Fernand, Duke of Belgarde, Madame de Valencay, Robespierre, the Vicomte d'Aronda, and Madame Elizabeth. The Revolution is plainly on its way.

Chapter one sits Trimousette in the green garden of her grandmother, the Countess of Floramour, stitching at her tambour frame with an open volume of Ronsard in her lap. She is wondering when she is to be married, and to whom. The match is being arranged, but nobody has given her any particulars. A pale, quiet girl with tragic black eyes, in a linen gown and hat, she might pass for a shepherdess of Arcady. The contents run through a present from the Duke, an earthquake, and Citizeness Belgarde.
66600-short-story-writing-an-art-or-a-tr:
N Bryllion Fagin wrote Short Story Writing: An Art or a Trade, issued in New York in nineteen twenty-three. Fagin was dean of a school of literary arts in Washington. He also taught short story writing at the University of Maryland. Thomas Seltzer published his course in book form.

Music gives his chapters their names: overture at the start and finale near the end. Between them he treats action and a thing he calls O Henryism. The moving pictures get a chapter as a new rival and market. One chapter, named with a German word for forbidden, lists what not to do. False endings, form, and effect round out a working writer's guide.
66658-australasia-triumphant-with-the-au:
A St John Adcock wrote Australasia Triumphant, with the Australians and New Zealanders in the Great War on land and sea. Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company first published it at London in January 1916, with thirty-six illustrations. The battered Emden, gone ashore on Cocos Island, fronts the book. A line from Tennyson heads the title: strong mother of a lion line, be proud of these strong sons of thine.

In his note Adcock owns it is too soon to tell the whole story at large. Much remains hidden for military reasons. He has collated the documents at hand into one connected narrative. He draws on official papers and on the dispatches of Sir Ian Hamilton. The reports of correspondents and the speeches of public men add their share. Letters and talks with wounded Anzacs in London complete his sources.
66746-brief-guide:
Brief Guide is a short hand book of the National Gallery of Art at Washington: its past and its works. Its first lines lay down its ground. The house, it says, is the prize of all the folk of the free states, set up by a vote of the law house and kept by state funds.

Its board, it tells, is made of four state men by right of post and five plain folk. The chief judge of the land chairs that board. By their rule the house gathers and keeps paints, carve works, and works on paper, the best of the stock of America and Europe. State funds run its days, but its works all come as gifts of plain folk. One great trust paid for its first hall.
66857-a-prevaricated-parade:
