W C Tuttle wrote this western tale, told in the voice of a cowhand who works for old man Whittaker. Tuttle had written Clean Crazy and Monkeying with Ancestors. A committee of four meets the night before in the town of Paradise: the teller, Scenery Sims, Hank Padden, and Whittaker himself. Their charge is to study the Fourth of July and judge whether it merits a celebration.

Hank reads the close of the Declaration aloud from a book, finger on the place. Whittaker rules that what they have heard is sufficient and plenty. Scenery backs the day, swearing he never cared for kings except in jack-pots. The vote is one-sided, and the tale rolls toward the parade of its title, with tall talk all the way.
67022-lyrics-legends-of-christmas-tide:
Lyrics and Legends of Christmas Tide, by Clinton Scollard, was printed at Clinton, New York, in 1906 in a second, enlarged edition. The first edition came in October 1904. Scollard writes short poems and tale poems for the Christmas season.

The list opens with A Bell, Christmas Elves, and The Christmas Angel. Nazareth Town and a Christmas masque follow. Other pieces name the Christmas minstrels, a Twelfth Night song, and Yule at Thengelfor. Ballads treat the eve of Yule, the hanging of the holly, and the maid of Bethlehem. Later poems name the three kings, the wise men, and the star of Bethlehem. A knight Christmas and a ballad of Kirkland Hills close the mid list. Verse fans get a full garland of Yule song and lore.
67268-the-life-of-jesus-christ-for-the-y:
William Hole painted a gallery of eighty paintings on the life of Jesus Christ, and this fourth volume holds his life in art for the young. A front plate shows Jesus brought before Pilate in the hall of judgment at dawn. Hole's own note walks the reader through the scene stone by stone.

He tells how the Romans oft set their courts in the open air, by gate, market, or road, so all could see and hear. Herod's palace, he shows, had a raised stone platform built for the work, with the judge's chair at its heart. Young readers get the Gospel tale in rich pictures with clear, learned notes.
67269-against-the-tide:
Against the Tide is a novel by Henry Bedford-Jones, writing as John Wycliffe. Dodd, Mead published it in New York in 1924. The contents divide the tale into three books. Each book carries a biblical motto. The first speaks of the hidden things of dishonesty.

The story opens at a wedding in Evansville, Indiana. The old Deming mansion blazes with light at noon. Thunder clouds brood over the Ohio river. Dorothy Deming is to marry Reese Armstrong that day. The best man, Macgowan, draws the bride aside. He speaks wonders of the groom to her eager ears. The house mirrors the city itself. Evansville borders both north and south, the narrator notes.
67605-the-oak-shade:
The Oak Shade, or Records of a Village Literary Association, is a set of tales and essays. A small town club made them, and one hand shaped the book. It came out at Philadelphia in the mid eighteen fifties. Its rights were set in law that year for its maker. A print house in the same street struck its pages.

Its parts open with a tale of a Dutch skin flint. Then come a plea for calm in our wants and a sick mum. A sly piece in praise of the lie joins them. A man of the old craft with a charm funnel fills the next part. The grace of a well tilled heart and the dream of a loafer close the set.
67951-my-secret-service-vienna-sophia-co:
The author of My Secret Service hides behind the name of the man who dined with the Kaiser. Doran published the book at New York in 1916, and it is dedicated to Lord Northcliffe. The catalog title is a scrap of his itinerary: Nish, Belgrade, Asia Minor, and more.

His contents promise the inside of wartime spying. The German spy system, three journeys, and work as a laborer at Krupp's great gun works all come in the first chapter. He traveled, he says, in chocolate, as a salesman spy. Vienna in war time follows: a subdued city, short of food, hating the English. Then come Sofia, Constantinople, and the Balkan capitals. Spy memoirs flooded the market in the war years, and this one sells the glamour of the game by a man who claims to have sat at the Kaiser's own table.
68056-thoughts-upon-the-african-slave-tr:
John Newton wrote this pamphlet against the African slave trade, printed in London in 1788 and sold for one shilling. Newton was rector of St Mary Woolnoth. Any profit went to the society that backed Sunday schools across England. A text from Matthew heads the title: do to men as you would have them do to you.

Newton writes of the trade that tore fellow creatures from their homes to stock the West India islands and, once, the American colonies. He notes that able pens had cast much light on the trade and that men of weight now pressed for its end. His hope is plain: that this stain on the national name will soon be wiped away.
68324-the-151st-field-artillery-brigade:
The 151st Field Artillery Brigade is a unit history by Richard Russell, published at Boston in 1919. Russell dedicates it to his old comrades and thanks the wife of General McNair and three officers for facts. The catalog title here is only the last word; the head gives the full name.

The tale opens at Camp Devens in Massachusetts in the fall of 1917. Men from every walk of life thronged the new camps after America declared war that April. Russell says the draft built a great democratic army from raw men. The brigade was formed from the 301st, 302nd, and 303rd regiments. Readers get a fresh, proud record of a New England gun brigade.
68373-the-gently-orbiting-blonde:
John Victor Peterson wrote a comic science fiction tale that ran in Infinity in April 1957, drawn by Engle. Its head note warns that antigravity may be hard to handle, but a woman scorned is harder. The narrator fears his wife Helene will let a secret slip to her bridge friends. Their living room became the training station for Space Satellite One.

Gladys, the gently orbiting blonde, is at the center of the facts he guards. On his wedding night he carried Helene across the threshold, then dashed to his basement lab. A glance at a sun chandelier had reminded him of the project. He forgot to kiss her first, a lapse he now regrets.
68829-mistake-inside:
James Blish wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Startling Stories in March 1948. Its scene is England two hundred years before bomb craters marked the landscape. Coffee houses still take precedence over the pub. A fire roars, and smoke from long clay churchwarden pipes makes a blue haze. Cheerful talk struggles through it.

The host stands in the doorway, fat hands on hips, surveying the scene. Someone invisible in the fog drinks a slurred, uproarious toast. A glass slams into the fireplace, its brandy coated fragments making small blue flames. Blish, later famous for Cities in Flight, began in the pulp magazines. The tale's title promises an identity trick.
69119-an-outlaw-s-pledge-or-the-raid-on-:
An Outlaw's Pledge, or The Raid on the Old Stockade, is the first number of the American Indian Weekly, by Colonel Spencer Dair, copyrighted in 1910 in Cleveland, Ohio. Its hero, Red Rogers, is a daredevil outlaw who breaks jail, killing four men, to keep a pledge made to a dying member of his gang.

Rose Landon, daughter of the man to whom the pledge was made, helps him escape and rides with him into the Bad Lands. Troopers, scouts, and a half-breed tracker named Alkali chase them to the old stockade. The cast list at the front gives away the shapes of the plot, as dime novels liked to do. It is fast, bloody, pulp Western fare of its day.
69375-the-automobile-owner-s-guide:
The Automobile Owner's Guide is a manual by Frank Scholl, issued by Appleton in 1920. It teaches owners how their cars work and how to keep them. The contents begin with the history of the gasoline engine. Buying a new or used car is treated next. Driving rules for city and country follow. What to do in an accident is also covered.

Engine parts fill the first full chapter. Valves and their grinding take the second. The working of a four-cycle engine is then explained. Six, eight, and twelve-cylinder engines are compared. The Knight sleeve-valve engine gets its own notice. Oils, greases, and their systems are treated in detail. Carburetion follows with named models of the day. Such guides served the first mass age of motoring. Owners were their own mechanics then.
6954-aikenside:
Mary Holmes opens Aikenside with an examining committee and a schoolgirl named Madeline Clyde, whose examination sets the story in motion. Grandpa Markham, a convalescence, a drive, and shadowings of what was to be follow, before a decision carries Maddy to Aikenside itself. Guy at home, a generous letter, Uncle Joseph, and holidays with Maddy and Lucy fill the middle chapters.

The later chapter titles trace womanhood, a burden that grows heavier, life at the cottage, and the interval before a marriage. Holmes, author of Lena Rivers and Tempest and Sunshine, writes a domestic tale of a girl's trials and growth. The novel moves from schoolroom to household, with duty, love, and patience as its steady themes.
69973-ingleside:
Madeline Leslie wrote Ingleside as a set of true scenes meant to prove one point: the misery of life without Christ, and the peace of life with him. Hodder and Stoughton printed this second edition in London. Leslie says the scenes are drawn from real life, falling under her own eye or told to her by friends who vouched for their truth.

Marion Howard, a young lady who gives her time and money to the poor, stands at the heart of the book. Around her sit the eccentric Mister Regy and poor Esther in her sorrows. A brother and sister from a foreign land lie in the same Home for the Sick, unknown to each other. Leslie had won readers with Tim the Scissors-Grinder, and she sends this book on the same errand of winning souls.
69974-fashion-parade:
Fashion Parade, Star Book number 189 of the American Thread Company, gives knit and crochet patterns. Its cover line promises patterns for him and her in one booklet. The price on the cover is twenty nine cents for the book. A jade suit with crocheted trim stands pictured in colour on the front.

A knitted jacket leads the patterns inside, in small, medium, and large sizes. Dawn knitting worsted from the thread company is the yarn named for the work. Four to five skeins of jade, needles, a hook, and ribbon make the list. Gauge runs nine stitches to two inches and six rows to one inch. Home knitters of the booklet era got a full wardrobe set in these pages.
70217-bruggil-s-bride:
Robert Young wrote "Bruggil's Bride," a science fiction story printed in Fantastic Universe in March 1960. Its bride is not born but built. She came off the production line of Androids, Incorporated, in September of the year 2241.

She stands five feet seven, weighs one hundred thirty-five pounds, and has flaxen hair and pale blue eyes. Her batteries are guaranteed for ten years. Her singing tapes are authentic Kirsten Flagstad, the great Wagner soprano. Shipped to New York, she opens the season in the best Tristan ever, say the die hard Wagner fans. Then she is switched off and stored with the rest of the cast. Young builds his tale on that cold shelf: what is owed to a singer who is also a machine.
71305-the-farmer-s-bride:
Charlotte Mew, an English poet, published The Farmer's Bride in a first form in 1916 and added eleven new poems for this edition of 1921. The Poetry Bookshop in London issued the book. Mew wrote short, intense poems, often in the voices of lonely country folk, and her fame grew slowly.

The title poem speaks in a farmer's voice about his bride, a shy girl who fears love and all things human. Her smile went out, he says, till she seemed more a frightened fay than a woman, and one night in the fall she ran away. The hunt for her, and what follows, gives the poem its ache. Mew's work, spare and strange, now holds a high place in modern poetry.
71939-gratitude:
Roy Norton wrote Gratitude, first of a series about the Competents. The Competents work a claim in Alaska in Norton's tales. The season ended as this story opens for the partners. They throw their last shovelfuls of dirt. Good-by is said to the homely cabin on the mountainside.

Shakespeare George found a verse in a magazine. He framed it above his bunk with care. The gratitude of men had oftener left him mourning, it ran. His partners smiled at the verse above his bunk. He mangled the lines whenever he tried to quote them aloud. He named Laughing Jim in that connection. Jim was bad through and through, without cause for mistake. Reckless charm covered half his misdeeds. No one remembers when he arrived in Marook, the tale adds. Norton gives the gold camp a study of thanks unthanked.
72433-proper-pride:
Proper Pride is a novel in three volumes, printed in London by Tinsley Brothers in 1882. No author is named on the title page. The tale opens far from home, in Malta, where a bright blue sky and a calm sea frame the busy streets of Valetta in December.

Two young officers, Cox and Brown, smoke outside a shop and grouse about the lack of sport on the isle. The contents point on to Alice Saville, Looton Park, a thunderbolt, and a scheme by Mrs Mayhew. Later heads name Wessex Gardens and a part called Eastward Ho. The book gives a full picture of garrison life, town talk, and the pull of home.
72513-the-slave-trade:
Theodore Jervey wrote The Slave Trade: Slavery and Color, published at Columbia, South Carolina, in 1925 by the State Company. A frontispiece shows Wade Hampton in 1889, quoted on the diffusion of the Negroes: it would be the salvation of the future. Jervey dedicated the book to Salley of the state historical commission. An excerpt had appeared in 1913.

Jervey, a Charleston newspaper man, writes the history of the African slave trade and of slavery in America from a South Carolina white man's standpoint of 1925. The introductory pages set out to correct, as he sees it, the errors of abolitionist history. Modern readers use the book as evidence of its own time's memory of slavery. Its facts and its frame must be read together and warily. It is a document of the Lost Cause in its scholarly dress.
72602-a-muramasa-blade:
A Muramasa Blade is a story of feudalism in old Japan by Louis Wertheimber. Ticknor of Boston put the book out in the year 1887 from Boston. Wertheimber held the rights from 1886 and gives it to his sister Emilie. The sword is the soul of the samurai stands as its motto. Five engravings on copper by a young Japanese artist fill the book.

Nakamura Munehiro of Tokio made the drawings and the engravings both. The preface calls the tale original, writ near a Japanese point of view. Turned into Japanese, it might pass for a native street tale, he holds. No incident stands strained and no character overdrawn by that measure. All historical allusions stand strictly true, culled from native chronicles with care. Wertheimber kept that treatment against the advice of literary friends. He hoped to bring the story closer to its own land's canons.
72999-the-suspicions-of-ermengarde:
Maxwell Gray, the pen name of Mary Gleed Tuttiett, published The Suspicions of Ermengarde with John Long in 1908. The novel opens in a pea-soup fog over Kensington Gardens. Ermengarde, sunk in a Chesterfield by the fire, finds the true simile for fog in the haunting horror of unpaid bills. The butcher's bill is enormous, and her husband Arthur takes such bills as coolly as the church collection. Chapter titles carry the pair from The Little Rift to the Train de Luxe and The Azure Shore.

The middle chapters move through the Casino, its gardens, and a sapphire necklace that returns late in the book. Gray had earlier written The Silence of Dean Maitland and The Reproach of Annesley. A Goethe epigraph in German fronts the title page. The story is a society novel of money worries behind a polished surface.
73250-there-is-a-tide:
J C Snaith wrote There Is a Tide, issued by D Appleton and Company in New York in MCMXXIV, with a copyright of nineteen twenty four. Snaith had earlier written Araminta, The Van Roon, The Sailor, and The Undefeated. A slight, pretty girl rides a boat express into England at the start. To her, all is new and odd. Her face is quick to show its feelings.

England strikes the girl as small in scale next to the land she came from. Neat small acres remind her of Noah ark toys. Trim farmsteads, hedgerows, and small villages with moss grown church towers peer through damp mist. By her side sits a cheap, battered grip, and a mate bag rides in the rack. Her bags have a second rate air, though her clothes are not bad. A tale of a stranger finding her tide in England follows.
73468-code:
Code, by Paul, tells the story of a criminal ship and a warning. No title page stands in this text; the tale opens at once. A queer hush hangs over the ship Cora. She lies at Beverstock, a small British port near Liverpool. Battered and dirty, she keeps a foreign register. Grim faced men go about their work without a word. A man in soiled dungarees appears at the gangway, nobody knows how. The stout chief engineer points out a tall figure climbing the gangway: Captain Bain.

Talk is barred on deck in port, the captain says, and takes Drake below. Who sent you, he asks. Dip Laplace, Drake answers, and hands over a crumpled wad of paper. Bain holds it to the light from the grimy port. Paul writes dockside crime in a hard, quiet style.
73524-the-butterfly-guide:
William Holland, director of the Carnegie Museum, wrote The Butterfly Guide in 1915 as a pocket manual for naming the commoner butterflies of the United States and Canada. The book holds 295 coloured figures showing 255 species and forms. Holland dedicated it to the Boy Scouts of America. Its aim is plain: a boy or girl in a field should be able to name what they have caught.

The opening chapters place butterflies in the animal kingdom and explain the jointed body plan of their group. Holland writes in clear words, as in his larger Butterfly Book, but keeps this volume small enough for a coat pocket. Each kind then gets its marks, range, and habits in brief form. For its day, the guide put sound museum knowledge into the hands of campers and young collectors at a low price.
7362-life-at-high-tide:
Harper's Novelettes series gathers ten short stories by different American writers, chosen by editors William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden. Margaret Deland, Anne O'Hagan, Grace Ellery Channing, and Mary Tracy Earle are among the contributors. All the stories had appeared in magazines within the previous five years, at a time when the American short story was coming into its own.

The editors' preface gives the book its theme. Each story turns on a critical moment in one life, or sometimes two, that reveals character rather than bringing fortune or ruin. A widow's pension, a guarded trust, and a yearly gift all test ordinary people under modern strain. Through those plain moments, the stories find a quiet idealism that never announces itself.
73679-the-metal-horde:
The Metal Horde, a science fiction story by John Campbell, imagines machines that learn to think. The magazine's editor sets the scene: calculating machines and robots grow yearly, and seismographs already find distant earthquakes. Machines might one day solve problems beyond our scientists, he muses. They might even state their own problems and work them out, a machine with almost a working brain.

Campbell takes that thought and runs with it into war among the planets. The tale's end credits one brilliant mind with making possible the defeat of the Sirians. A warning bought the precious hours his work on a deactivating field required. Without it, millions more would have died before escaping from Mars. Campbell, who wrote as a young man of science, packs the story with bold physics. It is early work from a writer who later shaped the whole field as an editor.
74374-the-20-mule-team-brigade:
The Twenty-Mule-Team Brigade is a story in jingles for the Pacific Coast Borax Company. Peter Newell drew the pictures for the small verse book of fun. Otis Kean held the rights in the year 1904 in New York. Twenty mules enlist as a band to fight the King of Dirt. Each warrior bears a gun charged with pure borax of the brand.

Their captain leads them first to the kitchen to begin the fight. Food is cooked there, so the room should be clean and bright. The Battle of Dish Pan Hill opens the war on grime in earnest. Tarnished tinware stands as a fort held by vicious dirty imps. Volleys of borax powder sweep the fort and rattle pot and pan. The imps drop their arms and run till all stands clean and bright. Tinware shines like burnished gold, or burnished tin, the verse corrects.
74522-my-hildegarde: My Hildegarde, by Rathborne, survives in this copy as the front matter of Street and Smith's Eagle Series number 329. The series is a New York line of popular fiction with elegant coloured covers. The publisher presents it as the pioneer line of copyright novels, unrivalled in sales and contents, its authors the foremost men and women of their time. The catalogue around the novel lists neighbouring numbers by Mary Holmes, Laura Jean Libbey, Charles Garvice, and May Agnes Fleming.
75017-look-on-the-sunny-side:
Ruth Lamb wrote Look on the Sunny Side, and Other Sketches, for the Religious Tract Society in London. Lamb also wrote Thoughtful Joe and Katie Brightside, tales for the young of the same sunny school. A front picture carries the text that is the book's rule, to be careful for nothing, but in everything by prayer to make requests known unto God.

Her sketches take children and working folk through small troubles toward cheer and trust. Sickness, poverty, and temper get met with faith and a smile, in the tract society manner. Such books filled Sunday school prize shelves for two generations. Readers get gentle Victorian sketches, meant to warm a child's heart toward patience and prayer.
75019-code:
Pierce, who wrote Sweet Water, tells this Prohibition sea story. A revered tradition of the sea, the headnote warns, may be confused with a scuttlebutt rumor. The rum runner Crayton has lain offshore a month, waiting to land whisky bottled in Scotland, labeled for the liners and officers' messes. Captain McNulty means to keep it from all of them, if he can elude the Coast Guard.

The cutter Chinook steams past, Captain Wold on the bridge. Wold knows the Crayton and the tricks in the book, and can neither be deceived nor bought. A blow is coming, and Pritt, who owns ship and cargo, suggests running in while the cutter shelters. McNulty refuses: a sailor is a sailor first, and there are codes a sailor never forgets, beginning with saving human lives and sailing your ship. Two captains of the old school will meet in the storm.
75039-a-new-discovery-for-finding-the-lo:
William Hobbs offered a new discovery for finding the longitude in a pamphlet printed at London and sold for six pence. The former impression was printed July 12, 1714. Hobbs humbly submits his plan to the lords appointed by the late act of Parliament for hearing proposals on the longitude. If the true hour and minute at the place of departure and at the place arrived can both be had, he begins, the difference of longitude follows truly.

For this purpose a spring movement of his design is proposed, to effect the same even to the tenth of a minute of time. If an error of a minute happens in practice, it must come from the air, not from any defect in his rules, he holds. The movement needs winding once in twenty six or twenty seven days. Crank or prophet, Hobbs speaks for a crowd of projectors.
75052-a-new-account-of-guinea-and-the-sl:
A New Account of Guinea and the Slave-Trade was printed in 1754 and gives a British view of the West African coast before 1750. The text keeps the old spelling and dates of the first edition, with a map running from the Senegal River to Cape Lopez. It deals with the Guinea coast, its kingdoms, its trade, and the traffic in enslaved people.

The book opens with the conquest of the kingdom of Whydah by the king of Dahomey. It goes on to describe local rule, markets, religion, and the forts and ships of the slave trade. Modern readers will find parts of it harsh and cold, since it treats human lives as goods. Yet it is a raw first-hand source on a trade that shaped three continents.
75098-hooking-a-sky-ride:
Hooking a Sky Ride is a short tale by Dan Morrissey, told in the first person by a boy of thirteen. He lives on a farm just outside San Antonio, Texas, in the days of the great war camps. A wire fence and a dirt road part his home from an army flight field.

A second field lies two miles off, and the whole town is ringed with camps and flight grounds. Planes hang thick as crows in the sky from dawn to dark. With his younger brother, the boy watches the field across the road with a craze that beats all boy tales of crime and the wild west. They talk of planes, read of planes, and dream of planes at night.
75494-the-workwoman-s-guide:
A Lady wrote The Workwoman's Guide in 1838. Simpkin, Marshall and Company issued it at London. Thomas Evans printed it at Birmingham. Its motto reads Method Shortens Labour. The frontispiece quotes Proverbs on the good wife. She stretches her hand to the poor, it says.

The guide teaches the untaught to cut out clothes. Home-made wear of all kinds fills its lessons. Upholstery gets full treatment too. Straw platting and bonnet making stand in the list. Knitting rounds out the home crafts taught. The author hopes to serve women of every rank, she writes. Duty or taste sets them to such work, she notes. A plain how-to book of its day, the guide preserves the cut and stitch of dress before the sewing machine ruled.
76156-altitude:
Leland Jamieson wrote Altitude, a short tale of free-balloon flight drawn from life in the army air service. Captain Conway is an expert on free balloons, and his ship, the Marie IV, is the love of his life in the air. Men who know her feats speak of the great silver sphere by name, as if she were a person.

In the hangar at dawn, the balloon tugs at her sandbags as a chill breeze sways her. Kisner, the aide who has flown with Conway on many past trips, works beside him in the basket. Talk in the tale turns on altitude records and on who shall fly this one. The tale prizes exact detail of gear, wind, and nerve.
77115-an-ice-cream-laboratory-guide:
Fisk and Ellenberger, teachers of dairy industry at Cornell University, wrote An Ice Cream Laboratory Guide for students. Orange Judd Company issued the book at New York in 1917. Its pages lay out the gear of the ice cream laboratory, the making of a standard mix, and the testing of ice cream for fat. Twenty-four exercises lead the student step by step, from a first look at the machines through the freezing of plain, fruit, nut, and custard ice creams.

Later work treats bricks and fancy moulded creams, parfaits, puddings, ices, sherbets, punches, and mousse. A score card for judging ice cream stands near the end, and the last exercises test how fat, binders, and milk solids change the end product. The guide shows how the making of a treat had become a science taught in college rooms.
77801-willie-and-lucy-at-the-sea-side:
Agnes Giberne, signing only A G, takes two small children to the sea in a tale for the very young. The Religious Tract Society issued it at London. William Clowes and Sons printed it.

Willie Gray wakes early on the great day. Nurse teases him for sleeping when Lucy is already dressed. He kneels for his morning prayers, said slowly and gravely as he was taught. Nine short chapters carry the holiday. The journey, the first sight of the sea, and spades and sand come first. A donkey ride and a rainy day follow. Rough weather and a row on the water close it. Giberne wrote many such gentle books. This one pairs a child's joy with small lessons on care and prayer.
77878-history-of-the-woman-s-temperance-:
Annie Wittenmyer wrote a history of the Woman's Temperance Crusade, entered for copyright in 1882. Wittenmyer was the first president of the Woman's National Christian Temperance Union. Her book calls itself a complete official history of the uprising of Christian women against the liquor traffic. That uprising grew into the gospel temperance movement.

Women tell much of the story in their own words. They marched into saloons and gambling dens, knelt in the snow to pray, and faced howling mobs. Some went to prison. Scenes in churches and homes sit beside scenes in the streets. Wittenmyer, who also wrote Woman's Work for Jesus, dedicates the book to those women and their union.
7806-a-boy-s-ride:
Gulielma Zollinger's A Boy's Ride, pictured by Fanny M. Chambers, opens in late May 1209 in the north of England, a land of vast forests where ash trees still unfold buds. A chilly east wind blows as a lad rides a bridle path a few miles southwest of York, into a very different England.

Pictures promise cries of yield in the king's name, shelter within walls, a lady's welcome, an oak-tree hiding place, a little spy, reeds snatched in flight, and a priest's disguise. Through Humphrey and Hugo's ride, the book gives young readers a medieval adventure of loyalty, danger, and quick wits.
78187-the-quarterly-of-the-oregon-histor:
The Quarterly of the Oregon Historical Society for December 1900 is volume one, number four. It is styled the Oregon Trail number. The society had been founded two years before. Young leads with a long essay on the trail. Jesse Applegate tells of a day with the cow column of 1843. A tribute to the ox whip follows. Simpson writes of the pioneers' camp fires.

Joaquin Miller gives two poems on the plains. Documents of the 1843 emigration close the number. It cost thirty-five cents, or a dollar a year. Members received it free with their dues. Such quarterlies saved the pioneers' own words. Applegate's day-by-day account is now famous. The issue is a foundation stone of Oregon history.
78197-tricks-of-the-trade:
Squire wrote Tricks of the Trade, a book of essays published at London by Martin Secker. The catalog title keeps only the last word. Squire, a poet and editor, dedicates the essays to Robert Lynd, calling them final essays in a not wholly admirable art. His other works, poems and imaginary speeches, fill the front list.

The contents open with How They Do It, a series on fellow writers, beginning with Belloc. Squire explains the tricks by which authors and editors work their effects, with the insider's malice and affection. The trade of the title is writing itself, and its tricks are style, timing, and persona. Literary London of the nineteen twenties is the setting. The book is a craftsman's tour of his own workshop.
7830-domestic-pleasures-or-the-happy-fir:
F. B. Vaux's Domestic Pleasures, or The Happy Fire-Side, offers talks on home happiness, opening with Cowper's lines on domestic bliss as the one joy of paradise to survive the fall. A frontispiece shows Eddystone Lighthouse as built by Lord Bywater in 1759, a mark of steady light.

In an address to young readers, Vaux recalls asking as a child whether a new book was true, since truth gave a volume new value. The children pictured here, she insists, are real. Through fireside talks, the book praises virtue nursed at home, where kindness, order, and faith grow.
78330-dressed-vegetables-a-la-mode:
Dressed Vegetables À La Mode is a cookery book by Mrs de Salis, issued by Longmans in 1900. In her preface, Harriet A. In her preface, Harriet De Salis says public demand brought her back to extend the series to vegetables.

The recipes give each dish a French name and exact quantities. American yams are sliced, trimmed oval and simmered in butter with nutmeg, then sauced with cream, castor sugar and lemon juice. Artichokes à la Barigoule are stuffed with a veal and suet forcemeat, topped with bacon and braised. The style is Edwardian fine cooking in miniature: rich, precise and unembarrassed by butter.
78372-the-crime-code:
The Crime Code, a mystery novel by William Le Queux, author of Poison Shadows, was published in New York in 1928 by Macaulay. In England the book appeared as Double Nought. Thirty chapters run from Threads of Iron through The Six Circles and a shop-window clue to a dark house and the conclusion. A heroine named Illona stands at the plot's center.

Chapter one begs the reader's pardon. The narrator owns his many shortcomings and denies any wish to pose as a hero. From the normal life of a young man about London, he says, one minute of ill fortune plunged him into doubt and misery. Hunted as a criminal, he kept his liberty by ruses. Le Queux writes his usual swift tale of secret crime across Europe.
78459-a-military-interlude:
A Military Interlude is a story of the American Revolution by Ernest Haycox, the Western writer. It is set in the snow at Valley Forge, in the bitter January of the army's suffering. Alva Jukes, a brash, hard-tempered soldier, stands in a hut doorway and looks at the white faces on the wretched pallets.

Jukes mocks the voice of a disliked colonel, asking the men what they have for supper, breakfast, and dinner. Fire-cake and water, comes the chorus each time. Outside, men drag a wood cart by rope while an officer rides past wrapped in a counterpane. Haycox writes the scene with grim humour and pity. The tale honours the common soldiers who starved and held on.
78581-partners-of-the-tide:
Joseph Lincoln wrote Partners of the Tide, a Cape Cod novel with a copyright of 1905, printed in New York. Lincoln had made his name with Cap'n Eri, another tale of the Cape. A front plate quotes a man who never dreamed he would come to be skipper of a coal hod, which sets the book's mix of pride and salt humor.

The tale opens at the Orham stage station, where Clark warms his boots at the stove and teases a boy at the lunch counter. Chapters follow the Thomas Doane, a lumber schooner, and the anchor of the Liberty. Wrecking and waltzing, a subscription ball, a burglar, and a captain's gamble fill the middle. Thanksgiving and a debt paid close a warm tale of shore folk.
78585-50-years-at-ringside:
Nat Fleischer, founder of The Ring magazine, wrote this memoir of fifty years at ringside, copyrighted in 1958. He calls himself a sports romanticist. For him the annals of the ring have no equal in appeal: two men, alone, tested for courage, skill, and stamina.

The contents run from his boyhood and reporter days to an interview with Roosevelt. Books follow on Jack Johnson and boxing's harlequin, on Tex Rickard and Uncle Mike Jacobs, and on adventures abroad. Donnybrooks, laughs, and oddities season the middle. The birth of The Ring and a summing up close it. Fleischer knew nearly every champion of his half century and tells their stories from his seat.
78588-personal-reminiscences-of-a-great-:
Josephine Butler wrote Personal Reminiscences of a Great Crusade, her own account of the campaign against the state regulation of vice. This new edition was printed at London in 1910. She dedicated it to the memory of Sir James Stansfeld, her parliamentary ally. A prefatory note points readers to the memoir of her edited by the Johnsons.

James Stuart's words there describe her. She was at home in every class of society. She was very beautiful and of a gracious presence, a good painter, and an extremely good musician. She was a bold rider, deeply in earnest, yet at times charmingly gay. The crusade fought the Contagious Diseases Acts and their continental sisters for forty years, and Butler's reminiscences are its classic history from inside.
78615-the-tide:
Mildred Cram writes a young widow's spring in The Tide, a Borzoi novel from Alfred A Knopf of New York, published in October 1924. A list of recent Borzoi novels fronts the book, naming Mary Borden, Carl Van Vechten, and Joseph Hergesheimer. Cram dedicates the book to her husband.

The tale opens as Lilah closes the apartment door after her father's funeral, pulling off her mourning veil with relief. She appraises the library he filled with books brought from Ohio to his Columbia professorship, and wants a bonfire of its sanctified ugliness. Something within her says she is free, and this is the beginning.
7887-fortitude:
Hugh Walpole's Fortitude, dedicated to Charles Maude, follows Peter Westcott from Scaw House through London life. Book one opens with an introduction to courage, a family sitting up for Peter, the dark shop of Zachary Tan, and Dawson's as a gate first of life, then of hell.

Later books move to a bookshop, Reuben Hallard, royal personages coming, a narrow street, and the roundabout at 72 Cheyne Walk, where success, an heir's birth, and wild men test Peter. Through fog in Charing Cross Road and rooms at Brockett's, Walpole traces how a boy holds fast.
79097-arcadian-adelaide:
Thistle Anderson, in private life Mrs Herbert Fisher, wrote Arcadian Adelaide, printed at Adelaide in 1905 by the Modern Printing Company. She dedicates the book to any kindred spirit whom duty compels to live in Adelaide, and who suffers there as the writer suffers. The tone is set before the first chapter.

In her foreword Anderson wonders whether any Adelaide reader will deign to glance through her pages. The book is a satire on the South Australian capital by a woman plainly bored and provoked by it. Arcadian, in her mouth, is a joke at the city's expense. Local readers took such books as an insult or a tonic, depending on taste. It preserves the voice of a clever outsider in a proud young city.
79442-the-man-that-rum-made:
The Man That Rum Made gathers temperance lessons and stories for the home circle, printed at Nashville in 1912. White and Avery-Stuttle edited the set for the Southern Publishing Association, a Seventh-day Adventist house. Its motto comes from Paul: every man that strives for the mastery is temperate in all things.

A picture story tells how rum made its victim, and another shows the effects of alcohol in panels. Old Joe the Drunkard runs to six chapters, and pieces tell of John Gough, the great temperance orator, and of the evils of the major's cigar. Tobacco gets its own warning from Talmage. The book is Sunday-school artillery against drink, aimed at the young.
79495-an-essay-on-the-slave-trade:
An Essay on the Slave Trade was printed in London in 1788, when Britain was debating whether to end the trade in enslaved Africans. The unnamed writer praises a clergyman's pamphlet that proposed terms both sides might weigh. He argues that lessons for ending the African trade can be found in how Europe once ended its own trade in human beings.

To make that case, he traces slavery in early Europe, where, he says, people were the main stock in trade and beaten prisoners were sold abroad. He names old slave markets at Rome, Bristol, and elsewhere, and translates an Icelandic account of one market near Gothenburg. His hope is that trade, farming, and Christian teaching will in time end the buying and selling of people.
79684-a-bear-raising-ride:
A Bear Raising Ride is a western tale by Ray Humphreys. Whiskers Graham, senior driver for the Wells Fancher Stage Company on the Como to Fairplay run, shrinks back from the Como barn boss. His leathery, weather beaten face shows horror and disgust.

Jim Burgess, the barn boss, holds up a bearskin overcoat, nothing more, he says. It belongs to Joe McGraw, the superintendent, who left it stored there last winter before his move to Fairplay. McGraw wants it brought down to him on the stage. Whiskers fixes faded blue eyes on the big coat and grunts. Is that not the same bearskin coat Bill Troy, McGraw uncle, wore the time he was shot through the head and killed by a rustler on Elk Creek. West tale fans get a cursed coat on a mountain stage road.
8189-the-bride:
Samuel Rowlands wrote The Bride, a poem first published in 1617, in the spelling of its original edition, with long s letters modernised and macrons expanded. Its modern history is curious: when the Hunterian Club issued Rowlands's complete works in 1872 to 1880. In two hundred and ten copies, the editor had to omit The Bride, since no copy was supposed to be extant. Twenty years later, a copy came to light, and the poem could at last be printed with an introductory note by Alfred Claghorn Potter.

The poem itself is Jacobean satire and social observation, in Rowlands's sharp, popular style. Its rediscovery makes the volume a small bibliographical romance as well as a literary text. For students of early modern poetry, it offers a rare Rowlands work, rescued from supposed loss.
8405-journalism-for-women-a-practical-gu:
E. A. Bennett wrote this practical guide for women seeking work in journalism, at a time when the field was opening to them. Contents cover the secret significance of journalism, the roads toward it, and style. They move on to the search for copy, corresponding with editors, the leading types of papers, and woman's sphere in journalism, ending with a conclusion for aspirants.

Bennett writes plainly about a trade: how to find subjects, write them up, and get paid, and what faults held women journalists back. The book is both a manual and a period document, showing what work was open to women and what barriers remained. Readers interested in media history, or in women's work, will find it frank and useful.
8853-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Jude, bondservant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes in Weymouth's version to those in God the Father, enfolded in his love, kept for Jesus Christ, and called. Mercy, peace, and love are wished abundantly. Jude had meant to write about their common salvation, but finds himself constrained instead to cheer them on to vigorous defence of the faith delivered once for all to God's people.

Certain persons, he warns, have crept in unnoticed, ungodly men spoken of in ancient writings, who pervert God's grace into an excuse for immorality and deny the Master. Jude answers with examples from Israel, angels, Sodom, and Enoch, and with a call to build up faith, pray, and show mercy. The letter is short and fierce, and Weymouth's plain English keeps its urgency intact. Readers meet the New Testament's sharpest warning against false teaching inside the church.
8859-true-to-the-old-flag-a-tale-of-the-:
G. A. Henty tells the American War of Independence from the loyalist side in True to the Old Flag, following a frontier family through the whole conflict. Contents run from a frontier farm, an Indian raid, and the fight at Lexington, through Bunker's Hill, scouting, the forest, Quebec, the surprise of Trenton, and a treacherous planter. The capture of Philadelphia, a settler's hut, Saratoga, a rescue, an island refuge, a great storm, and the siege of Savannah follow.

Henty's hero stays true to the king while neighbours choose rebellion, and the novel's sympathy lies firmly with the losing cause. That loyalist angle makes the book unusual among boys' war stories, and useful for seeing the Revolution from the other side. Young readers get a long, eventful campaign narrative, while adults can note how Henty's imperial loyalties shape a war most American books tell very differently.
8991-the-fur-country-or-seventy-degrees-:
Jules Verne wrote this adventure novel in French in 1873, and N. d'Anvers turned it into English the next year. It follows a party sent by the Hudson's Bay Company to build a trading fort far north in Canada, near the Arctic coast. The men, led by Lieutenant Hobson, face ice, wild beasts, and a land that shifts under their feet.

As the seasons turn, the fort's ground breaks away and drifts out to sea as a floating island of ice. The party must hunt, keep warm, and hold together while their home melts around them. Verne blends hard facts about the north with a tense tale of grit, and the result still reads as a vivid picture of life at the edge of the known world.
9054-the-young-woman-s-guide:
William A. Alcott, an American writer on health and morals, wrote this guide for young women in the 1800s, as a match to his Young Man's Guide. Alcott does not claim to cover every duty of a young woman's life. He picks those he felt other writers slighted, above all temperance, meaning self-control in all things.

Chapters urge care for health, good habits, sound friendships, and a useful, steady life at home and in the world. The advice now reads as old-fashioned, yet it shows plainly what middle-class America taught its daughters. Historians and general readers alike can learn much from its earnest, practical tone.
9183-wilfrid-cumbermede:
George MacDonald wrote this tale of a boy, a sword, and a haunted house, told in the first person. Wilfrid finds himself with an uncle and aunt, climbs a chimney stair, and meets a pendulum, a ghost, and lessons at school. A sword on the wall and a loss at Moldwarp Hall shape his youth.

Later chapters take him to an ice cave, the mountains, and Oxford, with Charley nursing him after a mishap. MacDonald mixes adventure with moral growth. The book still pleases as a boy's story with depth, wonder, and a strong sense of place.
9299-italian-letters-vols-i-and-ii-or-th:
William Godwin wrote this epistolary novel as Italian Letters, or the history of the Count de St. Julian, edited with an introduction by Burton Pollin. Volume One opens in Palermo, where the Count writes to the Marquis of Pescara on his father's death. He scorns fashionable forms of condolence, praising instead honest grief.

His friend Rinaldo, heir to fortune and title, weeps an unaffected tear, unspoiled by flattery. Letters trace love, honor, and Italian society through St. Julian's eyes. The novel remains an early Godwin work, formal, feeling, and rich in eighteenth-century manners.
9814-the-poetical-works-of-mark-akenside:
George Gilfillan edited The Poetical Works of Mark Akenside, opening with a life of the poet. Akenside, born at Newcastle in 1721 to a butcher father and Mary Lumsden, was baptized among Presbyterian Dissenters. Gilfillan notes the oddity of a butcher's shop birthing The Pleasures of Imagination, then cites like cases: Kirke White and others of humble trade. No decent calling, he argues, bars genius.

The volume pairs Akenside's poems, chiefly The Pleasures of Imagination, with Gilfillan's memoir. Akenside's verse favors lofty meditation on taste and fancy. A reader gets a Victorian edition of an eighteenth-century poet, with a life that defends humble birth.
a-boy-s-ride: Gulielma Zollinger tells a boys adventure of a ride through peril and pursuit. Its young hero seeks shelter within castle walls, finds guides and friends, and hides among oak trees and reeds. Illustrations follow scenes of flight, capture, and narrow escape across the countryside. The story mixes history and daring in a tale meant for young readers.
a-declaration-of-the-causes-which-mooved: Queen Elizabeth the First declares the causes that moved her navy's chief commanders on their voyage for Portugal. On June 30, 1589, English ships arrested vessels of corn and war provisions bound for Lisbon in the service of the King of Spain. The declaration justifies the seizure as an act of war at sea. It stands as a plain Tudor state paper on naval power and trade.
a-question-of-latitude:
Richard Harding Davis follows Everett, a young magazine writer known for honest attacks on graft and corruption. His editors trust him because no one has caught him in exaggeration or unfair play. Sent south on an assignment, Everett finds that the rules he lives by sit oddly in a hot, slow country where men do business differently.

The tale tests his code against local custom, a shady consul, and his own pride. Davis, a famous reporter of his day, writes with pace and clean detail. The story asks whether right and wrong shift with the climate, or whether a man must carry his own weather with him.
a-versailles-christmas-tide: Mary Stuart Boyd spends a Christmas-tide at Versailles in this 1901 volume, with fifty-three illustrations by A. S. Boyd. The contents run from the unexpected happening and Ogams through the town, the Christmas tree, New Year's Day, and ice-bound days to a haunted chateau, Marie Antoinette, and prisoners released. Illustrations of the summons, storm warnings, treasure trove, chestnuts in the avenue, and snow in the park accompany a holiday abroad.
abraham-lincoln-an-horatian-ode: Richard Henry Stoddard mourns Abraham Lincoln in an Horatian ode, published at New York in 1865. The title page records Lincoln born February 12, 1809, and assassinated on Good Friday, April 14, 1865. Epigraphs from Shakespeare cry confusion's masterpiece, sacrilegious murder breaking open the Lord's anointed temple, and an alarum bell ringing murder and treason. The ode answers assassination with classical measure and public grief.
adam-bede:
George Eliot's first full novel is set in the farming parish of Hayslope and organized in six books, as the contents show. The title figure, Adam Bede, is a skilled carpenter. Around him gather his brother Seth and the Methodist preacher Dinah Morris. The Poysers of the Hall Farm and Hetty Sorrel complete the circle. Hetty is the dairy maid whose beauty governs her small world.

Chapter titles trace the arc. They run from the preaching on the green and evenings in the wood to a birthday feast, a crisis, and a hidden dread. Then come a journey in despair, the tidings, a trial, a verdict, and hours in a prison cell. Hetty's fall through the young squire Arthur Donnithorne brings the catastrophe. Dinah's steadiness and Adam's slow forgiving close the book at a harvest supper and marriage bells.
aikenside:
Mary Jane Holmes lists her earlier novels on the title page. Maggie Miller, Lena Rivers, English Orphans, and Tempest and Sunshine stand among them. The book then opens in Devonshire. The good people there are quarreling about the minister and his wife. A school examination brings young Madeline Clyde before the examining committee, and her life changes with its result.

Twenty-four chapters follow Maddy through convalescence, a generous letter, life at Aikenside with the proud family there, holidays, a growing burden, and the interval before a marriage. Holmes was among the most widely read American novelists of her century, writing domestic tales of love, class, and conscience for an audience that bought her books by the hundred thousand.
an-essay-on-the-american-contribution-an:
Winston Churchill's An Essay on the American Contribution and the Democratic Idea argues that idealism is the American's ruling trait. Emerson and William James, he says, proclaimed it first. He quotes Firmin Roz's Sorbonne address on American idealism with approval. Europe mistook Americans for money grabbers whose philosophy is the dollar.

The essay marches through the national record: colonists animated by an ideal, a constitution ahead of its age, and democracy established in practice. Churchill confesses the failures frankly — Florida seized, Texas annexed, Mexico fought without unmixed pride. The war with Spain in 1898, fought to liberate Cuba, marks for him a transition in international ethics. America's contribution is an idea tested by its own betrayals. Written amid the Great War, the essay calls the republic back to its mission: democracy as a gift to be kept by being given.
an-international-episode:
Henry James wrote this novella about two young Englishmen who cross to America in the summer of 1874, as the opening pages state. Lord Lambeth and his friend Percy Beaumont land in a sweltering New York, ride up Broadway in a high coach, and find the bright, crowded city very odd. Their travels carry them to Newport, where American leisure society is on display.

There the young lord falls in with Bessie Alden, a quick, independent Boston girl, and an attraction grows that neither family quite approves. James builds the comedy from small collisions of manners: English reserve against American frankness, title against money, old assumptions against new ones. The tale is an early, light version of the international theme James returned to all his life.
britannica-1911-abode:
Abode receives a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The word, from abide, to dwell or wait, means in general a dwelling. English law narrows it below domicile: the place of a man's residence or business, fixed or passing.

Business can supply the abode though the man sleeps elsewhere, making the term looser than residence, defined in one case as where a man lives with family and sleeps at night. A solicitor's office stands as his abode for serving a notice of action. Public Health Act service at a place of business likewise holds good. Cases of 1835 and 1852 anchor the rulings, giving the small word a firm legal edge.
britannica-1911-accolade:
Accolade was the ceremony used in conferring knighthood, its name drawn from a word for the neck. The 1911 Britannica entry admits scholars disagree whether the original act was an embrace or a slight blow on the neck or cheek, since both customs are ancient. Gregory of Tours describes early French kings kissing new knights on the left cheek while giving the gilt shoulder-belt.

Blows softened over time. A blow with the naked fist, a real box on the ear, gave way to a gentle stroke with the flat of a sword on the neck or shoulders. British sovereigns still use that form when conferring knighthood. The word also names a brace joining staves in printed music.
britannica-1911-acosta-jose-de:
Jose de Acosta (about 1539-1600) was a Spanish Jesuit author. He was born at Medina del Campo. He joined the Jesuits in 1551. In 1571 the order sent him to Peru. He served as provincial there for five years. In 1583 he published a catechism in Quichua and Aymara. It was the first book printed in Peru. He returned to Spain in 1587. Opposition to his superior led to imprisonment. Later posts took him to Valladolid and Salamanca.

Writing made his lasting name. His Historia natural y moral de las Indias appeared in 1590. Translations into six languages followed quickly. Early books treat general questions of the New World. Middle books cover the physical geography of Mexico and Peru. Their natural history gets full treatment too. Final books describe native religion and government.
britannica-1911-acuna-christoval-de:
Christoval de Acuna (1597-about 1676) was a Spanish missionary and explorer. He was born at Burgos and became a Jesuit in 1612. Mission work took him to Chile and Peru. He rose to rector of the college of Cuenca. In 1639 he joined Pedro Texeira's Amazon expedition. His task was scientific observation for Spain's government. He was to draw up the official report.

Ten months of travel produced his narrative. He prepared it while awaiting a ship in Peru. Philip IV received the author coldly, tradition says. The king even tried to suppress the book. Portugal had just revolted from Spain. Madrid feared Lisbon would profit from Amazon intelligence. His New Discovery of the Great River of the Amazons appeared in 1641 anyway.
britannica-1911-agde:
Agde is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in the south of France, in the department of Herault. It stands on the left bank of the river Herault, thirty-two miles south-west of Montpellier. The count of 1906 gave it 7,146 people. The town lies at the foot of a dead volcano, the Montagne St Loup.

Agde is built of black volcanic stone, which gives it a gloomy look. Above the river stands the church of St Andre, part of it from the twelfth century. Till the Revolution it was a cathedral. It is a plain, massive church with walls like a fort, more stronghold than shrine. The Canal du Midi passes under the town walls. The mouth of the Herault forms a harbour, guarded by a fort.
britannica-1911-alarcon-juan-ruiz-de:
Juan Ruiz de Alarcón was a Spanish playwright born about 1581 at Tlacho in Mexico. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his move to Europe in 1600 for law study. He studied at Salamanca, then went back to Mexico for a time. In 1611 he returned to Spain and won success on the stage.

His best known play is La Verdad sospechosa, on a lying hero. Corneille later reshaped it as the Menteur in French. Alarcón was a hunchback who faced mockery and feuds with rivals. He answered with calm and cutting dignity, the entry stresses. Moral aims mark his plays more than those of his peers.
britannica-1911-alarcon-pedro-antonio-de:
Pedro Antonio de Alarcon, a Spanish writer who lived from 1833 to 1891, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Guadix, he studied at the university of Granada. He trained in law and theology in private and had a play staged before he came of age. He chose letters as his trade.

Alarcon helped edit a Cadiz newspaper and then moved to Madrid to seek a publisher. That bid failed, but work as a radical journalist in Granada won him notice. By 1854 he edited a republican journal in Madrid. His sharp attacks led to a duel with a rival poet. His first novel came out in 1855 and showed a fine prose style. Real fame came with his diary of the war in Africa. Fifty thousand copies sold in two weeks.
britannica-1911-alava-don-miguel-ricardo:
Don Miguel Ricardo de Álava, Spanish general and statesman born at Vittoria in 1770, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He served first in the navy as a young man. He had risen to captain of a frigate when he switched to the army at the same rank. As a marine he was present at Trafalgar on the flagship of his uncle.

In politics he took a very winding course over the years. At Bayonne in 1808 he stood among those who took a new charter from Joseph Bonaparte as king. After the national rising against France, he joined the party that fought beside the English. The Spanish Cortes made him their man at the English headquarters camp. Wellington held him in high favour and made him an aide de camp. By the close of the campaign he had risen to brigadier general.
britannica-1911-albornoz-gil-alvarez-de:
Albornoz, Gil Alvarez de, a Spanish cardinal born at Cuenca early in the fourteenth century, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His mother came from the Luna family, and his uncle was archbishop of Toledo. Educated at Saragossa and trained in law at Toulouse, he rose early through family influence. He became archdeacon of Calatrava and a member of the king's council while still young.

In 1337 Albornoz succeeded his uncle as archbishop of Toledo. He fought in person at Tarifa in 1340 against a great invasion from Africa and led his archbishopric's levy at Algeciras in 1344. A mission to Pope Clement VI at Avignon showed his diplomatic skill, and the pope made him cardinal in 1350. Sent to Italy as legate, he worked to restore papal authority in the states of the Church. Astute with men and an effective fighter, he paved the way for Urban V's return to Rome in 1362.
britannica-1911-alcalde:
Judging sits at the root of the Spanish title alcalde, a word taken from the Arabic al-quadi, the Cadi or judge. Every use of the title keeps some trace of that court role. An alcalde de corte judged cases at the palace court, with sway in and around the king's home.

Town life gave the word its lasting sense. A mayor of a town or village who also did the work of a justice of the peace was an alcalde, and that, the entry notes, is now the title's sole meaning. The post is filled by vote each year, and in Spain men have often found it a thankless one. Readers must not mix alcalde up with alcaide. That word springs from a separate Arabic term for a commander and means the man who governs a fortress.
britannica-1911-almagro-diego-de: Peru's conquest bound the Spanish commander Diego de Almagro (1475–1538) to Pizarro, first as partner and then as rival. He was born at Aldea del Rey, though one account calls him a foundling from the village that gave him his name. At Panama in 1525 he joined Pizarro and Hernando de Luque in their scheme. Their quarrel over territory ended with Pizarro ordering his execution in 1538.
britannica-1911-almeida-dom-francisco-de:
Death found Dom Francisco de Almeida (c. 1450–1510), Portuguese India's first viceroy, far from India, near the site of Cape Town. Stopping for water on 1 March 1510, he was killed in a fight with local people. Lisbon-born, he was the seventh son of the second count of Abrantes and came from one of Portugal's most honoured families. As a youth he fought under Ferdinand of Aragon in the Moorish wars of 1485 to 1492.

March 1505 brought his appointment as viceroy and a large fleet to command. Quiloa fell to him with little struggle; Mombasa he destroyed after stiff resistance. Forts rose at Angediva and Cannanore, a trade treaty was made with Malacca, and he ruled from Cochin. His son Lorenzo, serving under him, likely reached Ceylon before any other Portuguese, while another of his captains sighted Madagascar.
britannica-1911-arcade:
Arcade, in architecture, is a range of arches. Columns or piers support those arches. Church naves use arcades to separate aisles. Cloisters use them around covered walks. The Ducal Palace at Venice shows them famously. St Mark's Square shows them too. Italian palace courts display them commonly. Paris has them at the Palais-Royal. The Place des Vosges offers another example.

Rome holds the earliest known examples. The Tabularium is one such building. The theatre of Marcellus is another. The Colosseum completes the Roman trio. Diocletian's palace at Spalato shows a variant. Its arches rest directly on capitals. No entablature intervenes in that design. Decorative galleries on church façades count too. Blind arcades form part of the wall itself. Shopping passages took the name later. Burlington Arcade in London exemplifies that sense.
britannica-1911-argensola-lupercio-leona:
Argensola, Lupercio Leonardo de is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Spanish dramatist and poet of the golden age. Baptized at Barbastro on the fourteenth of December 1559 and schooled at Huesca and Saragossa, he became secretary to the duke de Villahermosa in 1585 and historiographer of Aragon in 1599. His tragedies drew praise from Cervantes, who said they filled hearers with wonder and delight.

Filis is lost, and the two surviving plays, printed only in 1772, are heavy copies of Seneca. His poems, printed with his brother's in 1634, join fine versions of the Latin poets to original satires. His echoing sonnets lend themselves to parody, though his diction is praised as singularly pure. The entry closes with his brother Bartolome, who followed him as historiographer of Aragon and wrote the Conquest of the Molucca Islands in 1609.
britannica-1911-avila-y-zuniga-luis-de:
Avila y Zuniga, Luis de (c. 1490-c. 1560), was a Spanish historian born at Placentia. Probably of low origin, he married a wealthy heiress of the Zuniga family and added her name to his own. He rose fast in the favor of the emperor Charles V.

Avila served as ambassador to Rome and became grand commander of the order of the Knights of Alcantara. He went with Charles to Africa in 1541 and served in the war of the league of Schmalkalden. His history of that war, printed in 1548, won wide fame and translation into five languages. The entry warns that his closeness to Charles makes the book strongly partial, its misrepresentations sharply criticized.
britannica-1911-aviles-pedro-menendez-de:
Avilés, Pedro Menéndez de (1519-1574), was a Spanish seaman and founder of St Augustine, Florida, born at Avilés in Asturias, one of nineteen children of a gentry family. At fourteen he ran away to sea and spent sixteen years as a corsair.

In 1549 Charles V set him to clear French pirates from Spain's north coast and the Canaries. From 1554 he commanded the flota, the convoy carrying trade between Spain and America, refusing bribes and guarding treasure so well that the emperor approved him warmly. The trade board, the Casa de Contratacion, hated his high-handed ways and had him jailed for twenty months on unknown charges before royal orders freed him. The entry's opening line credits him with founding St Augustine.
britannica-1911-ayala-don-pedro-lopez-de:
Ayala, Don Pedro Lopez de (1332-1407), was a Spanish statesman, historian, and poet born at Vittoria. He rose at the court of Peter the Cruel. He finally left that king's cause. In later campaigns he fought with honor. Twice he fell prisoner. The Black Prince took him in 1367, and the Portuguese took him in 1385.

Favored by Henry II and John I of Castile, Ayala became grand chancellor of the realm in 1398 under Henry III. His chief works are chronicles of the four Castilian kings of his lifetime, mostly scenes he witnessed himself, and so generally accurate. He also wrote a long satirical, teaching poem picturing his own experience and the morals of his age. He died at Calahorra in 1407.
britannica-1911-ayala-y-herrera-adelardo:
Ayala y Herrera, Adelardo Lopez de (1828-1879), was a Spanish writer and politician born at Guadalcanal, where he began writing plays for the town theatre as a boy. His early pieces were played by men only, since travelling companies never came and ladies did not act there.

At Seville university his studies were undistinguished, but playwright Garcia Gutierrez encouraged his stage ambitions. Settling in Madrid in 1850 with no friends or influence, he won the Teatro Español with a verse play in 1851 and made his name at once. Rioja, from 1854, was held his finest work. Government posts, party shifts from Moderates to Progressives, and campaign journalism in El Padre Cobos filled the same busy years.
britannica-1911-ayllon-lucas-vasquez-de:
Ayllon, Lucas Vasquez de (c. 1475-1526), was a Spanish adventurer and colonizer in America, born probably at Toledo. He sailed to Hispaniola with Ovando in 1502, served as magistrate in its towns, sat on its high court, and grew rich in trade.

Turning to the North American mainland, Ayllon sent Gordillo exploring in 1521 and won a charter from Charles V in 1523 to plant colonies. In 1526 he sailed himself with 500 colonists and about 100 African slaves, an early use of slave labor in what became the United States. His town of San Miguel, near the Pedee river by most accounts, sickened with fever; Ayllon died that October, slaves rose, and the survivors abandoned the place.
britannica-1911-azara-don-jose-nicholas-:
Azara, Don Jose Nicholas de (1731-1804), was a Spanish diplomatist born at Barbunales in Aragon, made Spanish agent and procurator-general in 1765 and ambassador at Rome in 1785. Long resident there, he collected Italian antiquities, patronized art, and played a leading, risky part in expelling the Jesuits from Spain.

Azara helped secure the election of Pius VI and served the pope through exile and death after France took Rome in 1798. As ambassador in Paris his government forced him to negotiate the treaty of San Ildefonso, which subjected Spain wholly to Napoleon, a master he personally liked. He died worn out in Paris in 1804, embittered, the entry says, by seeing what the French alliance would cost his country. His younger brother Felix won fame studying South American nature and boundaries.
britannica-1911-azoimide:
Azoimide, or hydrazoic acid, is a compound of nitrogen and hydrogen first isolated by Curtius in 1890. The entry walks through his route to it: benzoyl compounds treated with hydrazine, then nitrous acid, then boiled with alkali to free salts of the new acid.

An improved path runs through hippuric acid and its hydrazine derivative, ending with distillation of the sodium salt with dilute sulphuric acid. The pure acid is a colourless liquid of very unpleasant smell, boiling near room heat and extremely explosive. Its water solution attacks metals like zinc and iron, forming salts called azides, all of them explosive. In behavior it resembles the halogen acids, giving poorly soluble salts with lead, silver, and mercury.
britannica-1911-azurara-gomes-eannes-de:
Azurara, Gomes Eannes de ( ?-1474), was the second notable Portuguese chronicler, who came to letters in middle life and joined the royal library under Fernão Lopes during King Duarte's reign. By 1452 he held sole charge of it, and in 1454 he succeeded Lopes as chief keeper of the archives and royal chronicler.

His Chronicle of the Discovery and Conquest of Guinea was drafted by 1453. It is the standing authority for the early Portuguese voyages down Africa's coast. Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored those voyages. The chronicle also sketches Henry's life work. Royal commissions took him even to Africa for a year gathering material. The entry praises his labor and accuracy, while noting his court post kept him from telling the whole truth about his hero, Henry.
britannica-1911-bachaumont-louis-petit-d:
Bachaumont, Louis Petit de (1690-1771), was a French writer of noble family. He was brought up at the Versailles court. He passed his whole life in Paris. There he centred the salon of Madame Doublet de Persan. There, talk about art and books took the form of lively, malicious gossip.

The salon kept a news register dealing largely in scandal and in books the censor had suppressed. Bachaumont's name clings to its first volumes, published anonymously as Secret Memoirs for the History of the Republic of Letters, though his exact share is disputed. Others carried it to thirty-six volumes by 1779. The entry values the work as a historical source, above all for the banned literature of the age.
britannica-1911-balance-of-trade:
Balance of trade is an old term from the age of the mercantile theory, when trade was judged by how much gold and silver a country took in. The 1911 Britannica entry traces that view and the common belief that a surplus of precious metals meant profit for the nation.

Adam Smith's reply, that gold and silver are goods like any others, sits at the core of the piece. The entry then turns to modern talk of imports and exports, and to claims that an excess of imports is bad and an excess of exports is good. It tests those claims rather than taking them on trust.
britannica-1911-balboa-vasco-nunez-de:
Vasco Nuñez de Balboa (about 1475–1517) was a Spanish explorer of America, famed as the man who first reached the Pacific from the New World. Born at Jerez de los Caballeros, he sailed in 1501 with Rodrigo de Bastidas, then tried farming on Hispaniola and fell into debt.

In 1510 he joined Enciso's relief voyage, by some accounts hidden in a cask, and reached the ruined post of San Sebastian. The 1911 Britannica entry tells how he urged a move to Darien, helped found Santa Maria de la Antigua, and rose to lead the colony. From Darien he pushed inland toward the far sea he had heard of.
britannica-1911-baliol-john-de:
John de Baliol (1249–1315) was a king of Scotland. He was a son of John de Baliol of Barnard Castle and of Dervorguila, heiress of Galloway. On his elder brother's death in 1278 he became head of the family, with wide lands in England, France, and Scotland.

He came to notice in 1290, when the Scottish throne fell vacant on the death of Margaret, the Maid of Norway. Baliol claimed the crown through his mother's line from David, earl of Huntingdon. His chief rival was Robert Bruce. The 1911 Britannica entry tells how Edward I of England was called in to judge the claim, and first demanded to be owned as overlord of Scotland.
britannica-1911-balsham-hugh-de:
Hugh de Balsham (died 1286) was an English churchman, first noted as sub-prior of the monastery of Ely. When Bishop William of Kilkenny died in 1256, the Ely monks chose Hugh as bishop, against the wishes of Henry III, who had given the see's revenues to another man. The pope confirmed the choice in 1257.

Hugh set about repairing the harm done to the diocese. His lasting work came at Cambridge. In 1280 a charter let him swap the lay brethren of his hospital of St John for studious scholars. A second charter four years later set those scholars apart, and for them he founded and endowed Peterhouse. The 1911 Britannica entry keeps that founding as the core of his fame.
britannica-1911-balustrade:
Balustrade names a parapet or low screen made of a rail or coping held up on balusters, the small posts treated in the entry just before this one. It can guard a stair, a balcony, or a roof edge. The 1911 Britannica entry is brief and keeps to the forms the feature takes.

Sometimes a balustrade is purely decorative, set below the sill of a window that does not reach the ground. Sometimes carved foliage takes the place of the rail. Other so-called balustrades are made of upright stone slabs, pierced with open work. The entry points to the Ca' d'Oro at Venice and to the balconies of the minarets at Cairo as cases in point.
britannica-1911-balzac-honore-de:
Honoré de Balzac (1799–1850) was a French novelist, born at Tours on 20 May 1799. His father rose in army supply and hospital posts after the Revolution. Yet he had no real right to the name Balzac at all. The family name was Balssa, borne by day labourers and small peasants in the Tarn. Honoré himself added the de only after 1830.

The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, opens with that family history and the novelist's two sisters and younger brother, then follows his life and work in full. His mother, an heiress of strong faculty, outlived him. Laure, the elder sister and his favourite, later wrote his life, a fact the entry notes at the start.
britannica-1911-balzac-jean-louis-guez-d:
Jean Louis Guez de Balzac (1594–1654) was a French author, born at Angoulême in 1594. At eighteen he travelled in Holland with Théophile de Viaud, a friend who later became a bitter foe in print. The duc d'Épernon and his son, Cardinal de la Valette, backed him early and took him to Rome.

Letters made his name. His Lettres of 1624, written to friends and to great men at court, won wide praise. They earned him a place at the Hôtel de Rambouillet. Richelieu, though, never gave him the office he hoped for. Elected to the Academy in 1634, he kept up his letters from his château. The 1911 Britannica entry faults their empty, affected matter but credits their style with bringing new clearness and precision to French prose.
britannica-1911-banville-theodore-faulla:
Theodore de Banville was a French poet and wide ranging writer born at Moulins, son of a navy captain. His school years in Paris were, by his own tale, dull and lone. He took no part in the games of his peers, though no one dealt with him in a harsh way.

The 1911 Britannica entry says he left school with thin means and gave his life to letters. His first book of verse came out while he was still in his teens, and a second book soon after. The poems drew some blame, but won him the praise and friendship of two famed men of letters. From then on he wrote verse, plays, and reviews with a steady hand. A book of comic odes won full praise from the great Victor Hugo.
britannica-1911-bar-francois-de: François de Bar, a French scholar who lived from 1538 to 1606, gets a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied at Paris and joined the order of Saint Benedict. In time he became prior of the abbey of Anchin. There he gave his days to the rich stock of books in that house. Church history, most of all that of Flanders, was his field. He listed the abbey's hand-written books and wrote notes on many of them.
britannica-1911-barante-amable-guillaume:
Baron de Barante, who lived from 1782 to 1866, was a French statesman and historian. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his posts and books. He was born at Riom in June 1782, the son of a lawyer. He entered a top Paris school at sixteen and rose fast in state work.

Barante served as prefect, tax chief, and then a peer of France. He spoke for the liberal side in public life. After 1830 he served as envoy to Turin and to Saint Petersburg. When the monarchy fell in 1848 he quit public life for good. His history of the dukes of Burgundy won him a seat in the French Academy. Critics praised its tale and style but faulted its weak use of proof.
britannica-1911-barbe-marbois-francois-m:
Francois Barbe-Marbois, a French politician who lived from 1745 to 1837, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Metz and began his career as intendant of San Domingo under the old regime. At the end of 1789 he came back to France and put his service at the call of the new government.

In 1791 he was sent to Regensburg to aid talks on the lands of German princes in Alsace and Lorraine. Held on a charge of treason, he was soon set free. In 1795 he was picked for the Council of the Ancients, where his even tone drew a charge of royalism. At the coup of 1797 he was seized and shipped to French Guiana. Napoleon freed him, and in 1801 he took charge of the public treasury. In 1803 he made the treaty by which Louisiana was ceded to the United States.
britannica-1911-barricade:
Barricade, also spelled barricado, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a makeshift defence thrown up in a hurry. The word comes from the Spanish barricada, from barrica, a cask, because casks filled with earth were used early on to build such barriers. A barricade could be made of earth, paving stones, trees, or anything else close at hand that would slow an enemy down.

Street fighting is the use the entry stresses most. Barricades were most often raised across a street to block an advance. The word had a second, naval sense as well. On old wooden warships it named a fence or rail across the quarter-deck, held up by posts and strengthened with other material. That rail gave the crew some protection while the ship was in action.
britannica-1911-barthelemy-anatole-jean-:
Anatole Jean-Baptiste Antoine de Barthélemy (1821–1904), a French archaeologist and numismatist born at Reims, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Numismatics, the study of coins, is the field that made his name. He also worked on Brittany, publishing studies of the Breton revolution in 1858 and a large six-volume history of the old Breton bishoprics, with their monuments, between 1855 and 1879.

Coins dominate the list of his books. Barthélemy wrote popular manuals on ancient coinage and on medieval and modern coinage, both later revised, plus many technical papers in journals. Named studies cover Merovingian coinage, the Parisian coinage, and the origin of the tournois coinage, and he edited the numismatics volume for a national historical committee. Election to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-lettres came in 1897. A note on his younger brother Édouard's work on the old French nobility closes the entry.
britannica-1911-barthelemy-francois-marq:
François Barthélemy, marquis de Barthélemy (1747 or 1750–1830), a French politician, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Trained for diplomacy by his uncle, the abbé Jean Jacques Barthélemy, he served as secretary of legation in Sweden, Switzerland, and England. As minister in Switzerland he negotiated the treaties of Basel with Prussia and Spain in 1795, the agreements that took those powers out of the war against France.

High office brought sudden ruin. Elected to the Directory in May 1797 with royalist support, Barthélemy was arrested in the Fructidor coup that September and deported to French Guiana. He escaped, reached England by way of the United States, and returned after Brumaire to sit in the senate. He helped establish the consulship for life and the empire, then abandoned Napoleon in 1814, became a peer of France, and received his marquis title after the second Restoration.
