Most of the hosted text covers his son, Claude Prosper Jolyot Crébillon (1707–1777), a French novelist born in Paris. His satire L'Écumoire of 1734 brought disgrace, prison, and five years of exile. He later helped found the Caveau dining society and served as a censor from 1759. His best known novels include Les Amours de Zéokinizul and Le Sopha, both from 1740. He died in Paris on 12 April 1777.
britannica-1911-cressy-hugh-paulinus-de:
Hugh Paulinus de Cressy, born about 1605, was an English monk and church writer. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his start at Oxford. He entered at fourteen and won a fellowship at Merton College. He rose to dean of Leighlin in Ireland and canon of Windsor. He also served as chaplain to Lord Wentworth, later earl of Strafford. Travel abroad as a tutor took him to Rome.

At Rome in 1646 he joined the Roman Catholic Church. His account of that change came out at Paris the next year. Catholics prized it as a reply to attacks by Chillingworth. He entered the Benedictine order in 1649. For four years he served as chaplain to the queen at Somerset House. His chief work told the church history of England to the Norman Conquest. Only the first part was printed, at Rouen in 1668.
britannica-1911-cricklade:
Cricklade is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a market town in Wiltshire, England. Swindon lies nine miles to the south east. A count from 1901 gives the town 1517 people. It sits in the plain bordering the south bank of the Thames. The Thames and Severn Canal lies not far away. The cruciform church of Saint Sampson is its chief building. That church is mainly Perpendicular in style.

It has a fine ornate tower over its crossing. The small church of Saint Mary is also of interest. It has an Early English tower and a Norman chancel arch. Some agricultural trade goes on in the town. Legend makes Cricklade the home of Greek philosophers. That tale dates them before the Roman conquest. The name is given as Greeklade in Drayton's verse. In Saxon times the town owed its weight to the river crossing.
britannica-1911-curel-francois-vicomte-d:
Francois, Vicomte de Curel, a French playwright born in eighteen fifty four, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Metz, he was trained at a Paris school as a builder of works in iron and stone. Family wealth came from smelting works. He turned to letters all the same.

He began with two novels in the eighteen eighties. In eighteen ninety one three of his pieces were taken by a free stage house. The entry lists play after play from the years that came next. One paints the stiff pride of the old rural nobility. One tells of a mother who comes back to her children after twenty years apart. A later work takes on the clash of wealth and labour. The list shows a writer with a sharp eye for rank and change.
britannica-1911-cuvilles-francois-de:
François de Cuvilles, a French designer of buildings who lived from 1698 to about 1767, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He helped carry the French rococo taste into Germany. About 1720 the elector of Cologne called him to his court. In 1738 he became designer to the elector of Bavaria, and later to the emperor Charles the Seventh.

His style is called thin but often rich to a fault. He drew mirrors, rails for stairs, ceilings, and fireplaces. In the field of household goods he is noted for beds and chests of drawers. He also laid out parks and gardens. His books on design were put out by his son, who took his place at the court of Munich.
britannica-1911-cyanamide:
Cyanamide is a chemical compound, the amide of cyanic acid, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It is made by the action of ammonia on cyanogen chloride, bromide, or iodide. It can also be made by stripping sulphur from thiourea with mercuric oxide, the usual route. It forms white crystals that melt at 40 degrees and dissolve readily in water, alcohol, and ether.

Heated past its melting point, cyanamide joins with itself to form dicyandiamide. At 150 degrees that product turns in turn into melamine as the mass sets hard. The text then turns to its salts, with one metal or with two metals in their make up. Calcium cyanamide had won a place in farming by the time of writing. Its cheap making in the electric furnace had been found, and that use drives the rest of the piece.
britannica-1911-daguerre-louis-jacques-m:
Louis Jacques Mande Daguerre, a French painter who found a way to fix light views, fills an art life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Cormeilles in seventeen eighty nine, he first worked as a tax clerk. Stage paint for the opera soon drew him from that desk post. He helped paint wide views of Rome, Naples, London, and far towns. In eighteen twenty two he opened the Diorama show house at Paris with a peer.

Light shifts played on the views there to heighten their charm for crowds. Fire razed that house in eighteen thirty nine with his new work in it. He had long sought with Niepce a way to fix views by sun light. When Niepce died he worked on and found the plate craft named for him. Five steps of plate care made the fixed view that bears his name.
britannica-1911-decker-pierre-de:
Pierre de Decker, a Belgian statesman and author who lived from 1812 to 1891, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was schooled at a Jesuit school and studied law at Paris. He then worked as a journalist on the Revue de Bruxelles. In 1839 he was elected to the lower chamber, where he won a great name for oratory.

In 1855 Decker became minister of the interior and prime minister of Belgium. He tried to join the moderate parts of the Catholic and Liberal camps to settle the school question and other strife. The text calls that task an impossible one from the start. In 1866 he left politics for business, with dire results. Speculation cost him his good name and most of his fortune, though he was never shown to be more than a victim of sharp operators.
britannica-1911-dekker-jeremias-de:
Dekker, Jeremias de, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Dutch poet. Born at Dort in 1610, he was son of an Antwerp man. His father had fled to Holland for the reformed faith. The boy joined his father's trade at an early age.

Yet he found time to feed his love of letters and verse. On his own he learned English, French, Latin, and Italian tongues. His first poem reworked the Lamentations of Jeremiah in Dutch verse. Versions of Horace and Juvenal and takes on them came after. His best known work is a satire in praise of greed. Critics rank it with the Praise of Folly by Erasmus. He died at Amsterdam in November 1666.
britannica-1911-enfilade: Enfilade is a French military word, from a verb meaning to thread or pass through. It names fire directed along an enemy line or parapet, end to end. Such fire is most destructive and most crushing to morale, since few guns can be brought to bear against it. Against trenches enfilade is stronger still, as the enemy loses the cover of his works. Banks of earth called traverses are built across a line to block such fire.
britannica-1911-enschede: Enschede is a town in Overysel in Holland, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands near the Prussian frontier and is a rail junction south east of Hengelo. About twenty three thousand people lived there in 1900. The town is the centre of the cotton spinning and weaving trades of the Twente district. A rail line links it to the Westphalian coal fields. About two thirds of the town burnt down in 1862.
britannica-1911-episode:
Episode is an incident in the history of a nation, an institution, or a person, above all one that breaks an ordered course of events, an irrelevance. The entry is a short word-history. The word comes from a Greek term that had a set meaning in the ancient Greek tragedy. Aristotle defines it in the Poetics, chapter twelve, as all the scenes that fall between the choric songs.

In early Greek tragedy the parts spoken by the actors counted for less than those sung by the chorus. From that stage sense, the entry says, comes the modern meaning of the word, something that breaks off the course of events. The notice thus carries one word from the Athenian stage to the history book, where an episode now means any side incident that interrupts a larger story.
britannica-1911-epode:
Epode is the subject of a verse entry in the 1911 Britannica. In verse the epode is the third part of an ode. It followed the strophe and the antistrophe parts. It closed the move of the whole song form. Choirs sang first to one side and then the other. At a set point they joined and sang as one. A lead singer might sing for all at that point. That centre stance gave the part its Greek name.

A new song form grew with learned Greek verse. That form paired long and short iambic lines in turn. One poet is said to have made that form first. A later poet brought it to its highest pitch. The form held a firm place in choir verse. It spread to drama in speech and paired talk. Horace gave a whole book of odes that name.
britannica-1911-ercilla-y-zuniga-alonso-:
Alonso de Ercilla, who lived from 1533 to 1595, was a Spanish soldier and poet. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ties his fame to one long war poem. He was born in Madrid in August 1533. At fifteen he became a page to the heir of Spain.

Ercilla sailed to Chile to fight the Araucanian people there. He shone in the campaign but quarreled with a fellow soldier. His general condemned him to death for that clash in 1558. The sentence was cut to prison, and he soon fought again. Back in Spain he wed, won a knighthood, and ran royal errands. His poem La Araucana tells the Chile wars in three parts. The first part, written on the spot, sticks close to fact. Later parts drift into visions and side tales, the entry says.
britannica-1911-erode:
Erode is a town of British India in the Coimbatore district of Madras, standing on the right bank of the river Cauvery. The entry is short, a single short paragraph of civic facts. The river is crossed there by an iron railway girder bridge of 22 spans. The town's population in 1901 was 15,529.

Here the South Indian railway joins the South-Western line of the Madras railway, 243 miles from Madras. That junction is the town's chief claim to notice in the entry. There are exports of cotton and saltpetre, and the town has a steam cotton press. Nothing of the town's history, buildings, or people is given. A reader gets a railway junction's bare profile: a river, a long girder bridge, a cotton trade with its press, and a head count taken at the 1901 census.
britannica-1911-escovedo-juan-de:
Juan de Escovedo is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a Spanish politician. He died in 1578, the heading notes. He was secretary of Don John of Austria. He is chiefly notable as the victim of a mystery. He began life in the household of Ruy Gomez de Silva. Silva, prince of Eboli, was a most trusted minister. He served Philip the Second in his early reign.

By the prince's will, Escovedo was endowed for life with a post. That post was legal representative of the king in Madrid. He was also associated with Antonio Perez as a secretary. Those secretaries acted as agents of the king in dealings. After Lepanto in 1571, Don John launched on adventures of self seeking. Escovedo was appointed his secretary at that point. The intent was that he should act as a check on those follies.
britannica-1911-espronceda-jose-ignacio-:
Jose de Espronceda is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a Spanish poet. He lived from 1808 to 1842. He was the son of an officer in the Bourbon regiment. He was born near Almendralejo in March 1808. After the war he was sent to a school at Segovia. He later became a pupil of the poet Lista in Madrid. In his fourteenth year his verses caught his master's eye.

He had joined a secret society by that age. He was sentenced to five years' seclusion in a convent. In that Franciscan convent at Guadalajara he began an epic. The poem was called Pelayo, and fragments of it survive. He escaped to Portugal and thence to England. There he found Teresa, whom he had met at Lisbon. In 1830 he eloped with Teresa to Paris. He took part in the July revolution there.
britannica-1911-fabert-abraham-de:
Abraham de Fabert, a marshal of France who lived from 1599 to 1660, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the son of a famous printer who served Henry the Fourth well in civil and military ways. At fourteen Fabert entered the Gardes françaises. He got a commission in 1618 and became a major in 1627. He stood out again and again in the wars of the period.

Fabert showed bravery at La Rochelle, Exilles, Avesnes, and Maubeuge. In 1642 Louis the Thirteenth made him governor of the fortress of Sedan. He became lieutenant-general in 1651. At the siege of Stenay in 1654 he brought in new methods of siegecraft. Those methods looked ahead to the great improvements of Vauban. In 1658 he was made a marshal of France. He was the first commoner to reach that rank. He died at Sedan in May 1660.
britannica-1911-feller-francois-xavier-d:
Francois Xavier de Feller (1735-1802), Belgian author, was born at Brussels on 18 August 1735. He entered a Jesuit school at Reims in 1752, showing strong gifts for mathematics and physical science, and began his novitiate two years later. In honour of the apostle of India he added Xavier to his name. He taught at Luxembourg and Liege, then held the theology chair at Tyrnau in Hungary from 1764, returning to Belgium in 1771.

When the Jesuits were suppressed in 1773, Feller gave the rest of his life to study, travel and writing. Driven from Belgium by the French invasion of 1794, he lived at Paderborn and then Ratisbon, where he died on 23 May 1802. His works run to more than 120 volumes. They include a Catechisme philosophique of 1773, printed under an anagram pen name, and his chief work, a historical and literary dictionary first published at Liege in 1781.
britannica-1911-fermat-pierre-de:
Pierre de Fermat, a French mathematician who lived from 1601 to 1665, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Montauban, he worked with Blaise Pascal on the traits of numbers while still young. From that work grew early steps toward the maths of chance. He also found new ways to handle curves and their high and low points.

Fermat is famed most as a founder of the modern theory of numbers. His notes were writ in the margins of a Greek maths book. His son printed them in 1670, after his death. One note states the famed problem that a sum of two like powers cannot equal a third, for powers above two. Fermat also served as a counsellor at Toulouse. He was praised there for legal skill and strict honesty.
britannica-1911-ferrand-antoine-francois:
Antoine François Claude Ferrand, who lived from 1751 to 1825, was a French statesman and political writer. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born in Paris on the fourth of July 1751. At eighteen he joined the parlement of Paris. He fled France with the first band of emigrants in the Revolution. He served the prince of Condé, then sat on a council of regency for the royal cause. He lived at Regensburg till 1801.

Back in France, Ferrand still worked for the kings in secret. In 1814 he was made minister of state and head of the posts. He signed the act that seized the goods of Napoleon. His bill to restore the lands of the emigrants drew a famed line between two kinds of royalist. He was made a peer and joined the Academy in 1816. He held his hard royal views till his death in 1825.
britannica-1911-feuquieres-isaac-manasse:
Isaac Manasses de Pas, Marquis de Feuquieres, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Feuquieres was a French soldier, born in 1590. His family had given many commanders to the civil wars of the last century. He entered the royal army at the age of thirty.

Distinction came quickly to him. He served in the Valtelline in 1626 and at the siege of La Rochelle in 1628. There he was taken prisoner by the defenders. In 1629 he rose to the rank of marechal de camp. He fought on the southern frontiers of France and held posts in Lorraine. Then he was sent as ambassador into Germany, where he dealt with Wallenstein. In 1636 he led the French corps serving with the duke of Weimar's army. The entry traces a soldier whose sword and tongue both served his king.
britannica-1911-fleury-andre-hercule-de:
André Hercule de Fleury (1653-1743) was a French cardinal and statesman who in effect ruled France, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells how. He was born at Lodève, the son of a tax collector, and was schooled by the Jesuits in Paris. He became a priest, then almoner to the queen, and in 1698 bishop of Fréjus.

He won his chance as tutor to the young heir to the throne, gaining a hold on the boy's mind that never broke. When the regent Orleans died in 1723, Fleury let the duke of Bourbon take the top post first. In 1726 he took power into his own hands and sent Bourbon into exile. Made a cardinal that year, he ran the state with care and thrift. By 1738 the budget showed a surplus in place of the usual shortfall.
britannica-1911-florian-jean-pierre-clar:
Jean Pierre Claris de Florian (1755-1794) was a French poet and writer of romances, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives his life in outline. He was born at the château of Florian near Sauve, in the department of Gard. His Spanish mother died while he was a small child. His uncle and guardian, the marquis of Florian, had married a niece of Voltaire and brought the boy to Ferney.

In 1768 he became a page in the household of the duke of Penthièvre, who stayed his friend for life. He studied at the artillery school at Bapaume and gained a captain's post in a dragoon regiment through his patron. When the Revolution came he retired to Sceaux but was found and jailed. His time in prison was short, yet he died within months of his release, in September 1794.
britannica-1911-foix-paul-de:
Paul de Foix (1528-1584) was a French prelate and diplomatist. He studied Greek and Roman literature at Paris and law at Toulouse. Shortly after finishing his course he lectured on civil law there and won a great reputation. At nineteen he was made councillor of the parlement of Paris. In that post he spoke for mild measures toward persons accused of Lutheranism. He was arrested for it, but escaped punishment and later regained the court's favour.

At the end of 1561 Foix was sent as ambassador to England, where he stayed four years. He then went to Venice and returned to England to negotiate a marriage between Queen Elizabeth and the duke of Anjou. More missions followed under Henry III. He was made archbishop of Toulouse in 1577 and ambassador to Rome in 1579. The entry follows a career that moved between the law courts, the church and the embassies of France.
britannica-1911-folard-jean-charles-chev:
Jean Charles, Chevalier de Folard (1669-1752), was a French soldier and military author born at Avignon on 13 February 1669. Reading Caesar's Commentaries first woke his love of war, and he ran away from home to join the army. He soon saw active service. Young as he was, he wrote a manual on partisan warfare, a manuscript that passed at his death to Marshal Belleisle. In 1702 he became a captain and aide-de-camp to the duke of Vendome in Italy.

In 1705 Folard won the cross of St Louis for a gallant feat of arms and stood out at the battle of Cassano, where he was badly wounded. During his slow recovery he formed the tactical theories he spent most of his life setting out. He served again in Italy in 1706 with credit. The entry follows his campaigns and then his writings on the order of battle and the column in attack.
britannica-1911-fontenelle-bernard-le-bo:
Bernard le Bovier de Fontenelle (1657-1757), French author, was born at Rouen on 11 February 1657. He died in Paris on 9 January 1757, having very nearly reached the age of one hundred. His father was an advocate settled at Rouen. His mother was a sister of the two Corneille, the great dramatists, so literature ran in the family. He was educated at the Jesuit college in his native city, where his teachers quickly saw his gifts.

Fontenelle stood out for the extraordinary precocity and range of his talents. His Jesuit teachers, who valued those gifts, wished him to join their order. The entry follows the long life that opened from that schoolroom: a career in letters stretching across two centuries of French writing. Few authors of the age lived so long, or kept a name alive from the reign of the young Louis XIV into the middle of the eighteenth century.
britannica-1911-forbin-claude-de:
Claude de Forbin (1656-1733), French naval commander, was born in Provence in 1656, of a family of high standing. High-spirited and ungovernable as a boy, he ran away from home. Through an uncle's influence he entered the navy and served his first campaign in 1675. He left the navy briefly for the army, then returned to his first choice. Under D'Estrees he made the American campaign, and under Duquesne the campaign of Algiers in 1683, standing out everywhere for headlong courage.

The strangest episode of Forbin's life was his mission to Siam, where France hoped to bring Christianity and European ways. Forbin sailed with the chevalier de Chaumont, holding the rank of major. The entry follows him through the Siamese court and home again, then through his later sea fights. His memoirs keep the flavour of a sailor who fought as hard in peace as in war.
britannica-1911-fournier-l-heritier-clau:
Claude Fournier l'Heritier (1745-1825), French revolutionist called l'Americain, was born at Auzon in Haute-Loire on 21 December 1745. He was the son of a poor weaver. He went to America to seek his fortune and set up at San Domingo making tafia, a rough kind of rum. A fire cost him his money. Back in France he threw himself into the Revolution with enthusiasm, and he took a leading hand in organizing the popular armed force behind its great coups.

Fournier's influence showed in the insurrections of October 1789, July 1791, and June and August 1792. He stood on bad terms with most of the politicians, Marat above all, and spent much of his time in prison or in disgrace. The entry follows the street fighter whom the Revolution used and distrusted in turn. His American years gave him his nickname.
britannica-1911-fourtou-marie-francois-o:
Marie Francois Oscar Bardy de Fourtou (1836-1897), French politician, was born at Riberac in Dordogne on 3 January 1836. He represented his native department in the National Assembly after the Franco-German War. There he proved a useful follower of Thiers, who made him minister of public works in December 1872. He was minister of religion in the short cabinet of May 1873, the only member of the Right whom Thiers took into that ministry of a week's life.

As minister of education, religion and fine arts under the duc de Broglie, Fourtou used his powers to serve clerical ends. As minister of the interior in 1877 he brought back the administrative methods of the Second Empire. With a known Bonapartist as his secretary, he replaced republican officials with Bonapartist partisans across France. The entry presents a minister of order whose purges of 1877 became a byword in the young Third Republic.
britannica-1911-franceschi-piero-de:
Piero de' Franceschi (about 1416-1492), generally named Piero della Francesca, was an Italian painter of the Umbrian school. Tradition says his father, a woollen-draper named Benedetto, died before his birth, and that Francesca was his mother. The entry corrects the tale: his mother's name was Romana, and his father lived through many years of Piero's career. The painter is also named Piero Borghese, from his birthplace, Borgo San Sepolcro in Umbria, and the family still exists as Martini-Franceschi.

Piero first had a scientific education and became adept in mathematics and geometry. That early bent shaped his growth as a painter to a large degree. He had more science than either Paolo Uccello or Mantegna, his contemporaries in the study of perspective.
britannica-1911-frayssinous-denis-antoin:
Denis Antoine Luc Frayssinous (1765-1841), French prelate and statesman, was born of humble parents at Curières in Aveyron on 9 May 1765. His fame rests on the conferences of Saint-Sulpice, lectures on dogmatic theology given in Paris from 1803 to 1809. Crowds came for his clear argument and graceful speech, until bold words in 1809, after Napoleon seized the pope, brought a ban.

Restored with the Bourbons, he became court preacher and almoner to Louis XVIII, then bishop of Hermopolis, a member of the French Academy, and head of the university. In 1824 he took office as minister of public instruction and church affairs, and his term is marked by the recall of the Jesuits. His lectures, printed in 1825 as Défense du christianisme, ran through 15 editions in 18 years. Forced out in 1828, he later tutored the duke of Bordeaux and died in 1841.
britannica-1911-free-trade:
Free trade names the policy of letting trade between countries run with no protective duties in the way. First urged in France and held by thinkers in many lands, it was taken up as a settled system by Great Britain alone among great trading nations, from 1846 onward. The entry first clears away older senses of the term, used for chartered company disputes and even for smuggling.

The case rests on exchange itself, as Adam Smith showed: in a free bargain both sides gain, so wider exchange means wider gain. Nations, like workshops, do best when each makes what it is fittest to make. Gladstone is quoted counting cheap postage, the end of taxes on print, and the repeal of the Navigation Act within the same freeing code. A long closing survey weighs free trade against protection and socialism, and lists the leading books on both sides.
britannica-1911-freycinet-charles-louis-:
Charles Louis de Saulces de Freycinet (1828- ), French statesman, was born at Foix on 14 November 1828. Trained at the École Polytechnique, he entered state service as a mining engineer. In 1858 he managed traffic for the Midi railway company, showing a rare gift for organisation. A noted report on the work of women and children in English factories followed.

In 1870 he ran Gambetta military cabinet and raised army after army. His direction of field generals brought friction, and Bourbaki eastern campaign ended in ruin. Senator from 1876, he became minister of public works in 1877 with a vast railway and canal plan. He headed the government in 1879 and again in 1882. His refusal to join the British attack on Alexandria ended French sway in Egypt. As minister of war from 1888 he held the post five years and built a general staff.
britannica-1911-freycinet-louis-claude-d:
Louis Claude Desaulses de Freycinet (1779-1842), French navigator, was born at Montélimart on 7 August 1779 and entered the navy in 1793. In 1800 he sailed with his brother under Captain Baudin in the Naturaliste and Géographe to chart the south and south-west coasts of Australia. An inlet and a cape on that coast still carry his name.

Back in Paris in 1805, he prepared the maps and finished the narrative of the Baudin voyage, printed from 1807 to 1816. In 1817 he commanded the Uranie on a three-year scientific cruise for pendulum measures, geography, magnetism, weather, and natural history across the Pacific and South America. Though the Uranie was lost on the Falklands on the way home, his collections and notes were rich. The voyage account filled 13 quarto and 4 folio volumes. He entered the Academy of Sciences in 1825 and died in 1842.
britannica-1911-frontenac-et-palluau-lou:
Louis de Buade, comte de Frontenac (1620-1698), was governor and lieutenant-general for the French king in New France, Canada. He entered the army young and served under the prince of Orange in Holland in 1635. He fought in the Low Countries and Italy, taking many wounds. He rose to colonel in 1643 and maréchal de camp in 1646 after the siege of Orbitello.

Marriage without consent, separation, and lavish living left him deep in debt. In 1669 he won glory leading French troops sent to defend Crete. He reached Quebec as governor on 12 September 1672 and pushed expansion against the wishes of Colbert. Quarrels with the intendant and with Bishop Laval, above all over drink licences, ended in his recall in 1682. He had built the fort at Cataraqui that bore his name. Restored later, he died at Quebec in November 1698, deeply mourned by the Canadians.
britannica-1911-galliffet-gaston-alexand:
Gaston Alexandre Auguste de Galliffet (1830-1909), marquis and prince de Martignes, was a French general born in Paris. The 1911 Britannica entry follows a career begun in 1848 that took him to Sevastopol, Italy, Algeria and Mexico. At the storming of Puebla in 1863 he was badly wounded.

In the Franco-German War he led the Chasseurs d'Afrique in the famed charge at Sedan and was taken prisoner. He then fought against the Paris Commune, earning a lasting name for severity there. Later he commanded army corps, won a European reputation on cavalry questions, and served as war minister from June 1899 to May 1900. He died on 8 July 1909.
britannica-1911-ganymede:
Ganymede, in Greek myth, was the son of Tros, king of Dardania, and Callirrhoë. The 1911 Britannica article calls him the most fair of all mortals. The gods carried him off to Olympus to pour drink for them. In the later tale Zeus did the deed himself, in the shape of an eagle. As payment, Zeus gave the boy's father a team of deathless horses, or a golden vine in some accounts.

Later ages linked Ganymede with the Nile and its life-giving floods. Star watchers matched him with Aquarius, the water bearer in the zodiac. So the cup bearer of heaven became the guard of the water supply on earth. The entry also notes how his tale was used to lend honour to the love of boys in Greece. Art took up the scene too, in a bronze group by the sculptor Leochares.
britannica-1911-gayangos-y-arce-pascual-:
Pascual de Gayangos y Arce (1809-1897) was a Spanish scholar and Orientalist, born at Seville on 21 June 1809. The 1911 Britannica entry has him schooled near Blois from age thirteen, then studying Arabic under Silvestre de Sacy from 1828. Treasury and foreign-office posts followed in Spain.

From 1836 he worked in England, writing for English periodicals and translating Almakkari's History of the Mahommedan Dynasties in Spain, published 1840-1843. Ticknor, the entry notes, owed him much help. In 1843 he became professor of Arabic at Madrid, holding the chair until 1881, then directed public instruction and sat as a senator. His last years went on cataloguing Spanish manuscripts in the British Museum. His best-known work treats Spanish romances of chivalry. He died in London on 4 October 1897.
britannica-1911-geestemunde:
Geestemunde is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a sea port town in Germany on a great river bank. A small stream parts it from a sister port town just north. Rail links it to the old trade city of Bremen inland.

The entry gives a count of more than twenty three thousand souls. The whole town is new, born when its first basin was dug in the late fifties. Wide basins take in the largest sea ships that call there. Its fish market is the chief one in the whole empire. Prices set at its sale hall rule fish prices across the land.
britannica-1911-genlis-stephanie-felicit:
Stephanie de Genlis was a French writer and teacher from a noble but poor house in Burgundy. The 1911 Britannica entry dates her birth to the mid seventeen hundreds. It notes her odd start in life. At age six she was made a canoness in a noble chapter. She took a grand title from a town at that time.

The entry stresses that all her schooling was done at home. It left gaps she spent her life to fill. Her harp skill and quick wit won praise in Paris while she was still a girl. Wed at sixteen to a colonel, she kept up her drive to learn and to teach. In time she joined a royal house as lady in wait. She then took charge of the young girls of that house as their guide.
britannica-1911-gentileschi-artemisia-an:
Artemisia and Orazio Gentileschi, Italian painters, are the subject of a joint entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Orazio, born at Pisa in the fifteen sixties, studied under his half brother Aurelio Lomi. In time he passed his teacher in skill. He later went to Rome to work.

In Rome he worked with the landscape painter Agostino Tasi. He painted the figures for the landscape grounds in that artist's works. Works in a Roman palace and in the great hall of the Quirinal are named. Some accounts credit those hall figures to him, while others dispute the claim. The entry sets out both sides of that question.
britannica-1911-georgswalde:
Georgswalde, a town of Bohemia in Austria, gets a brief place note in the 1911 Britannica. It lies north east of Prague by rail. With three joined villages it forms one commune. Its folk count for nineteen hundred was eight thousand one hundred thirty one. The town ranks as one of the old work towns of Bohemia.

Linen cloth is its chief trade, shared with the town of Rumburg near by. One joined village, Philippsdorf, drew crowds for a new cause. From eighteen sixty six tales of cures at an image of the Virgin made it a shrine. A grand new church rose there in eighteen eighty five to hold the image and its guests.
britannica-1911-gerando-marie-joseph-de:
Marie Joseph de Gerando (1772-1842) was a French philosopher, born at Lyons on 29 February 1772. The 1911 Britannica entry follows a life brushed by revolution: he fought in besieged Lyons in 1793, barely escaped death, and fled to Switzerland and Naples. Back in France, he served as a cavalry private at twenty-five.

His turn came with a prize essay for the Institute, on the influence of symbols on thought. Posts followed in quick order: the interior ministry in 1799, governor of Catalonia in 1812, and the council of state. He opened a Paris course in public and administrative law in 1819, and was made a baron in 1837. The entry lists his works, headed by the Histoire comparee des systemes de philosophie, with books on the education of deaf-mutes and on public charity. He died at Paris on 9 November 1842.
britannica-1911-gerlache-etienne-constan:
Belgian politician and historian Etienne Constantin de Gerlache, born in Luxemburg in seventeen eighty five, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied law in Paris and practised there for a time. He then settled at Liege, after the kingdom of the Netherlands was set up.

As a member of the states general he was a keen voice of the opposition. He backed a pact of Catholics and Liberals that paved the way for the revolt of eighteen thirty. He held posts in the interim government that followed. As president of congress he moved that Leopold of Saxe Coburg be invited to become king of the Belgians. He led the chamber of representatives in eighteen thirty two. For thirty five years he presided over the court of appeal.
britannica-1911-giers-nicholas-karlovich:
Nicholas Karlovich de Giers, who lived from 1820 to 1895, was a Russian statesman. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his slow rise in foreign service. He was schooled at the lyceum of Tsarskoye Selo. Lack of patrons and his Protestant, German stock held him back. At eighteen he joined the eastern desk of the ministry. Twenty years of junior posts in south east Europe followed. In 1863 he rose to envoy in Persia.

Six years in Persia led to posts in Switzerland and Sweden. In 1875 he took charge of the eastern desk and aided Prince Gorchakov. He had married that chief's niece. His gift for hard work was tested at once. Revolt in Herzegovina had just broken out. Russian volunteers were slipping to Serbia with quiet state connivance.
britannica-1911-girard-philippe-henri-de:
Philippe Henri de Girard (1775-1845) was a French mechanician, born at Lourmarin on 1 February 1775. The 1911 Britannica entry ties his name to flax-spinning machinery. Napoleon in 1810 offered a million francs for the best machine to spin flax, and Girard produced what was required.

The reward never came. Having borrowed against it to pay for the work, Girard fell into deep money trouble, and in 1853, after his death, his heirs got only a small pension. He left France in 1815 to build flax mills at Hirtenberg in Austria. In 1825 he went to Poland and raised a flax factory near Warsaw, round which the village of Girardow grew. He also built a Danube steamer in 1818. He died at Paris on 26 August 1845, creditors still pressing.
britannica-1911-girardin-delphine-de:
Delphine de Girardin (1804-1855) was a French author, born at Aix-la-Chapelle on 26 January 1804. The 1911 Britannica entry makes her the daughter of Madame Sophie Gay, raised amid a brilliant literary circle. Two volumes of poems came in 1824 and 1825, and a visit to Italy in 1827 ended with her crowned in the Capitol at Rome.

In 1831 she married Emile de Girardin, and a new career opened. Her Paris sketches in La Presse, signed Charles de Launay, were gathered as Lettres parisiennes in 1843 and won a brilliant success. The entry lists her romances and plays, from La Canne de Monsieur de Balzac to Lady Tartufe. Gautier, Balzac, Musset and Hugo frequented her drawing-room. She died on 29 June 1855. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; her entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-girardin-emile-de:
Emile de Girardin (1802-1881) was a French publicist, born at Paris in 1802, the son of General Alexandre de Girardin. The 1911 Britannica entry clears away a false tale of Swiss birth in 1806, recognized as wrong in 1837. His first book, the novel Emile of 1827, dealt with his own birth and early life.

His power was cheap print. His Journal des connaissances utiles had 120,000 subscribers, and his Almanach de France of 1834 ran to a million copies. In 1836 he founded La Presse at forty francs a year, opening the age of cheap journalism. A duel with Armand Carrel marked his early career. The entry follows his turns through 1848, his later papers La Liberte and Le Petit Journal, and his attacks on MacMahon in 1877. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; his entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-gironde:
Gironde is a maritime department of south-western France, formed from four divisions of the old province of Guyenne. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 4,140 square miles and 823,925 people in 1906. It takes its name from the Gironde estuary, where the Garonne and Dordogne unite, and faces the Bay of Biscay to the west.

The west of the department is the Landes: morass and sandy plain planted with pines. A long line of pine-bound dunes holds it from the sea. The lakes of Carcans and Lacanau and the Bay of Arcachon lie there. The east is hill and dale, very fertile in the Gironde valley. The estuary runs about 45 miles, two to six miles wide, its islands and mud banks splitting it into two channels. The long entry continues through rivers, produce, towns and history.
britannica-1911-glanvill-ranulf-de:
Ranulf de Glanvill (died 1190) was chief justiciar of England and the reputed author of a book on English law. The 1911 Britannica entry says he was born at Stratford in Suffolk, in a year unknown, and first comes to view as sheriff of Yorkshire from 1163 to 1170. At Alnwick in 1174 the king of Scots surrendered to him.

In 1180 he became chief justiciar, and in effect viceroy during Henry II's frequent absences abroad. The entry credits him with helping complete Henry's judicial reforms. Richard I removed and imprisoned him until a heavy ransom was paid; freed, he took the cross and died at the siege of Acre in 1190. His name rests on the Tractatus de legibus, the treatise on the laws and customs of England that he wrote or supervised, a practical guide to procedure in the king's court.
britannica-1911-glucoside:
A glucoside is a substance that yields a sugar when broken down. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says the sugar is most often glucose. The split is made by plain chemistry or by a ferment. The name first covered plant products of this kind. Their other half was most often a sharp scented compound. Some known cases break that rule, such as sinigrin.

The name has since spread to made goods in the lab. It now covers ethers formed from glucose in acid and alcohol. Even cane sugar is classed in the group by some. Not all glucosides yield glucose, though. Some give rhamnose or iso-dulcite instead. Much work has gone into the non sugar half of these compounds. Their make up has been found for many of them. Some have been built up again in the lab from scratch.
britannica-1911-goeje-michael-jan-de:
Michael Jan de Goeje (1836-1909) was a Dutch scholar of eastern languages, and his career is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Friesland, he took to Arabic early under the teachers Dozy and Juynboll. He earned his doctorate at Leiden in 1860, then spent a year studying manuscripts at Oxford.

The entry lists his editions of Arabic texts, with his great edition of Tabari as the most valued of them. In 1883 he became professor of Arabic at Leiden, a post he held until 1906. It also notes his work on town affairs and schools in Leiden, his lead role at a congress of scholars in Algiers in 1905, and the honors he received.
britannica-1911-goes-damiao-de:
Damiao de Goes, a Portuguese humanist who lived from 1502 to 1574, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born of a noble family at Alemquer in February 1502. Under King John the Third he served abroad from 1523 on state and trade tasks. He traveled over most of Europe and knew its top scholars.

Goes was a friend and pupil of Erasmus from 1532 and took his degree at Padua in 1538. At Louvain in 1542 he led the defense when the French besieged the town. Back in Portugal, foes charged him with Lutheran leanings. Still, in 1548 he was made chief keeper of the archives. In 1558 he was charged to write a history of King Manoel's reign.
britannica-1911-gohrde:
Gohrde is a forest of Germany, in the Prussian province of Hanover, just west of the Elbe between Wittenberg and Luneburg. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it an area of about 85 square miles. It is famous for its oaks, its beeches and its game preserves.

Two historical notes fill the rest of the short entry. On 16 September 1813 the allies under Wallmoden won a victory in the forest over French forces under Pecheur. The hunting-box standing in the forest was built in 1689 and restored by Ernest Augustus, king of Hanover. It is known to history for the constitution of Gohrde, promulgated there in 1719. The notice is a brief gazetteer piece: size, trees, game, the one battle, and the one document.
britannica-1911-golden-horde:
Golden Horde was the name of a body of Tatars who overran much of eastern Europe in the middle of the 1200s, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. They founded in Russia the Tatar empire known as the Empire of the Golden Horde, or Western Kipchaks. They invaded about 1237 under Bātū Khan, a grandson of Jenghiz Khan.

After sweeping across Russia, they pushed into Silesia, Poland, and Hungary, and beat Henry II of Silesia at Liegnitz in 1241. That win cost so much that Bātū turned back and settled in a splendid tent on the Volga, whence the name golden camp. The article then lists his heirs and tells how, after the death of Jānī-Beg, the empire fell into confusion among rival khans.
britannica-1911-gongora-y-argote-luis-de:
Luis de Gongora y Argote (1561-1627) was a Spanish lyric poet, born at Cordova on 11 July 1561. The 1911 Britannica entry has him studying law at Salamanca from fifteen, taking only an ordinary pass degree. Cervantes praised him in the Galatea in 1585, the year he took minor orders and gained a canonry at Cordova.

Ordained about 1605-1606, he lived mostly at Valladolid and Madrid, stabbing at everything, a contemporary said, with his satirical pen. Honour came late and slight: honorary chaplain to Philip III, through the duke of Sandoval. His poems, sonnets, odes, ballads and the larger Soledades and Polifemo, carry the tortuous estilo culto that bears his name. The entry censures his Latinisms and obscurity, yet calls him a man of rare genius, spoiled only in his imitators. He died at Cordova on 24 May 1627.
britannica-1911-gontaut-marie-josephine-:
Marie Josephine Louise de Gontaut is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. She lived from 1773 to 1857 and was born in Paris. Her father had charge of the young king Louis the Sixteenth as a boy. She learned with the Orleans children as a girl. When revolt broke out she fled France with her mother. They went first to Coblenz and then to England.

In England she wed a French lord and later came back to France. At court she cared for the young heirs of the crown. She had charge of the prince who was heir to the throne. In 1827 she was made a duchess in her own right. She followed the exiled royal house to Scotland and to Prague. A clash with a court lord led to her dismissal in 1834.
britannica-1911-goudimel-claude:
Claude Goudimel was a composer of the 1500s, born about 1510, most likely at Besançon, as this 1911 Britannica article argues. He calls himself a native of that town in print, which weighs against a claim that he was born near Avignon. Little is known of his early schooling, but his fine Latin letters show a good classical training alongside his music.

He is thought to have led a music school in Rome in 1540, with Palestrina said to be among his pupils. Later in Paris he helped issue a setting of Horace's Odes in 1555. His weightiest work was a four-part setting, out in 1565, of the French Psalms of Marot and Beza. The tunes, long credited to him, are now known to come from popular songs of the time, and some are still sung by the French Protestant Church.
britannica-1911-gouvion-saint-cyr-lauren:
French marshal Laurent Gouvion Saint Cyr, born at Toul in seventeen sixty four, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At eighteen he went to Rome to study painting. He kept up art study in Paris, but never took painting as his trade.

In seventeen ninety two he was chosen captain in a volunteer unit. He served on the staff of a general, and rose fast. Within two years he was a general of division. He led the centre of an army on the Rhine in seventeen ninety six. His cool head aided a famed retreat that year. He later led the army of Italy, then a wing in Germany. In eighteen hundred he won a victory at Biberach.
britannica-1911-grain-trade:
The grain trade is the subject of a survey entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry opens by using the trade to show how complex modern life had become. The ordinary bread sold in Great Britain, it notes, draws on produce from nearly every country outside the tropics. That single loaf thus maps a world system.

Wheat has been grown from remote antiquity, the text explains. In a wild state it is practically unknown today. Claims that it was found wild between the Euphrates and Tigris have never been confirmed. Unless the plant is cared for with effort, the species dies out fast. Modern trials in cross breeding are then introduced.
britannica-1911-granada-luis-de:
Granada, Luis de is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Spanish preacher and writer on the religious life. Born in 1504 at Granada to poor parents named Sarria, he lost his father young. A child of the Alhambra, he served as page in the house of the alcalde and was schooled with the sons of the house when his gifts showed.

Sent to Valladolid for study, he was then made prior of the ruined convent of Scala Caeli in the mountains of Cordova. He rebuilt the house over eight years and began his work as a zealous reformer. His famed Guia de Peccadores was laid on the Index in 1559 under charges of heresy. The ban was lifted in 1576, and his works kept their worth for later readers.
britannica-1911-granvella-antoine-perren:
Antoine Perrenot de Granvella is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a church prince and envoy born in France in fifteen seventeen. His father rose to be chief aide to the emperor of the age. The son read law and divinity at schools in Italy and Louvain.

The entry tells how he became a bishop at the age of twenty three. He sat at great diets and at the first meets of a famed church council. His skill in talks won him hard and fine tasks from the court. That work taught him the cross tides of politics in all Europe. His name ranks high among the church statesmen of his era.
britannica-1911-gray-john-de:
John de Gray is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a bishop of Norwich. He died in 1214, the heading notes. He entered the service of Prince John as a young clerk. When John took the throne in 1199, Gray rose fast. He became bishop of Norwich in September 1200. The king then tried to force him into the primacy in 1205. That move began John's long, fatal quarrel with Pope Innocent the Third.

Gray was a hard working royal officer in many fields. He served in finance, in justice, and in action. He used his place to enrich himself and his kin. In 1209 he went to Ireland as justiciar. He pushed the English frontier north and west there. He fought campaigns on the Shannon and in Fermanagh. In 1212 he met a great defeat in that work. His skill with money may explain the king's favour.
britannica-1911-gray-walter-de:
Walter de Gray (died 1255) was an English prelate and statesman, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry follows his rise under King John. He was a nephew of John de Gray, bishop of Norwich, and was educated at Oxford. Royal favour drove his fast advance in church and state. He became the king’s chancellor in 1205, and bishop elect of Lichfield in 1210.

Gray was not allowed to keep that bishopric in the end. He became bishop of Worcester in 1214 and gave up the chancellorship that year. He stood with John when the king signed Magna Carta in June 1215. Soon after, he left England on the king’s business. While he was away, he was pressed into the archbishopric of York. His election owed much to the good offices of John and of Pope Innocent the Third.
britannica-1911-grenade:
A grenade, says the 1911 Britannica, takes its name from the French word for a pomegranate, whose shape the weapon copies. It is a small spherical explosive vessel thrown by hand. Hand-grenades served in war in the 16th century, though the word also meant a shell fired from a gun, a sense surviving in the German Granate.

From about 1660 special troops called grenadiers threw them, and they appear through the wars of the 17th and 18th centuries. Obsolete in the 19th century, they found a new lease of life in the 20th. At the siege of Port Arthur in 1904, modern hand-grenades with powerful explosives proved very effective. The entry ends with peaceful cousins: glass grenades of chemicals for putting out fires, and strong-smelling vessels used to find defects in a drain or sewer.
britannica-1911-gribeauval-jean-baptiste:
Jean Baptiste de Gribeauval (1715-1789) was a French artillery general, son of a magistrate of Amiens, born there on 15 September 1715. The 1911 Britannica entry has him entering the royal artillery as a volunteer in 1732. Twenty years of regimental duty and scientific work followed, and in 1752 he captained a company of miners.

Lent to the Austrian army in the Seven Years' War, he served as a general of artillery. The siege of Glatz and the defence of Schweidnitz were his chief exploits, rewarded with the cross of the Maria Theresa order. Back in France he rose to lieutenant-general, yet spent years in disfavour. Only in 1776, as first inspector of artillery, could he carry out the reforms that are his chief title to fame. The entry points to his published tables of artillery construction and the 1776 regulation. He died in 1789.
britannica-1911-grimoard-philippe-henri-:
Philippe Henri, comte de Grimoard (1753-1815), was a French soldier and military writer. The 1911 Britannica entry has him entering the royal army at sixteen. In 1775 he published his Essai theorique et pratique sur les batailles. Louis XVI soon placed him in his own military cabinet, chiefly for schemes of army reform.

By the Revolution he was among the king's most valued counsellors, in politics as in war, though only a colonel. He was marked out as the next minister of war. In 1791 he prepared the scheme of defence for France that later served the Committee of Public Safety well. The events of 1792 ended his military career, and the rest of his life went to military books. The entry lists them: campaigns of Turenne, light troops, the conquests of Gustavus Adolphus, lives of Frederick the Great and others.
britannica-1911-guibert-jacques-antoine-:
Jacques Antoine Hippolyte Guibert (1743–1790) was a French general. He was also a leading military writer. Born at Montauban, he campaigned in Germany from age thirteen. His father was chief of staff to Marshal de Broglie. Guibert won the cross of St Louis in Corsica. He also won a colonel's rank there in 1767. His Essai général de tactique appeared in 1770.

That book was the finest essay on war of its age. It was translated into English, German and even Persian. Its broad view of Europe's military state sets it apart. One passage foresaw a coming revolution in war. National armies, it argued, would beat standing armies. Frederick the Great received Guibert warmly in 1773. From 1775 he helped St Germain reform the French army. St Germain's fall dragged Guibert down with him. The Revolution recalled him to the War Office.
britannica-1911-guichen-luc-urbain-de-bo:
Luc Urbain de Bouëxic, comte de Guichen (1712–1790), was a French admiral. He entered the navy in 1730 as a garde de la Marine. Promotion came slowly at first. He reached lieutenant de vaisseau only in 1748. Post captain followed in 1756. The cross of St Louis came in 1748. In 1775 he commanded the training frigate Terpsichore. Rear-admiral followed in 1776.

France had become the ally of the Americans in the War of Independence. Guichen fought at Ushant in July 1779. In 1780 Rodney opposed him in the West Indies. Guichen handled his fleet with great skill and caution. He kept the weather gauge and denied Rodney a close action. The French islands suffered no harm that campaign. In December 1781 Kempenfelt caught his convoy in the Bay of Biscay. Twenty transports were taken and the mission failed. Guichen lacked Suffren's fighting instinct, the verdict runs.
britannica-1911-harlay-de-champvallon-fr:
Francois de Harlay de Champvallon (1625-1695) was the fifth archbishop of Paris. He was born in that city on 14 August 1625. His uncle held the see of Rouen before him. The young Harlay was given the abbey of Jumieges fresh from school. At just twenty-six he followed his uncle as archbishop of Rouen. In 1671 he moved to the see of Paris.

Harlay was made a commander of the order of the Saint Esprit and joined the French Academy. The king named him for a cardinal's hat in 1690. In his early years he stood firm with Mazarin and is said to have helped bring him back from exile. His private life drew much talk, but he had skill in affairs and fine speech. He won the lasting favour of Louis XIV by backing the rights claimed for the French church in 1682.
britannica-1911-hassam-childe:
Childe Hassam, an American painter of scenes and land views, gets a short art note in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Boston, he learned in Paris with Boulanger and Lefebvre as his guides. The bright school of France soon shaped his hand and eye. He struck a style of his own in bold hue and pure dabs of paint. Prize wins at world fairs crowd the short note in a long row.

Paris gave him a bronze prize in eighteen eighty nine for his work. Chicago, Boston, and more towns gave him prizes in the years that came next. A gold prize from a Philadelphia school stands out in that list. He held seats in art groups in America, France, and Germany. The note stays a bare list of posts and prize years for the most part.
britannica-1911-herberay-des-essarts-nic:
Nicolas de Herberay des Essarts (d. about 1557) was a French translator, born in Picardy, who served in the artillery. At the express wish of Francis I he turned the first eight books of Amadis de Gaul into French, printing them between 1540 and 1548. Other hands translated the books that followed. His rendering made the Spanish romance a French classic of its age.

His other work also came from Spanish. It includes L'Amant maltraité de sa mye in 1539, the first book of the chronicle of Dom Florès de Grèce in 1552, and L'Horloge des princes in 1555, taken from Guevara. He also translated the works of Josephus, printed in 1557, the year of his death. The Amadis he began later crossed the Channel: Anthony Munday turned it into English in 1619. Readers meet in this short life one of the men who carried Spanish romance into French print.
britannica-1911-herrera-fernando-de:
Fernando de Herrera, a Spanish poet who lived from about 1534 to 1597, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Seville and took minor orders in the church. He wrote fervent love poems to the countess of Gelves. The entry warns that these may be cool feats of craft in the manner of Petrarch.

Most space goes to his notes on the poems of Garcilaso de la Vega, printed in 1580. Those notes drew him into long feuds with other men of letters. His odes on the battle of Lepanto and on Don John of Austria are praised most. They earn him first place among the poets of Andalusia, the entry holds.
britannica-1911-herrera-y-tordesillas-an:
Antonio de Herrera y Tordesillas is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a Spanish historian. He lived from 1549 to 1625. He was born at Cuellar in the province of Segovia. Both his parents came of good family stock. After study in his own land, he went to Italy. There he became secretary to Vespasian Gonzago. When Gonzago was made viceroy of Navarre, Herrera came back to Spain.

Gonzago praised his skill to King Philip the Second. The king made him first historian of the Indies. He also made him a historian of Castile. With a good salary, Herrera gave his life to writing. He kept his posts into the reign of Philip the Fourth. That king made him secretary of state near his death. He died at Madrid in March 1625. His general history of the Indies is his most prized work.
britannica-1911-hirsch-maurice-de:
Maurice de Hirsch, a banker and giver who lived from 1831 to 1896, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Munich, he came from a famed German Jewish family. His grandfather was the first Jewish landowner in Bavaria to be ennobled. His father was banker to the Bavarian king and became a baron in 1869.

Hirsch went into business at age seventeen and joined a Brussels banking house in 1855. He made a large fortune from rail grants in Austria, Turkey, and the Balkans. Gains from sugar and copper deals added to his wealth. He lived in splendour in Paris, London, and Hungary. Yet much of his time went to help for Jews who faced persecution. He gave a million francs twice to a French Jewish school alliance. His largest work was aid for Jews in Russia.
britannica-1911-hita-gines-perez-de:
Gines Perez de Hita, born about 1544, was a Spanish novelist and poet from Mula in Murcia. The 1911 Britannica entry notes his service in the war against the Moriscos in 1569 to 1571. He wrote a rhymed history of Lorca in 1572 that stayed unprinted until 1889. Wide fame came from a later work on the last days of Granada.

That work claims to rest on an Arabic source by one Aben Hamin, a made up name. In truth it is a historical novel, perhaps the first of its kind to win readers. Its first part tells with great colour how the Emir court fell. Court life there is drawn with warmth that shaped later tales of Spain.
britannica-1911-hooch-pieter-de:
Pieter de Hooch (1629–c. 1678) was a Dutch painter, a native of Rotterdam who wandered early to Haarlem and the Hague. In 1654 he was back in Rotterdam, marrying Jannetje van der Burch of Delft. From 1655 to 1657 he belonged to the painters' guild of Delft. Then all trace of him is lost until about 1668, when he appears in Amsterdam. Dated pictures prove him alive in 1677, and he died probably soon after.

De Hooch is one of the kindliest painters of homely subjects Holland has produced, a fellow pupil, it seems, of van der Meer and Maes. He painted only one large canvas, which burned at Rotterdam in 1864. His small pieces show perfect finish and a fine eye. He is most at home in interiors lit by shifting daylight through doors and windows. Drawing-rooms with dancing ladies and cavaliers suit him, but cottages and courtyards with housewives and children suit him better.
britannica-1911-houdetot-elisabeth-franc:
Elisabeth Françoise Sophie de la Live de Bellegarde, comtesse de Houdetot (1730–1813), was born in 1730 and married the comte de Houdetot in 1748. In 1753 she formed a union with the marquis de Saint-Lambert that lasted until his death. Fame came to her from one chapter of Rousseau's Confessions, where he tells of his own unreturned passion for her.

Asked about that account, Madame de Houdetot replied that Rousseau had much exaggerated. A view quite different from his can be found in the memoirs of Madame d'Epinay, her sister-in-law. The short entry adds a pointer to Saint-Marc-Girardin's study of her relations with Rousseau, in the Revue des deux mondes of September 1853. Her own life, long and mostly private, is known to posterity chiefly through the two writers who quarrelled over her portrait.
britannica-1911-iriarte-y-oropesa-tomas-:
Tomas de Iriarte y Oropesa, a Spanish poet who lived from 1750 to 1791, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Orotava on the island of Tenerife, he was educated at Madrid under his uncle, the king's librarian. At eighteen he began his writing life by translating French plays for the royal theatre.

In 1770 he issued an original comedy under an anagram of his name. He then became an official translator and later keeper of records in the war office. A long teaching poem on music in 1780 drew some notice in Italy and at home. His fame rests chiefly on his literary fables of 1781, set in many metres. They mock writers and their methods with wit, though the entry says their merit has been much overstated.
britannica-1911-iturbide-augustin-de:
Augustin de Iturbide was emperor of Mexico from May 1822 to March 1823, and his rise is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in September 1783 at Valladolid in Mexico. His father was an Old Spaniard from Pampeluna who had settled there with his creole wife. The boy got a better schooling than was then the rule in Mexico.

He joined the army and in 1810 held a lieutenant's post in the regiment of his home town. That year the rising under Hidalgo broke out, and Iturbide served in the royal army. He had great courage and a gift for the war of small bands. In December 1813 he and General Llano beat Morelos at Valladolid, and he won again at Pururuan the next month. By 1815 he led the army of the north, but charges of graft and cruelty brought his recall in 1816.
britannica-1911-joinville-francois-ferdi:
Francois Ferdinand Philippe Louis Marie, Prince de Joinville (1818-1900), was a French prince and naval officer, and his career fills an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Third son of Louis Philippe, king of the French, he was born at Neuilly and trained for the navy, becoming lieutenant in 1836.

The entry recounts his first fame at the bombardment of San Juan de Ulloa in 1838, where he took a Mexican general prisoner with his own hand. In 1840 he brought Napoleon's remains home from Saint Helena. He bombarded Tangier in 1844, rose to vice-admiral, and fell with his family in the revolution of 1848.
britannica-1911-joinville-jean-sire-de:
Jean de Joinville is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French lord and writer of history in Old French. Born in twelve twenty four, he led a noble house in Champagne. His land lay near Paris and felt the pull of the royal court.

The entry ranks him as the second great prose voice of his tongue. He first came to court for the knighting of a royal prince. Seven years on he took the cross and sailed with the saint king. War taught him hard lessons in craft and in command. His book of that crusade keeps his name fresh through the ages.
britannica-1911-jouy-victor-joseph-etien:
Victor Joseph Étienne de Jouy, a French dramatist who lived from 1764 to 1846, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Versailles, he took an army post at eighteen and sailed for South America with the governor of Guiana. He came home at once to finish his studies, then served again, this time in India.

India gave him bold adventures that he later turned to use in his writing. Back in France for the Revolution, he fought with honour and rose in rank, but he would not drink a toast to Marat and had to flee for his life. Fresh charges of secret letters to an English envoy were thrown out, yet he quit the army, worn by attack and by his wounds. He turned to the stage, and his opera La Vestale, with music by Spontini, ran for a hundred nights in 1807.
britannica-1911-jovellanos-gaspar-melcho:
Gaspar Melchor de Jovellanos, a Spanish statesman and author, was born at Gijon in Asturias in seventeen forty four. He chose law and studied at Oviedo, Avila, and Alcala. In seventeen sixty seven he became a criminal judge at Seville. His honesty and skill won him a judgeship in Madrid in seventeen seventy eight. Two years later he joined the council of military orders.

In Madrid he took a good place in its learned societies. For one such society he wrote his best known work, a report on a draft farm law. When his friend Cabarrus fell, Jovellanos spent seven years in near exile at Gijon. There he founded a school for reform in his home province. In seventeen ninety seven he came back as minister of justice.
britannica-1911-juge-boffille-de:
Boffille de Juge (d. 1502) was a French Italian adventurer and statesman of the del Giudice family of Amalfi, which followed the fortunes of the house of Anjou. When John of Anjou was beaten in Italy in 1461 and fled to Provence, Boffille went with him. The Angevin princes charged him with upholding their claims on Catalonia by force of arms.

Louis XI of France drew Boffille into his own service, made him a chamberlain, and gave him the vice royalty of Roussillon and Cerdagne in 1471. Lands taken from others followed, among them the countship of Castres in 1476, and he handled talks with Flanders and England. His marriage in 1480 to Marie d'Albret fixed his standing in the south. He sat as a judge at the trial of René of Alençon and served with zeal. Then the bishop of Castres regained his see, and the heirs of Nemours sued for Castres.
britannica-1911-jussieu-de:
De Jussieu is the name of a French family that came to note at the close of the 16th century and for a hundred and fifty years was famed for its botanists. The entry, which sits in a file shared with jury and justice material, gives the chief members in turn. Antoine (1686–1758) succeeded Tournefort at the Jardin des Plantes and edited his works, while practising medicine among the poor.

His brother Bernard (1699–1777) published little, but in 1759 he set out the plants of the Trianon garden by his own plan of grouping, the basis of his nephew's great work. Joseph (1704–1779) spent thirty six years in South America with a survey party and sent home the first seeds of the Peruvian heliotrope. The nephew, Antoine Laurent (1748–1836), issued the Genera plantarum in 1789, the base of modern plant grouping. His son Adrien carried the line on, and with him the dynasty closed.
britannica-1911-kenealy-edward-vaughan-h:
Edward Vaughan Hyde Kenealy (1819–1880) was an Irish barrister and author, born at Cork on the 2nd of July 1819, the son of a local merchant. He was trained at Trinity College, Dublin, called to the Irish bar in 1840 and to the English bar in 1847, and built a fair practice in criminal cases. In 1868 he became a queen's counsel and a bencher of Gray's Inn.

His fame came only in 1873, when he acted as leading counsel for the Tichborne claimant. His violent handling of the case became a public scandal. After the verdict went against his client, he started a paper to plead the cause and attack the judges. His conduct ran so far that in 1874 his Inn disbenched and disbarred him. He then raised a stir across the country over his grievances, and in 1875 he was elected to parliament for Stoke. No member would present him when he took his seat.
britannica-1911-keratry-auguste-hilarion:
Auguste Hilarion, Comte de Kératry (1769–1859), was a French writer and politician, born at Rennes on the 28th of December 1769. Coming to Paris in 1790, he fell in with Bernardin de St Pierre. After twice being jailed in the Terror he withdrew to Brittany, where he gave himself to letters until 1814.

In 1818 he went back to Paris as deputy for Finistère and sat in the Chamber until 1824, becoming one of the known liberal leaders. He was re elected in 1827, took an eager part in the making of the July monarchy, was named a councillor of state in 1830, and in 1837 a peer of France. After the coup d'état of 1851 he left public life. His writings range from early tales and verse to studies of morals, beauty in art, and the history of France.
britannica-1911-kersaint-armand-guy-simo:
Armand Guy Simon de Coetnempren, Count of Kersaint, was a French sailor and lawmaker in this 1911 Britannica life. Born at Paris in seventeen forty two, he came of an old sea house. His father was a famed sea chief of the French fleet. He joined the navy in seventeen fifty five as a young boy. Brave work on his father ship won him a post in seventeen fifty seven.

By seventeen eighty two he held the rank of captain in the fleet. At the great revolt he took the side of the plain born sea men. A tract by his hand hit the rights of birth with sharp words. He set a plan to rebuild the navy, but the hall turned it down. In the hall he backed the fall of King Louis in seventeen ninety two.
britannica-1911-koninck-laurent-guillaum:
Laurent Guillaume de Koninck (1809–1887) was a Belgian palaeontologist and chemist, born at Louvain on the 3rd of May 1809. He studied medicine at the university of his home town and became an assistant in its chemical schools in 1831. In 1856 he was made professor of chemistry at Liége, a post he held for the rest of his life.

From about 1835 Koninck spent his free hours on the Carboniferous fossils found near Liége. He became known above all for his work on the mollusca, brachiopods, crustacea and crinoids of the Belgian Carboniferous limestone. The Geological Society of London gave him its Wollaston medal in 1875. In 1876 Liége made him professor of palaeontology. His books include a text on inorganic chemistry (1839) and a large study of the fossil animals of the Belgian Carboniferous beds (1842–1844). He died at Liége on the 16th of July 1887.
britannica-1911-la-badie-jean-de:
Jean de la Badie (1610–1674) was a French divine, founder of the school called the Labadists. He was born at Bourg, near Bordeaux, on the 13th of February 1610, the son of the governor of Guienne. Strong views on prayer, on the direct work of the Holy Spirit, and on grace and predestination set him against his order, and he left it. He became a preacher at Bordeaux, Paris and Amiens, where in 1640 he was made a canon.

Cardinal Mazarin's enmity drove La Badie to a Carmelite hermitage at Graville. A study of Calvin's Institutes showed him his true home, and in 1650 he joined the Reformed Church and took the chair of theology at Montauban. At Orange from 1657 he ruled his flock with strict discipline, against dancing and cards. His teaching held the church to be a fellowship of the born again, with baptism for believers only.
britannica-1911-la-bourdonnais-bertrand-:
Bertrand François, Count Mahé de la Bourdonnais (1699–1753), was a naval commander born at Saint Malo on the 11th of February 1699. He joined the French India Company as a lieutenant in 1718. Made captain in 1724, he showed such courage at the taking of Mahé that the town's name was added to his own. In 1735 he became governor of the Île de France and the Île de Bourbon,.

War with Britain put La Bourdonnais at the head of a fleet in Indian waters. He saved Mahé, relieved Dupleix at Pondicherry and had a share in the siege of Madras in 1746. His quarrel with Dupleix then ruined him. On reaching France he was arrested in 1748 on a charge of dishonest rule. He spent over two years in the Bastille and was cleared at his trial in 1751, but his health was broken. He died at Paris on the 10th of November 1753.
britannica-1911-la-calprenede-gauthier-d:
Gauthier de Costes, seigneur de la Calprenède (c. 1610–1663), was a French novelist and dramatist, born at the Château of Tolgou, near Sarlat in Dordogne, in 1609 or 1610. He studied at Toulouse, then came to Paris and joined the regiment of the guards. In 1650 he became a gentleman-in-ordinary of the royal household. He died in 1663 from a kick by his horse.

La Calprenède wrote long heroic romances that Boileau held up to scorn. They include Cassandre, in 10 volumes (1642–1650), Cléopatre (1648) and Faramond (1661). Les Nouvelles (1661) came out under his wife's name but is generally held to be his. His plays have less life than the novels at their best. The finest of them, Le Comte d'Essex (1638), gave Thomas Corneille ideas for his own tragedy of that name.
britannica-1911-la-chaise-francois-de:
François de la Chaise (1624–1709) was confessor to Louis XIV. He was born at the château of Aix in Forey on the 25th of August 1624, a grandnephew on his mother's side of Père Coton, confessor of Henry IV. He entered the Society of Jesus young and taught philosophy at Lyons. In 1674 he was named confessor of Louis XIV,.

With Madame de Maintenon, La Chaise worked to end the king's tie with Madame de Montespan, and the king's marriage to Maintenon was held in his presence . In the long fight between Louis XIV and Pope Innocent XI over the Gallican Church he backed the royal right. He must bear a large share of blame for the revoking of the Edict of Nantes, though not for the cruel steps taken against the Protestants. Towards the Jansenists he used a calming hand on the king's zeal.
britannica-1911-la-chalotais-louis-rene-:
Louis René de Caradeuc de la Chalotais (1701–1785) was a French jurist, born at Rennes on the 6th of March 1701. For sixty years he was procureur général at the parliament of Brittany. A keen foe of the Jesuits, he drew up in 1761 a memoir on the constitutions of their Order that did much to bring about its suppression in France. In 1763 he printed an "Essay on National Education,".

The same year a fight began between the Estates of Brittany and the governor, the duc d'Aiguillon. The parliament took the Estates' side and forbade taxes they had not approved. Two rude anonymous letters then reached the minister Saint-Florentin, and three experts in handwriting swore they were La Chalotais's work. He was arrested with his son and four others. Voltaire told how, in his prison at Saint Malo, he lacked even ink to write his defence.
britannica-1911-la-chaussee-pierre-claud:
Pierre Claude Nivelle de la Chaussée (1692–1754) was a French dramatist, born in Paris in 1692. In 1731 he printed an Épître à Clio, a poem defending verse in tragedy. He was forty before his first play, La Fausse Antipathie (1734), appeared. Le Préjugé à la mode (1735) followed, then L'École des amis (1737). After a failed attempt at tragedy he came back to comedy with Mélanide (1741).

In Mélanide the kind called comédie larmoyante stands fully formed: comedy made to draw tears, not laughter. The new way broke the sharp line between tragedy and comedy, and it led on to the domestic drama of Diderot and Sedaine. Critics struck hard at it. Piron mocked him in a famous epigram, and Voltaire scorned the tearful comedy, though he wrote a play of the sort himself. L'École des mères (1744) and La Gouvernante (1747) rank with his best work.
britannica-1911-la-cloche-james-de:
James de la Cloche (1644?–1669) is a figure whom Lord Acton brought into English history in 1862. Acton worked from papers found by Father Boero in the Jesuit archives at Rome. The papers support a claim: that Charles II had a natural son, James, born at Jersey. A Jesuit register shows that a Jacobus de la Cloche, aged 24 and from Jersey, entered the house of novices at Rome on the 2nd of April 1668.

Those papers purport to be written by Charles II at Whitehall, in 1665 and 1667. In both, Charles owns James as his natural son, yet says that to own him in public would imperil the peace of the kingdoms. A further paper is a letter in which Charles tells Oliva, general of the Jesuits, of his wish to be received in secret into the Roman Church. James, once ordained, is to come to England and receive him.
britannica-1911-la-condamine-charles-mar:
Charles Marie de la Condamine (1701–1774) was a French geographer and mathematician, born at Paris on the 28th of January 1701. He was trained for the army, but turned to science and travel. After a scientific trip in the Levant in 1731, he joined Louis Godin and Pierre Bouguer in the expedition sent to Peru in 1735. Its task was to fix the length of a degree of the meridian near the equator.

La Condamine fell out with his chiefs, and the party was beset by troubles. At last he split from the rest, went from Quito down the Amazon, and reached Cayenne. His was the first scientific exploration of that river. Back in Paris in 1744, he printed his measures and travels with a map of the Amazon in 1745. His journal of the South American voyage came out at Paris in 1751. He died at Paris on the 4th of February 1774.
britannica-1911-la-cruz-ramon-de:
Ramón de la Cruz (1731–1794) was a Spanish dramatist, born at Madrid on the 28th of March 1731. He worked as a clerk in the ministry of finance. His fame rests on the sainetes, short farcical sketches of city life played between the acts of a longer piece. He wrote three hundred of them.

La Cruz printed a choice of his sainetes in ten volumes at Madrid between 1786 and 1791. He died on the 5th of March 1794. The best of the pieces, such as Las Tertulias de Madrid, are praised as delightful pieces of satiric observation of Madrid life.
britannica-1911-la-cueva-juan-de:
Juan de la Cueva (1550?–1609?) was a Spanish dramatist and poet, born at Seville. About 1579 he began writing for the stage. His fourteen plays were printed in 1588, and they are the first signs of the methods that Lope de Vega would bring to full growth. Cueva dropped the Senecan model that had ruled Spain until then. He took his themes from national legend, from history, from fresh victories and from the life of his own day.

That mix of epic and real elements, and his use of many metres, prepared the way for the Spanish romantic drama of the 17th century. His play El Infamador has a special interest: its character Leucino looks ahead to the classic type of Don Juan. As a force that set things moving, Cueva counts for much in history.
