His epic poem La Conquista de Bética (1603) shows his weakness as an artist.
britannica-1911-la-dixmerie-nicolas-bric:
Nicolas Bricaire de la Dixmerie (c. 1730–1791) was a French man of letters, born at Lamothe in Haute-Marne. While still young he moved to Paris, and the rest of his life was spent in literary work. He died on the 26th of November 1791. His many books cover tales, literary history and praise of great writers.

Among his works are the Contes philosophiques et moraux (1765) and Les Deux Âges du goût et du génie sous Louis XIV et sous Louis XV (1769). That book sets the two ages side by side and gives the verdict to the latter. He also wrote L'Espagne littéraire (1774), an Éloge de Voltaire (1779) and an Éloge de Montaigne (1781).
britannica-1911-la-fayette-gilbert-motie:
Gilbert Motier de La Fayette (1380–1462) was a marshal of France, brought up at the court of Louis II, duke of Bourbon. He served under Marshal Boucicaut in Italy and became seneschal of the Bourbonnais in 1409. In the English wars he was at the taking of Soubise in 1413 and of Compiègne in 1415, and was made lieutenant-general in Languedoc and Guienne. He failed to hold Caen and Falaise against Henry V, but held Lyons against the duke of Burgundy in 1418.

Successes on the Loire won La Fayette the government of Dauphiny and the marshal's office in 1420. He led the Franco-Scottish troops at Baugé in 1422, was taken at Verneuil in 1424 and soon freed, and fought with Joan of Arc at Orleans and Patay in 1429. His last campaign was in Normandy in 1449. He died on the 23rd of February 1462.
britannica-1911-la-fayette-louise-de:
Louise de La Fayette (c. 1616–1665) was one of the fourteen children of John, comte de La Fayette, and Marguerite de Bourbon-Busset. As maid of honour to Anne of Austria she caught the eye of Louis XIII. Richelieu had pushed her forward, hoping she would offset the sway of Marie de Hautefort. The plan misfired. The king made Louise the keeper of his grievances against the cardinal, and she urged him to resist Richelieu's rule, yet she refused to become his mistress.

In 1637 Louise left the court for the convent of the Filles de Sainte-Marie. Louis still visited her there, and they wrote to each other. Richelieu seized the letters and, by cuts and false changes, broke the trust between them. At her death in January 1665 Louise was superior of a convent of her order that she had founded at Chaillot.
britannica-1911-la-harpe-jean-francois-d:
Jean François de La Harpe (1739–1803) was a French critic, born in Paris on the 20th of November 1739, of poor parents. Orphaned at nine, he was schooled on a scholarship at the Collège d'Harcourt. At nineteen he was jailed for some months, charged with writing a satire on his patrons at the college. His tragedy Warwick, played at court in 1763, was perhaps the best play he ever wrote. The plays that followed failed,.

La Harpe corresponded with Voltaire, who thought well of him and let him correct his verses, and for a time he and his wife were guests of Voltaire at Ferney. From 1786 he lectured on literature at the new Lycée. Those lectures, printed as the Cours de littérature ancienne et moderne, show him at his best, standing apart from the quarrels of the day. There his fame rests.
britannica-1911-la-mothe-le-vayer-franco:
François de La Mothe Le Vayer (1588–1672) was a French writer, born in Paris of a noble family of Maine. His father was an advocate at the parlement of Paris. François took his father's place at the parlement, but gave up the post about 1647 for travel and letters. His Considérations sur l'éloquence française (1638) won him a seat in the Academy. His work on the education of the dauphin (1640) caught Richelieu's eye.

In 1649 Anne of Austria gave La Mothe Le Vayer the schooling of her second son, and later the finishing of Louis XIV's neglected education. From that work came a row of books for the prince, on seven subjects for the prince (1651–1658). The king made his tutor historiographer of France and a councillor of state. His treatise of 1668, on the small certainty there is in history, marks the start of historical criticism in France.
britannica-1911-la-motte-antoine-houdar-:
Antoine Houdar de La Motte (1672–1731) was a French author, born in Paris on the 18th of January 1672. His comedy Les Originaux failed wholly in 1693,. Four years later he was writing operas and ballets, among them L'Europe galante (1697). His tragedy Inès de Castro (1723) had a huge success at the Théâtre Français. He became a champion of the moderns in the revived quarrel of the ancients and moderns.

Madame Dacier had printed a translation of the Iliad in 1699. La Motte, who knew no Greek, built a verse translation of his own (1714) on hers. He defended the moderns in the Discours sur Homère and in his Réflexions sur la critique (1716). He entered the Academy in 1710 and later went blind. His fame rests on the fine prose of his views, and he died at Paris on the 26th of December 1731.
britannica-1911-la-noue-francois-de:
François de La Noue (1531–1591), called Bras-de-Fer, was one of the Huguenot captains of the 16th century, born near Nantes. His first deed was the taking of Orleans in 1567 at the head of fifteen horsemen. He led the rearguard at Jarnac in March 1569, was taken at Moncontour that October,. At the siege of Fontenay in 1570 a bullet shattered his left arm, and a mechanic of Rochelle made him an iron arm with a hook for his reins, hence his name.

After the peace of 1570 La Noue fought the Spaniards in the Netherlands and was taken at Mons in 1572. Charles IX then sent him to reconcile La Rochelle to the king after the massacre of St Bartholomew. The townsmen would not treat, and La Noue served as general of La Rochelle from 1574 to 1578. Back in the Low Countries he took several towns and captured Count Egmont in 1580.
britannica-1911-la-place-josue-de:
Josué de La Place (1606?–1665), in Latin Placaeus, was a French Protestant divine, born in Brittany. He studied philosophy at Saumur and then taught it there. In 1625 he became pastor of the Reformed Church at Nantes. In 1632 he was made professor of theology at Saumur. His theses of 1640, on the state of fallen man before grace, drew suspicion for liberal views on original sin.

La Place held that Adam's first sin was not directly charged to his descendants, and the synod of Charenton in 1645 condemned that view, without naming him. He himself drew a line between direct and indirect imputation. After his death his teaching, like Amyraut's, was rejected in the Formula consensus of 1675. He died on the 17th of August 1665. His defence fills three volumes (1649–1651), and his work on the imputation of Adam's sin came out in 1655. A collected edition of his writings appeared at Franeker in 1699.
britannica-1911-la-revelliere-lepeaux-lo:
Louis Marie de La Révellière-Lépeaux (1753–1824) was a French politician, a member of the Directory. He was born at Montaign on the 24th of August 1753. He studied law at Angers and Paris and was called to the bar in 1775. A deputy in 1789, he later sat on the council of Maine-et-Loire. In 1792 the department sent him to the Convention. In November 1792 he proposed the decree by which France offered protection to foreign nations fighting for liberty.

La Révellière-Lépeaux voted for the death of Louis XVI, but stood apart from the extremists. Proscribed with the Girondins in 1793, he hid until the fall of Robespierre in July 1794. He became president of the Directory. His policy was marked by bitter hostility to the Christian religion, which he hoped to replace with the new cult of theophilanthropy.
britannica-1911-la-rochefoucauld-francoi:
François de La Rochefoucauld (1613–1680), born in Paris on the 15th of September 1613, is remembered as the greatest maxim writer of France and one of her best memoir writers. While his father lived he bore the title prince de Marcillac. He joined the army before he was sixteen, married Andrée de Vivonne, and fought in the annual campaigns with great bravery, though with little credit for military skill.

Drawn into the intrigues around Anne of Austria by Madame de Chevreuse, he was briefly shut in the Bastille and more than once ordered to retire to his father's estates. His failure in the Fronde came from scrupulousness rather than want of courage: a mind that saw both sides of a question was slow to act. His Maxims grew out of that world of court and civil war.
britannica-1911-la-rochefoucauld-liancou:
François Alexandre Frédéric, duc de La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt (1747–1827), French social reformer, was born at La Roche Guyon on the 11th of January 1747. A visit to England led him to set up a model farm at Liancourt, with imported cattle. He installed spinning machines on his estate and founded a school of arts and crafts for soldiers' sons, which in 1788 became the École des Enfants de la Patrie under royal protection.

Elected to the states-general of 1789, he tried to uphold the crown while pushing reforms. On the 12th of July he warned Louis XVI of the danger and answered his cry of revolt with the famous words, "Non, sire, c'est une révolution." He became president of the Assembly on the 18th of July. After the 10th of August 1792 he fled to England and then America, returning to Paris in 1799.
britannica-1911-la-sabliere-marguerite-d:
Marguerite de La Sablière (c. 1640–1693) was the wife of Antoine Rambouillet, sieur de la Sablière, a Protestant financier who administered the royal estates. Well taught in Latin, mathematics, physics and anatomy, she made her house a meeting-place for poets, scientists and courtiers of Louis XIV. About 1673 she took La Fontaine into her home and for twenty years freed him from every material care. The traveller François Bernier also lived in the house, and his abridgment of Gassendi was written for her.

Her one serious passion, for the marquis de La Fare, ended in 1679 when he left her. From then she gave herself to good works, spending much time in the hospital for incurables. Her husband died the same year, and she was later converted to Roman Catholicism. She died in Paris on the 8th of January 1693.
britannica-1911-la-salle-st-jean-baptist:
St Jean Baptiste de La Salle (1651–1719) founded the order of Christian Brothers. He was born at Reims, the son of a rich lawyer whose influence got him a cathedral canonry while he was still young. There he opened a school giving free elementary teaching to poor children. The work grew, assistants gathered round him, and he gave up his canonry to devote himself wholly to education. His assistants were formed into a community, and a training-school for teachers was set up at Rouen.

In 1725, six years after his death, the pope recognized the society as the "Brothers of the Christian Schools." Its members took monastic vows but did not seek the priesthood. Confined mostly to France in its first century, the order spread across western Europe in the 19th century. When La Salle was canonized in 1900, the brothers numbered about 15,000.
britannica-1911-la-tour-maurice-quentin-:
Maurice Quentin de La Tour (1704–1788), French pastellist, was born at St Quentin on the 5th of September 1704 and came to Paris in 1727. Pastel was not yet a distinct branch of painting when Rosalba Carriera brought it into fashion in 1720. From 1737 La Tour exhibited the first of a series of some 150 portraits that were the glory of the Salon for thirty-seven years. He entered the academy in 1746, became painter to the king in 1750, and was made a councillor the year after.

His rare gift was to satisfy his fashionable sitters and his fellow artists at once: the flattery was hidden behind a just and striking likeness he hardly ever missed. His portraits of Rousseau, Voltaire, Louis XV, the queen and the dauphin are both documents and masterpieces. The life-size Madame de Pompadour, shown at the Salon of 1755, became the chief ornament of the cabinet of pastels in the Louvre.
britannica-1911-lacepede-bernard-germain:
Bernard Germain Étienne de la Ville, comte de Lacépède (1756–1825), French naturalist, was born at Agen on the 26th of December 1756. His father educated him carefully, and reading Buffon's Natural History as a boy fixed his life's interest. He also composed music: two unpublished operas won Gluck's high approval, and he published a Poétique de la musique in 1781–1785. Treatises on electricity and physics won him Buffon's friendship.

In 1785 Buffon made him sub-demonstrator at the Jardin du Roi and set him to continue the Histoire naturelle. His continuations covered the oviparous quadrupeds and serpents (1788–1789) and the reptiles (1789). He sat in the legislative assembly, then left Paris during the Terror. When the garden became the Jardin des Plantes he took the chair for reptiles and fishes. His Histoire naturelle des poissons ran from 1798 to 1803, and his Histoire des cétacés followed in 1804.
britannica-1911-lacretelle-pierre-louis-:
Pierre Louis de Lacretelle (1751–1824), French politician and writer, was born at Metz on the 9th of October 1751. He practised as a barrister in Paris, sat in the Legislative Assembly, and belonged to the moderate Feuillants. After the 10th of August 1792 he left public life. In 1803 he entered the Institute. Under the Restoration he was a chief editor of the Minerve française, and he wrote an essay on the 18 Brumaire.

His younger brother Jean Charles Dominique, called Lacretelle le jeune (1766–1855), was a historian and journalist, born at Metz. He served as secretary to the duc de La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt, then joined the Journal de Paris under Suard, alongside André Chénier and Antoine Roucher. His monarchist sympathies and his reporting of the trial and death of Louis XVI put his life in danger; he enlisted in the army, and returned to Paris after Thermidor.
britannica-1911-lalaing-jacques-de:
Jacques de Lalaing (c. 1420–1453), Flemish knight, served first the duke of Cleves and then Philip III the Good, duke of Burgundy. He won great renown by his prowess in the tiltyard. The duke trusted him with embassies to the pope and to the king of France in 1451, and afterwards sent him to put down the revolt of the people of Ghent. Lalaing was killed on that expedition.

His biography, Le Livre des faits de messire Jacques de Lalaing, has been published several times. It is mainly the work of the Burgundian herald and chronicler Jean le Fèvre, called Toison d'or, with the Flemish historiographer Georges Chastellain and the herald Charolais also taking part.
britannica-1911-lalande-joseph-jerome-le:
Joseph Jérôme Lefrançais de Lalande (1732–1807), French astronomer, was born at Bourg on the 11th of July 1732. His parents sent him to study law, but he lodged at the Hôtel Cluny, where Delisle had his observatory. Astronomy drew him in, and he became pupil of Delisle and Lemonnier. Lemonnier sent him to Berlin to observe the lunar parallax in concert with Lacaille at the Cape of Good Hope. The success of that work won him admission to the Berlin Academy and the post of astronomer.

In 1759 he published an edition of Halley's tables, with a history of the comet whose return he had helped Clairault to calculate. In 1762 Delisle resigned his Collège de France chair in Lalande's favour, which he held for forty-six years. His house became a seminary, with Delambre, Piazzi and Mechain among his pupils, and his transit-of-1769 publications brought fame.
britannica-1911-lally-thomas-arthur-comt:
Thomas Arthur, comte de Lally (1702–1766), French general, was born at Romans in 1702, the son of an Irish Jacobite officer. He entered the French army in 1721, fighting Austria in 1734. At Fontenoy in 1745 he led his regiment, made brigadier on the field. He served Charles Edward at Falkirk. He was made maréchal de camp at Maestricht in 1748.

In 1756 he took command in India, reaching Pondicherry in April 1758. Pride and ferocity undid him: his officers disliked him, his soldiers hated him, and he trampled on caste traditions. He failed at Tanjore and retired from the siege of Madras when the British fleet arrived. Beaten by Coote at Wandiwash in 1760, he capitulated at Pondicherry in 1761. Sent to England as a prisoner, he insisted on returning on parole to face treachery charges. After two years in prison, he was sentenced to death on the 6th of May 1766 and beheaded three days later.
britannica-1911-lally-tollendal-trophime:
Trophime Gérard, marquis de Lally-Tollendal (1751–1830), was born at Paris on the 5th of March 1751. He was the legitimized son of the comte de Lally, and learned the secret of his birth on the day of his father's execution. He resolved to clear his father's memory. Voltaire backed him, and in 1778 he persuaded Louis XVI to annul the decree that had sentenced Lally. The Rouen parlement, to which the case went back, again found Lally guilty in 1784, and later courts never admitted his innocence.

In 1789 Lally-Tollendal sat in the states-general. He opposed Mirabeau's "tyranny" and condemned the renunciations of the 4th of August 1789, then emigrated to England. In 1793 he offered to defend Louis XVI at his trial, but was not allowed to return. He came back under the Consulate; Louis XVIII made him a peer of France, and in 1816 he entered the French Academy.
britannica-1911-lamballe-marie-therese-l:
Marie Thérèse Louise of Savoy-Carignano, princesse de Lamballe (1749–1792), was born at Turin on the 8th of September 1749. In 1767 she married Louis Alexandre Stanislaus de Bourbon, prince of Lamballe, . Her husband died the following year, and she lived at Rambouillet until the dauphin's marriage brought her back to court. Marie Antoinette, charmed by her gentle manners, made her a companion and appointed her superintendent of the household against the king's wish.

From 1785 to the Revolution she was the queen's closest friend. She followed the queen to the Tuileries. In 1791 she visited England to appeal for help for the royal family, then returned. Imprisoned in the Temple after the 10th of August, she was moved to La Force. Refusing the oath against the monarchy, she was given over to the mob on the 3rd of September, and her head was carried on a pike before the queen's windows.
britannica-1911-lamennais-hugues-felicit:
Hugues Félicité Robert de Lamennais, a French priest and writer on faith and politics, lived from 1782 to 1854, and the 1911 Britannica gives him a long life entry. Born at Saint Malo, he was a shipowner's son meant for trade. Long hours in an uncle's library, reading Rousseau and Pascal, shaped his path.

His first book, of 1808, urged a revival of the church in France, and Napoleon's police seized it as a risk. It still woke the ultramontane spirit that later shaped church and state. He turned next to a French version of a monk's guide by Louis de Blois. In 1814 he and his brother wrote against bishops being named without the pope's leave. Fearing the Hundred Days, he fled to London and taught French to keep alive. He was ordained priest in 1816, after much doubt on his call.
britannica-1911-lamettrie-julien-offray-:
Lamettrie, Julien Offray de, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a French thinker. Born at St Malo on the 25th of December 1709, he first read church lore. He then switched with speed to the study of medicine as a trade. In 1733 he went to Leiden to learn under Boerhaave.

Back in Paris in 1742, he won a post as surgeon to the guards. In a bout of fever he watched his own quick pulse stir his thoughts. From that he held that mind acts spring from changes in the brain. His first book on the soul caused such an outcry that he fled. At Leiden he set out his full creed in a book on man as a machine.
britannica-1911-lamoriciere-christophe-l:
Christophe Léon Louis Juchault de Lamoricière (1806-1865) rose as a French general through the long war in Algeria. Born at Nantes, he entered the Engineers in 1828, served in Algeria from 1830, and reached high rank by 1840. Service at Isly in 1844 and a spell as acting head of Algeria led to his capture of Abd el-Kader in 1847.

Politics followed soldiering. He sat in the Chamber of Deputies, held the war ministry for a time under Cavaignac, and stood against Louis Napoleon from 1848 to 1851. The coup of December 1851 brought arrest and exile. In 1860 he led the papal army in Italy and was badly beaten at Castelfidardo that September, then lived out his last years in quiet retirement in France.
britannica-1911-lannoy-guillebert-de:
Guillebert de Lannoy (1386-1462) served the dukes of Burgundy as chamberlain, held the fort of Sluys as governor, and wore the order of the Golden Fleece. Missions took him to France, England, Prussia, Poland, and Lithuania, and he helped settle the treaty of Troyes in 1420.

In 1421 Henry V of England sent him to Palestine to test whether the kingdom of Jerusalem might be raised again. His account of that road, covering Syria and Egypt, reached print centuries later, in 1826 and again in 1842. The record here is short: a life of errands between courts, closed by one long eastern journey and the book it left behind.
britannica-1911-lapparent-albert-auguste:
Albert Auguste Cochon de Lapparent is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Lapparent was a French earth scientist who lived from 1839 to 1908. He was born at Bourges in December 1839. After study at a famed Paris school, he joined the corps of mines. He helped draw up the earth map of France. In 1875 he became professor of earth science at the Catholic Institute in Paris.

The article lists his memoir on a district of France for the national survey. In 1880 he served as president of the French earth science society. His treatise on earth science, printed in the early eighteen eighties, is called the best European textbook of its kind. His other works cover coal, sea level, earthquakes, and old glaciers. For many years he edited a journal of earth science. He died in Paris in 1908.
britannica-1911-las-casas-bartolome-de:
Bartolome de Las Casas, for a time bishop of Chiapa in Mexico, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in fourteen seventy four, he is known as the Apostle of the Indies. He was a son of Seville. His father sailed with Columbus on the trip that found the New World.

The father sent the boy to Salamanca, where he took his degree. In fourteen ninety eight the son sailed with his father to the West Indies. Four years later he went to Haiti with the new governor. In fifteen ten he was made a priest on that isle, the first priest so made in the new lands. He then went to Cuba to help plant the isle. There he saw a mass slaying of the native folk and tried in vain to stop it. That sight set the course of his famed life.
britannica-1911-lauria-roger-de:
Roger de Lauria, who died in 1305, was an admiral of Aragon and Sicily. The 1911 Britannica article calls him the chief figure in the sea war that grew from the Sicilian Vespers. His father backed the Hohenstaufen cause. His mother came to Spain with Costanza, heir of Manfred, when she wed Peter of Aragon. Roger was raised at that court and given lands in Valencia.

In 1282 the revolt of the Sicilian Vespers threw off French rule on the island. Sicily took Peter the Third as king, and in 1283 he gave Roger command of his fleet. That same year Roger beat a French fleet off Malta. From then to the peace of 1303 he won at sea again and again. His fleets served Aragon in the waters of south Italy and off the coast of Catalonia.
britannica-1911-lauriston-jacques-alexan:
Lauriston, Jacques Alexandre Bernard Law, Marquis de, is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French soldier and envoy. He was born at Pondicherry on the first of February 1768 and died in 1828. His father was a general officer in the French army. The young Lauriston got his first commission near 1786.

He served with the guns and on the staff in the early campaigns of the Revolution, and rose to brigadier of artillery in 1795. He quit in 1796, then came back in 1800 as aide-de-camp to Napoleon, a school friend from cadet days. He ran the artillery school at La Fere and went as special envoy to Denmark. He was picked to carry the peace of Amiens to England in 1802. By 1805 he was a general of division.
britannica-1911-lautrec-odet-de-foix-vic:
Odet de Foix, vicomte de Lautrec, was a French soldier who lived from 1488 to 1528 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His house traced its line to Pierre, a grandson of Archambaud de Grailly. Odet and his two brothers served Francis the First as captains. Their sister became the king mistress, and that bond won them high offices.

Lautrec fought in the Marignano campaign of 1515. The next year he took charge of the Milanese and ruled it so harshly that French rule became hateful there. He held the duchy against a Spanish army in 1521. At the Bicocca in 1522 he was crushed and had to quit Milan. Mutiny among his Swiss troops had forced that battle on him against his wish. Made marshal of France, he led the army of Italy again in 1527.
britannica-1911-leon-luis-ponce-de:
Luis Ponce de Leon was a Spanish poet and mystic born in a town of Cuenca. He entered the great college at Salamanca as a boy of fourteen, then joined a strict order of friars. In time he won a chair of church study there, with a chair of sacred letters added some years on.

The 1911 Britannica entry peaks with his clash with the church court. He was charged for his rendering of a book of songs from the Bible into Spanish, and for his doubts on the Latin text in church use. He lay in jail for more than four years. The charges were then dropped, and he was freed with a mere warning. Back at his post, he was charged once more, with no result. His famed prose works were writ in jail or soon after.
britannica-1911-leon-moses-de: Moses de Leon (died 1305) was a Jewish scholar born in Leon, Spain. He died at Arevalo. His fame rests on the Zohar. That book is the most weighty work of the Kabbala. It was put out under the name of a second-century rabbi. Later study showed it to be far newer. Moses built it from old matter with real genius. His wandering life drew blame. The depth of the book itself stands firm.
britannica-1911-lescure-louis-marie-jose:
Louis Marie Joseph, marquis de Lescure (1766-1793), fought for the French crown against the Revolution. Born near Bressuire, he left the École Militaire at sixteen. A cavalry company in the Royal-Piémont regiment was his post. Hostile to the new ideas, he left France in 1791, then soon came back.

On 10 August 1792 he helped guard the Tuileries from the Paris mob. Flight to Clisson followed. When Vendée rose, royalists freed him from prison and made him a leader. He fought at Thouars and took Fontenay and Saumur in 1793. A failed stroke at Nantes came next. With La Rochejaquelein he beat Westermann near Cholet on 19 September. Death took him on 15 October near La Tremblaye.
britannica-1911-ligne-charles-joseph-pri:
Charles Joseph, prince de Ligne (1735-1814), was at once a soldier and a man of letters. Brussels was his birthplace and Hainaut his house's home. As an Austrian subject he joined the imperial army young. Bravery in the Seven Years' War showed at Breslau, Leuthen, Hochkirch, and Maxen. High rank came fast after the peace.

Friendship with Joseph II put him near the throne. Vast estates let him live in great style. Travel took him through courts, camps, and salons across Europe. In 1787 he rode with Catherine II to the Crimea and took a Russian marshal's rank. Belgrade's siege saw him in 1788. Asked to head the Belgian revolt, he refused with a jest. French troops ate up his Brabant lands in 1792-1793. His eldest son fell in the Argonne. Vienna held his last years, spent much in writing.
britannica-1911-littleton-sir-thomas-de:
Thomas de Littleton is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English judge and law writer born near fourteen hundred and seven. He took his mother name and her lands in Worcestershire. No firm proof shows that he went to a university at all.

The entry traces his rise as counsel, town clerk, and county officer in turn. His name shows up in famed letter sets of the age as a known pleader. He taught law at a London inn on a great old statute. Grants of land came to him as thanks for work as counsel. His fame rests most on his book on land tenures in English law.
britannica-1911-lomenie-de-brienne-etien:
Etienne Charles de Lomenie de Brienne, born in Paris in seventeen twenty seven, was a French churchman and man of state. His family came from Limousin and dated from the fifteenth century. After a bright school career he entered the Church as the best road to high place. He became a doctor of theology in seventeen fifty one. Doubts were raised about the soundness of his thesis.

He rose fast, to bishop of Condom and then to archbishop of Toulouse. His friends included Turgot, Morellet, and Voltaire, and he joined the French Academy. He wrote notes for Turgot on social questions, one on poverty being much praised. In seventeen eighty seven he led the Assembly of Notables. He attacked the tax plans of Calonne and then took his place in charge of finance.
britannica-1911-longueville-anne-genevie:
Anne Geneviève, duchesse de Longueville (1619–1679), is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the only daughter of Henri de Bourbon, prince de Condé, and the sister of Louis, the great Condé. She was born in the prison of Vincennes, where her parents were held for standing against the regent's favourite. She was raised in strict style by the Carmelites in Paris. In 1642 she wed the duc de Longueville, a widower twice her age.

The match was not a happy one, but her place at court grew as her father rose in the regency. She was the guiding spirit of the first Fronde, drawing her brother Conti and her husband to the rebels' side. She failed to win over Condé himself, whose faith to the court broke that first rising.
britannica-1911-louvois-francois-michel-:
François Michel le Tellier, marquis de Louvois, was war minister to Louis the Fourteenth of France and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Paris on 18 January 1641. His father taught him the work of state and wed him to an heiress. The young man won the trust of the king.

In 1666 he took his father place as war minister. Turenne saw his gifts in the war of Devolution and taught him how to supply armies. After peace in 1668 Louvois set to work to rebuild the French army. The years to 1672 were years of hard preparation. While others found allies and money, Louvois found soldiers for Louis.
britannica-1911-luckenwalde: Luckenwalde is a town in the Prussian province of Brandenburg, on the river Nuthe. The short 1911 Britannica note sets it 30 miles south of Berlin on the main line to Dresden. Its count in 1905 was 22,263 people. Cloth and wool mills there rank among the most extensive in Prussia. Other work covers cotton printing, dye works, brewing, and the making of metal and bronze goods. A monastery stood on the site in the 1100s, but the town itself dates from the reign of Frederick the Great.
britannica-1911-lucy-richard-de:
Richard de Lucy, called the loyal, who died in eleven seventy nine, was chief justiciar of England. A 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry traces his career. He first shows up late in the reign of Stephen as sheriff and justiciar of Essex.

When Henry the Second came to the throne, Lucy shared the top law post with the Earl of Leicester. After that earl died in eleven sixty eight, Lucy held the post alone for twelve years. He was a close aide and friend of the king. He was among the first royal men to be cast out by the church in the Becket dispute. In eleven seventy three he helped crush a revolt of barons. He led the royal side at the battle of Fornham.
britannica-1911-luna-alvaro-de:
Alvaro de Luna, constable of Castile and a great lord of Spain who died in fourteen fifty three, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the base born son of a noble of Castile. His uncle, a high church lord of Toledo, brought him to court as a page in fourteen ten. There he soon won a firm hold on the young king.

In the years of rule by the king uncle, the page was kept to a mere place of service. When that uncle was made king of a next realm, the rule fell to the queen mother. Then the young man rose to great weight at court. The king held him in a love that men of the age laid to witch craft. Round the king stood lords with greed and no shame.
britannica-1911-macedo-jose-agostinho-de:
José Agostinho de Macedo, Portuguese poet and prose writer who lived from 1761 to 1831, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Beja of a plebeian family. Latin and rhetoric were his studies with the Oratorians in Lisbon. In 1778 he took vows as an Augustinian friar.

A turbulent bent spoiled that path for him from the start. He spent a great part of his time in prison for his conduct. Superiors moved him from one convent to another in vain hope of calm. At last he gave up the monk habit to live loosely in the capital. In 1792 he was unfrocked by the church. Aid from strong friends then won him a papal brief that freed him in form.
britannica-1911-macmahon-marie-edme-patr:
Marie Edme Patrice Maurice de MacMahon, a French marshal and head of state, fills a 1911 Britannica life. Born in eighteen oh eight at the chateau of Sully, he came of an Irish line exiled with James the Second. Trained at Saint Cyr, he first fought in Algeria. Brave raids and the siege of Constantine made his name there. He rose to lead a large force by the mid fifties.

In the Crimean War his storm of the Malakoff works brought the fall of Sebastopol. In Italy in eighteen fifty nine a bold push at Magenta won the day for France. The prize was a marshal baton and a duke title from that field. Rule in Algeria went less well, with loud plaints and two bids to quit. War with Prussia then called him home.
britannica-1911-mailly-louise-julie-comt:
Louise Julie, Countess de Mailly, born in seventeen ten, was a mistress of King Louis the Fifteenth of France. A short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls her the daughter of the Marquis de Nesle. She was the eldest of three sisters. Each sister in turn became a favourite of the king.

In seventeen twenty six she wed her cousin, Louis Alexandre de Mailly. The king had paid her court from seventeen thirty two. She became his titled mistress only in seventeen thirty eight. She did not use her place to grow rich or to meddle in affairs of state. Her sister, the Duchess of Chateauroux, took her place. Mailly had to leave the court in seventeen forty two.
britannica-1911-maintenon-francoise-d-au:
Francoise de Maintenon, the second wife of King Louis the Fourteenth of France, was born in a prison. Her father, son of a famed friend and general of a past king, lay jailed as a rebel of the Protestant faith. Her mother, a staunch Catholic, had the child baptized in her own faith, with grand sponsors.

The 1911 Britannica entry follows a hard childhood across the sea and back. Freed, her father took the family to Martinique, lost what coin he had at cards, and died there. Her mother brought the girl home in want, and gave her to a kinswoman who made her glad but drew her to the Protestant faith. When that came out, the state moved the child to her godmother, who pressed her back to Rome.
britannica-1911-mairet-jean-de:
Jean de Mairet, who lived from 1604 to 1686, was a French playwright. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica marks his role in stage rules. He was born at Besancon and baptized in May 1604. He went to Paris to study in about 1625 and staged a first play that year.

His best work, Sophonisbe, came out in 1634. Its strict use of the unities opened the age of regular tragedy. Mairet had fought for those rules in print years before. He also attacked Corneille hard in the row over The Cid. Envy of that rival may have ended his stage work. He later served his home province in Paris, then retired. He died at Besancon in 1686.
britannica-1911-maistre-joseph-de:
Joseph de Maistre, who lived from 1754 to 1821, was a French envoy and fierce polemical writer. The 1911 Britannica entry places his birth at Chambery in an old noble house. His father led the senate of Savoy, and Joseph rose in that state service. He joined the senate himself and wed Francoise de Morand in 1786.

When French republican troops seized Savoy he fled into exile at Lausanne. There in 1796 he issued his first great work, Considerations on France. That book set out his stark views on revolt, rule, and faith. The entry opens the tale of a thinker who fought the age with his pen.
britannica-1911-maistre-xavier-de:
Xavier de Maistre, a French writer who lived from 1763 to 1852, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the younger brother of Joseph de Maistre. Born at Chambéry in October 1763, he served young in the Piedmontese army. Under arrest at Turin after a duel, he wrote his famed fantasy there.

That book, A Journey Round My Room, appeared in print in 1794. When France annexed Savoy, he left its service for a Russian commission. He campaigned under Suvarov and followed the marshal to Russia. In disgrace with his general, he kept himself by painting miniatures at St Petersburg. Posts in the capital followed, and he saw hard service in the Caucasus. Wounded there, he rose to the rank of major-general. He married a Russian lady and settled in his adopted country. His other tales, all of modest size, include a leper story of great tenderness.
britannica-1911-malesherbes-chretien-gui:
Chrétien Guillaume de Lamoignon de Malesherbes, who lived from 1721 to 1794, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French statesman from a famed legal family, born at Paris. Trained for the law, he became president of a Paris tax court in 1750. He later served as counsel for the defence of King Louis the Sixteenth.

Much of the article deals with his charge of the press under his father, the chancellor. For eighteen years he kept close ties with the leading writers of Paris. His help, one writer claimed, made Diderot's great Encyclopaedia possible. The piece then turns to 1771, when he spoke out boldly against a new court system. That protest brought him swift banishment from the capital.
britannica-1911-malherbe-francois-de:
Francois de Malherbe, born at Caen in fifteen fifty five, was a French poet, critic, and translator. His family held some standing, though its claims to old noble rank were not proved. He was the eldest son of a king's counsellor in the courts at Caen. His schooling was rich, at Caen, at Paris, at Heidelberg, and at Basel. At twenty one he chose arms over the gown.

Malherbe entered the household of Henri d'Angouleme, a natural son of Henry the Second. He served that prince as secretary in Provence and wed there in fifteen eighty one. He seems to have written verse in those years, but poor verse by report. When his patron died he had no set work for a time. He lived in Provence and in Normandy for many years. His poem The Tears of Saint Peter came out in fifteen eighty seven.
britannica-1911-mandeville-jehan-de:
Jehan de Mandeville, called Sir John Mandeville, is the name claimed by the compiler of a singular book of travels, and this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article examines the claim. The book was written in French and published between 1357 and 1371. Translations into many tongues made it hugely popular. A few added words in one English version gave Mandeville the false credit of fathering English prose.

In his preface the compiler calls himself a knight born and bred at St Albans. He says he crossed the sea on Michaelmas Day 1322. His travels, as told, covered Turkey, Armenia, Tartary, Persia, Syria, Arabia, Egypt, and India. He says he served the sultan of Egypt in his wars and was often at Jerusalem. He wrote in Romance, as more widely understood than Latin.
britannica-1911-manny-sir-walter-de-mann:
Sir Walter de Manny (died 1372) was a soldier of fortune and the founder of the Charterhouse, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens his career. He was a younger son of Jean de Mauny of Hainaut. He claimed descent from the counts of that land. Manny was a patron and friend of the chronicler Froissart.

In the chronicles of Froissart, the deeds of Manny hold a large and likely inflated place. He seems first to have come to England in 1327. He came as an esquire of Queen Philippa. He took a marked part in the Scottish wars of Edward the Third. In 1337 he was given command of an English fleet. The next year he crossed to the continent with the king. There he proved himself in the campaigns that followed.
britannica-1911-manucode:
Manucode is the name of a small group of birds akin to the birds of paradise. A long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the word to a Malay name that means bird of the gods. The name was used for birds of paradise in general for over two hundred years. In English it came to rest on this one small group.

The birds wear a glossy steel-blue coat of much beauty. Their outer and middle toes are joined for part of their length. The males have a windpipe coiled in a strange way on the breast. That coil goes with a loud, clear voice. The group lives only in the Papuan region and the Cape York peninsula. The entry sorts its kinds and weighs which forms count as true species.
britannica-1911-marbot-jean-baptiste-ant:
Jean Baptiste Antoine Marcelin de Marbot, a French soldier who lived from 1782 to 1854, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at La Riviere, the son of a general who died in the defence of Genoa. He joined the army of the republic as a volunteer in 1799. He rose fast and served as aide to Marshal Augereau in the war of 1806 and 1807.

He then served with great credit in the Peninsular War under Lannes and Massena. He showed as a bold leader of light horse in the Russian war of 1812 and the German campaign of the next year. He was slow to heal from wounds he took at Leipzig and Hanau. In the Hundred Days Napoleon made him a general of brigade, and he was wounded at Waterloo. Cast out at the Restoration, he came home in 1819.
britannica-1911-marca-pierre-de:
Pierre de Marca is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Marca was a French prelate and historian, born at Gan near Pau in 1594. His family moved in legal circles and kept the Catholic faith. That loyalty held even after the Reformed religion was set up in Navarre.

He studied law at Toulouse and practised with success at Pau. Ambition drew him toward a larger stage. He called loudly for King Louis the Thirteenth to intervene by arms in Bearn. His first writing, published in 1618, urged the restoring of Catholic worship there. After the short campaign of 1620, church lands taken by Protestants were given back. Marca played his part in that settlement, and the entry follows his rise from lawyer to church statesman.
britannica-1911-marignac-jean-charles-ga:
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac (1817-1894) was a Swiss chemist born at Geneva on 24 April 1817. At sixteen he entered the Ecole Polytechnique in Paris. From 1837 to 1839 he studied at the Ecole des Mines. He then spent a short time in Liebig's lab at Giessen and in the Sevres porcelain works. In 1841 he became a teacher of chemistry at Geneva.

In 1845 Marignac took the chair of the study of minerals as well. He held both posts till ill health forced him to give them up in 1878. He died at Geneva on 15 April 1894. His name is known for his careful fixes of the weights of atoms. He did that work for twenty-eight elements. He meant to test Prout's famous guess about those weights. He gave much of his life to the rare earths and to sorting them apart.
britannica-1911-marignolli-giovanni-de:
Giovanni de Marignolli, a traveller to the Far East in the fourteenth century, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born most likely before 1290 to a noble family of Florence. In 1338 an embassy from the great khan of Cathay reached the pope at Avignon. Its letters asked for a spiritual guide for Christians at that court.

The pope named four legates, with Marignolli third on the list. A large party set out in December 1338 by way of Naples and Constantinople. They crossed the Black Sea and the steppes to the khan of the Golden Horde. At Almaligh they built a church, sang masses, and baptized converts. They reached Peking in 1342 and were well received by the khan. Chinese records fix that year by a note on great horses brought from Europe as gifts.
britannica-1911-marigny-enguerrand-de:
Enguerrand de Marigny (1260-1315) was chamberlain and chief minister of Philip IV of France, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. Born at Lyons-la-Forêt in Normandy, of an old family of the smaller baronage, he entered the service of a royal chamberlain as a squire. He then joined the household of Queen Jeanne, who made him an executor of her will.

After two royal servants fell in battle in 1304, Marigny became Philip's grand chamberlain and chief minister. He won lands, money, and the king's full trust, and acted as the tool of Philip's plans. He shared the public hatred the king drew by debasing the coinage. In 1314 he addressed the estates general and won more taxes for the Flemish war, at the cost of much fresh ill will from the princes of the blood.
britannica-1911-marivaux-pierre-carlet-d:
Marivaux, Pierre Carlet de Chamblain de, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life. Born at Paris on the 4th of February 1688, he was a French writer. His father was a money man of Norman stock named Carlet. The son took the added names that became his famed pen name.

The father ran the mint at Riom, where the boy was raised. He showed a taste for letters early in his young life. At age eighteen he writ his first play for the stage. It came out in print in 1712, when he was twenty-four. His early care went to novels more than to plays. Three novels came from his pen in the years 1713 to 1715. They followed Spanish tales and the grand novels of old.
britannica-1911-martens-frederic-frommho:
Frederic Frommhold de Martens is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Russian expert in law between nations, born in Livonia in eighteen forty five. He joined the foreign ministry as a young man and taught law at the same time. His books on war rights and consuls won note at once.

The entry calls his great set of Russian treaties his chief work of all. That set prints the texts in two tongues with long notes on how each deal came to be. The notes rest in part on state papers not yet in print. His long list of studies lifted the fame of Russian law schools abroad. Kings and courts sought his counsel on hard points of world law.
britannica-1911-matos-fragoso-juan-de:
Juan de Matos Fragoso (about 1614-1689) was a Spanish playwright of Portuguese descent. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places his birth in the Alemtejo region. He took a law degree at Evora, then moved to Madrid for the stage. A link to Perez de Montalbán opened that world to him there.

He had a sharp gift for what crowds wanted to see. Better talents than his sought his help as a joint author. His first printed play came out in 1651, with more in 1658. Fame lasted past his death, yet the entry judges his plays weak on reading. Fine phrases and honor points grow tedious in his work, it says.
britannica-1911-mauleon-savari-de:
Savari de Mauleon died in 1236 and was a French soldier of his age. The 1911 Britannica life makes him son of Raoul, lord of Mauleon. He took the side of Arthur of Brittany in the wars of his youth. In 1202 foes seized him at Mirebeau and jailed him at Corfe. King John freed him in 1204 and won him to his own cause.

John made him seneschal of Poitou in the next year after that. In 1211 he helped Count Raymond besiege Simon de Montfort in arms. The king of France bought his sword in 1212 for a fleet. That fleet was smashed in the Flemish port of Damme soon after. Mauleon then went back to John and fought for him in 1215.
britannica-1911-maupassant-henri-rene-al:
Guy de Maupassant was a French novelist and poet of the nineteenth century. He lived from eighteen fifty to eighteen ninety three. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at the Chateau of Miromesnil in Seine Inferieure in France.

Maupassant was schooled at Yvetot and at the Rouen lycee in youth. He entered the ministry of marine as a clerk after school days. He split his time between rowing trips and literary gatherings in Paris. Those meets were held at the house of Gustave Flaubert, a family friend. Writers like Turgenev, Daudet, and Zola met the quiet young athlete there.
britannica-1911-mena-juan-de:
Juan de Mena (1411–1456) was a Spanish poet, born at Córdova in 1411. In his twenty-fourth year he entered the university of Salamanca, and he studied later at Rome. His learning won him the post of Latin secretary at the court of Castile. He later became the writer of the king's past for John II and a magistrate at Córdova. One account says he died of natural causes in 1456. The tale of the people says he died in a fall from his mule.

Though Mena was the king's writer in name, he had no share in the chronicle of John II. The claim that he wrote the first act of the Celestina is set aside in the article. Three true samples of his heavy prose live on.
britannica-1911-mena-pedro-de:
Pedro de Mena is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a Spanish sculptor. He died in 1693, the heading notes. He was born in the town of Adra. He was a pupil of his father in the craft. He also studied under the master Alonzo Cano. His first conspicuous success came at a convent in Granada. That was the convent of El Angel in that city. 

Saint Diego and Santa Clara stand among those early works. In 1658 he signed a contract for major work. The work was the choir stalls of Malaga cathedral. It extended over four years of labour. Other works stand in churches across Spain. Madrid holds his Madonna and child and Saint Joseph. Polychrome figures of his stand in the church of Saint Isidore. A statuette of Saint Francis is held at Toledo. Between 1673 and 1679 he worked at Cordova.
britannica-1911-mendoza-antonio-hurtado-:
Mendoza, Antonio Hurtado de is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Spanish playwright. He was born near the end of the sixteenth century, in Asturias, and died in 1644. He became a page to the count de Saldana. Cervantes picked him out as a rising poet in 1614.

He rose fast in favour under King Philip the Fourth. The king made him a private secretary and ordered plays from him for the royal theatre at Aranjuez. In 1623 the king gave him the orders of Santiago and Calatrava. His peers courted him and called him the discreet man of the palace. He stayed on good terms with most fellow playwrights of his day. He died, it seems after a fall from favour, at Saragossa in September 1644.
britannica-1911-mendoza-diego-hurtado-de:
Diego Hurtado de Mendoza is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Mendoza was a Spanish novelist, poet, diplomat, and historian. He was born at Granada in 1503, a younger son of its governor. The famed marquis of Santillana was his great-grandfather.

At the university of Salamanca he dropped a plan to take holy orders. He served the emperor Charles the Fifth in Italy instead. Between campaigns he attended lectures at Bologna, Padua, and Rome. In 1537 he was sent to England on a delicate marriage mission. The mission failed, yet he kept the emperor's full trust. In 1539 he became ambassador at Venice, a post of the first rank. There he patronized the Aldine printers and gathered Greek manuscripts. The entry shows a man of letters thriving at the centre of empire.
britannica-1911-mendoza-pedro-gonzalez-d:
Pedro Gonzalez de Mendoza, a Spanish cardinal and statesman who lived from 1428 to 1495, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the fourth son of the marquess of Santillana. He was born at Guadalajara in New Castile, the chief seat of his family, in May 1428. The house of Mendoza claimed descent from the lords of Llodio. It had been settled in Old Castile since the eleventh century.

The article traces the family's rise through battles and royal gifts. His father, the marquis, was a poet of note. Loyalty to the Crown was the family's standing policy. Pedro, a younger son, was sent into the Church with no calling for it. The article calls him a worldly, political prelate. In 1452, at twenty-four, he was made bishop of Calahorra.
britannica-1911-michel-claude:
Claude Michel, known as Clodion, lived from 1738 to 1814 and was a French sculptor born in Nancy. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him to Paris in 1755 to his uncle workshop. Lambert Sigisbert Adam, a clever sculptor, trained him there for four years. On his uncle death he passed to the teaching of Pigalle in Paris.

Prizes came fast, the grand prize for sculpture in 1759 and a silver medal in 1761. Rome drew him in 1762, and busy years of work followed there from 1767. Catherine the Second sought him for Saint Petersburg, but he chose Paris instead. Chapters, states, and crown offices all ranked among his many patrons.
britannica-1911-millipede:
The 1911 Britannica article on the millipede treats the best known members of a group of jointed animals. Science knows them as the Diplopoda. They were once classed with the centipedes as one order. Modern writers split the groups apart. The split rests on where the breeding openings sit on the body.

The article then sets out the build of the class. A clear head bears at least three pairs of limbs. Each body ring has a top plate, a bottom plate, and side plates. A pair of legs joins each ring at the bottom plate. The article notes odd points in the ring structure. It treats the millipedes with two smaller kin groups for ease. Long figure notes on species and jaws open the piece.
britannica-1911-molay-jacques-de:
Jacques de Molay (died 1314) was the last grand master of the Knights Templars, and his fall is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born of a noble but poor family in Franche-Comte about the middle of the thirteenth century, he entered the order in 1265 at Beaune. He likely went east at once to fight for the Holy Land.

The entry says he was chosen grand master about 1295, and after the Templars were driven from Palestine he gathered their remnant in Cyprus. In 1306 Pope Clement V called him to Paris, in secret league with the king of France to crush the order. In October 1307 every Templar in France was arrested.
britannica-1911-molde: Molde is a brief notice in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a small seaside town in Norway, in the county of Romsdal. It lies 204 miles by sea north-east of Bergen and has little trade. Its wealth is its view: the broad Molde Fjord with long low islands, and jagged peaks rising to 6,010 feet. Steamers from Hull, Newcastle, Hamburg, and Antwerp call here, and Molde is the port for the tourist route through the Romsdal.
britannica-1911-moncey-bon-adrien-jeanno:
Bon Adrien Jeannot de Moncey, duke of Conegliano, was a marshal of France who lived from 1754 to 1842. His life is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Besancon, the son of a lawyer. As a boy he twice joined the army, and his father got him out both times.

He won a post at last in 1778 and backed the French Revolution in 1791. In the wars of 1793 and 1794 he rose fast on the Spanish front and helped force Spain to make peace. Napoleon sent him over the St Gothard pass into Italy in 1800, made him a marshal, and gave him the dukedom in 1808. That year he led a corps in Spain and drove on Valencia.
britannica-1911-monstrelet-enguerrand-de:
Enguerrand de Monstrelet (about 1400-1453) was a French chronicler from Picardy. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places his home and posts at Cambrai for most years. He served as bailiff and then provost for the cathedral chapter there. He saw Joan of Arc in talk with Philip of Burgundy after her capture.

His Chronique carries on the work of Froissart for a new age. Two books cover the years from 1400 to 1444 in full. A clumsy sequel later stretched the work to 1516 without his hand. Rich documents fill his pages, though his telling is called dull. A clear bias toward Burgundy colors his claims of fairness.
britannica-1911-montaigne-michel-de:
Michel de Montaigne (1533-1592) was a French essayist. He was born, as he himself tells us, late in the morning of 28 February 1533. The family name was Eyquem. The name Montaigne came from the estate the family held, bought by his grandfather. The name was long thought to be of English stock. Long English rule in Gascony and Guienne gave much room for English settlers to come in.

Later research traced a family of Eyquems in the region from a time well before Eleanor of Aquitaine wed Henry II of England. No link has been proved between that older family and the essayist's kin. The Eyquems had ties to Bordeaux for some time. Montaigne's father, Pierre Eyquem, dealt in trade. His grandfather Ramon had dealt in herrings, as Scaliger notes with a sneer.
britannica-1911-montalban-juan-perez-de:
Juan Perez de Montalban was a Spanish stage writer, poet, and tale teller born at Madrid in the early sixteen hundreds. At age eighteen he took a degree in church study, was ordained priest some years on, and was made a clerk to the Inquisition court.

The 1911 Britannica entry says he began to write for the stage as a youth under the guide of the great Lope de Vega. His prose tales of love and marvels sold wide and were much loved. His father, a Madrid publisher, put out a stolen copy of a famed sharp book, which lit a fierce row. The strain of that fight, of overwork, and of his masters death broke his mind, and he died young. His last work sang the praise of his dead master.
britannica-1911-montalembert-charles-for:
Charles Forbes Rene de Montalembert is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French writer and historian born in London in eighteen ten. His house was an old one with roots deep in the west of France. His father fled France in the revolt and served in foreign arms.

The entry tells how the son grew up in Sweden while his father served there. Too young to sit as a peer, he still held weight by pen and mind. He held broad views but broke with the new regime on faith. He sought a church free from the grip of the state. That stand shaped his long fight in French public life.
britannica-1911-montalembert-marc-rene-m:
Marc Rene Montalembert, who lived from 1714 to 1800, was a French fort builder. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica credits him with a new fort method. Born at Angouleme, he joined the French army in 1732. He fought on the Rhine and in Bohemia and Italy.

Vauban writings drew Montalembert to the art of strong walls. He founded a gun works at Ruelle and served with allied Swedes. His forts dropped the maze like trace of older plans. In its place he set a plain wall plan massed for fire. Guns could then crush a besieger works with sheer weight of shot. France corps barred him from print for fifteen years. His book came out at last in the 1770s. German builders took up his polygonal method in the next age.
britannica-1911-montchretien-antoine-de:
Antoine de Montchretien, a French writer who lived from about 1576 to 1621, is covered in a 1911 Britannica article. He was the son of a drug seller at Falaise. In a duel he killed his foe and fled to England. Help from King James let him come back to France.

Montchretien set up a steel works, then left it in 1621 to fight on the Huguenot side in civil war. He was killed in a clash that same year. His plays list Sophonisbe, David, Aman, and Hector. In 1615 he printed a prized work on trade and state wealth, drawn in chief from Jean Bodin. Critics praise his prose style.
britannica-1911-montfaucon-bernard-de:
Bernard de Montfaucon, who lived from 1655 to 1741, was a French scholar and monk. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens at his birth in a family castle. Born to a noble line, he was meant for the army. He spent his youth in the castle library, reading in many tongues. He did serve two years in Germany under Turenne. Ill health and his parents' deaths turned him back to books.

In 1675 he joined the Maurist monks at Toulouse. Years in abbey libraries honed his Greek. Paris called him in 1687 to help edit the church fathers. Three years in Italy let him hunt texts not held in Paris. He then settled at the abbey of Saint Germain in Paris. There he built his name on great works of old learning. His edition of Athanasius was still held the best of that father. He died without warning in December 1741.
britannica-1911-montfort-simon-de:
Simon de Montfort, earl of Leicester, an English statesman and soldier who died in twelve sixty five, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in France about the year twelve hundred, he was the fourth and last son of a famed crusade lord. His father had held and then lost the earldom of Leicester.

Of the youth of the young Simon, the text says no tale stands on record. He came to England in twelve thirty and bound himself to Henry the Third. With the nod of his last live brother, he won back the family earldom. For a time he was not liked by the English. He stood close to the royal side at first. He gave an early sign of deep faith and of a firm will. The entry sets up the man who would shake a realm.
britannica-1911-montgaillard-jean-gabrie:
Jean Gabriel Maurice Roques, comte de Montgaillard (1761–1841), was a French agent in state affairs. He was born at Montgaillard, near Villefranche, on 16 November 1761. His parents were of the lesser nobility, and he was schooled at the military school of Sorèze. There he drew the eye of the comte de Provence, later Louis XVIII. After some years of service in the West Indies, he came back to France.

In 1789 Montgaillard was set up in Paris as a secret agent in talks with other states. He fled to England after 10 August 1792, but he came back to Paris six weeks later. His safety there was most likely bought by service to the new rule of France. He was at work for the Bourbon princes again when he met Francis II of Austria at Ypres in 1794.
britannica-1911-montgomery-gabriel-seign:
Gabriel Montgomery, a French soldier born about fifteen thirty, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He rose to a post in the Scots guards of the king of France. His father led that same guard. In his first years he took part in work to crush the new faith party in France.

By chance he caused the death of King Henry the Second in a tilt in fifteen fifty nine. That blow cast him from grace, and he went home to his lands in Normandy. There he read deep in church themes and took up the cause of the reform side. In fifteen sixty two he joined a great prince of that side. He took a town and held Rouen for a month past odds. In a later war he seized two tracts in the south west.
britannica-1911-montmorency-anne-duc-de:
Anne de Montmorency was a duke and constable of France in the sixteenth century. He lived from fourteen ninety three to fifteen sixty seven. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Chantilly, he grew up with the future King Francis the First.

Anne fought in Italy in fifteen fifteen and shone at Marignano battle. He helped guard Mezieres and led Swiss troops in Italy soon after. Made marshal of France in fifteen twenty two, he was caught at Pavia. Freed, he helped shape the treaty of Madrid with Spain after that. In fifteen thirty eight he rose to constable, then fell from favour. He returned to high office when Henry the Second took the throne.
britannica-1911-montmorency-mathieu-jean:
Mathieu Jean Felicite de Montmorency-Laval, a French politician who lived from 1766 to 1826, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Paris in July 1766. He served with his father in America and came home full of ideas of freedom. In 1789 he was sent to the states-general, where he joined the Third Estate and sat on the left.

In 1790 he moved the end of coats of arms. After the fall of the assembly he joined the army on the frontier, but the revolt of August 1792 turned him from his first views. He took no part in affairs under the empire. At the Restoration he became a peer of France. In 1821 he served as minister of foreign affairs under Villele. He urged armed action in Spain, then resigned late in 1822 and was made a duke.
britannica-1911-montmorin-de-saint-herem:
Armand Marc, comte de Montmorin de Saint Herem, lived from 1745 to 1792. The 1911 Britannica life presents him as a French statesman of the old regime. He came of a cadet branch of a noble house of Auvergne. As a youth he waited on Louis the Sixteenth when he was dauphin. He then served as ambassador of France at Madrid in Spain.

From Madrid he was called at short notice to govern Brittany. In 1787 the king chose him to lead foreign affairs for France. He took that post in the place of Vergennes that year. Montmorin held Necker in high regard and backed his sway at court. When Necker fell in July 1789, Montmorin left office with him.
britannica-1911-montpensier-anne-marie-l:
Montpensier, Anne Marie Louise d'Orleans, Duchesse de is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the French memoir writer known as la grande mademoiselle. Born at the Louvre on the twenty-ninth of May 1627, she was a daughter of Gaston of Orleans, brother of Louis the Thirteenth. Her mother was Marie de Bourbon, heiress of the Montpensier house. Royal on both sides and heiress to huge wealth, she seemed marked for a splendid match. She was bred to hope for the throne itself in marriage with Louis the Fourteenth, eleven years her junior.

On the second of July 1652 she saved Conde's beaten troops by opening her gates and firing the Bastille cannon on the royal army. Years later her wish to marry the Gascon Lauzun drew the king's consent, then its withdrawal.
britannica-1911-montresor-claude-de-bour:
Montresor, Claude de Bourdeille, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a French intriguer. Born about 1606, he was grandnephew of the writer Brantome. He became the chief favourite of Gaston, duke of Orleans, in 1635. Gaston was the weak brother of King Louis the Thirteenth.

In 1636 he planned the murder of Cardinal Richelieu at Amiens camp. The plan failed through the sheer lack of nerve of Orleans. He spent six years on his estate in forced quiet rest. In 1642 he joined the Cinq Mars plot against Richelieu as well. On its fall he fled to England and lost his estates. Later plots landed him in the Bastille and at Vincennes.
britannica-1911-montreuil-gerbert-de:
Gerbert de Montreuil, a French trouvère of the 1200s, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He wrote the Roman de la violette, a verse romance. Around 1221 he dedicated the poem to the Countess Marie of Ponthieu. The piece is short, but it traces the tale and its long afterlife.

In the story, Count Gerard of Nevers stakes his lands on his wife Euriant's fidelity. The traitor Lisiard slanders her and seems to win the wager. After many trials the lie is exposed and Euriant is restored. Other forms of the same tale appear in French verse and in the Decameron. Shakespeare built his play Cymbeline on that line of the story. A prose version later gave Weber the matter for his opera Euryanthe, staged in 1823.
britannica-1911-montrond-casimir-comte-d:
Casimir de Montrond was a French agent in the work of envoys, son of an army officer. His mother was a writer of the royalist side, said to be the hand behind a famed song of the south. In the terror years the young Montrond was jailed in Paris, where he met a divorced duchess of note.

He bought her freedom and his own with a sum of gold, the 1911 Britannica entry says. They wed and fled to London, but the match proved a sad one and they split on their return to Paris. Turned to the world of fashion, he won fame for his wins in love and in cash. He was the close friend and secret agent of a great statesman, and his inside grasp of the game let him make a vast pile on the stock mart.
britannica-1911-montyon-antoine-jean-bap:
Antoine Jean Baptiste Robert Auget, Baron de Montyon, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was a French philanthropist who lived from 1733 to 1820. He was born in Paris in December 1733. His father was a senior accounts officer. Montyon was educated for the law.

He became advocate at the Châtelet in 1755. In 1760 he was made master of requests to the council of state. He then served as intendant of Auvergne, Provence, and La Rochelle in turn. He had shown great independence of character more than once. In 1766 he protested against a noted accusation of the day. In 1771 he refused to suppress the local courts of justice, against orders. He was made a councillor of state in 1775. In 1780 he was attached to the court in an honorary office.
britannica-1911-moraes-francisco-de:
Francisco de Moraes, a Portuguese writer of romance who lived from about 1500 to 1572, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Little is known of his life save a few posts. He kept the purse of the house of King John the Third. In 1540 he was in Paris in the train of a Portuguese envoy.

His fame rests on one book, the romance of chivalry called Palmeirim de Inglaterra. He is thought to have written it in France in 1544. Some critics held that he merely turned a Spanish tale into Portuguese. The entry holds that proof points the other way. The tale is praised for its clear plot, well-drawn folk, and fine style. It stands as a classic of its tongue, and Cervantes spared it in his mock burning of such tales.
britannica-1911-moratin-leandro-antonio-:
Leandro Fernandez de Moratin, a Spanish playwright and poet born in seventeen sixty, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Madrid, he was the son of a poet father who set him to learn the trade of a jeweller. His own gift for verse showed early all the same.

At age eighteen he won second prize from the Academy for a heroic poem on the fall of Granada. Two years later a verse satire on the popular poets of the day won wide note. He went to France on a state task in seventeen eighty seven. His first play came in seventeen eighty six, but church foes had it pulled fast from the stage. The entry traces a writer caught between court, church, and stage. It is a useful start on Spanish drama of his time.
britannica-1911-moratin-nicolas-fernande:
Nicolás Moratín, a Spanish poet of rules, is noted in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Madrid in 1737, he learned law at Valladolid school. In 1772 he was called to the bar in his home city. Four years on he took the chair of poetry at the college. He backed French methods in the Spanish theatre of his day.

In 1762 Moratín lashed the home stage in a sharp tract. His blows at the old church plays helped get them banned. His own plays in the French mould fared cold with crowds. La Petimetra and Lucrecia were never staged at all in his life. Two later tragedies played to no great success on the boards. His light songs and his bull fight tract show his best gift.
britannica-1911-mornay-philippe-de:
Mornay, Philippe de, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a French Protestant. Born at Buhy in Normandy in 1549, he is known as Du-Plessis-Mornay. In 1572 he went on a secret mission for Admiral de Coligny. The task took him to William the Silent, prince of Orange.

He got clear of the St Bartholomew massacre by a Catholic friend's aid. He then took refuge in England till late in 1573. Back in France he fought in the wars of Henry of Navarre. In 1575 the duke of Guise took him prisoner in the field. Not known for who he was, he was ransomed for a small sum. He wed Charlotte Arbaleste at Sedan soon after that time. His founding of the university at Saumur is also told.
britannica-1911-morny-charles-auguste-lo:
Duc de Morny, who lived from 1811 to 1865, was a French statesman. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes his birth as a court secret. He was the natural son of Queen Hortense of Holland. That made him a half brother of Napoleon the Third.

A false birth record gave Morny a cover name and rank. He served as an army officer in Algeria in the 1830s. Back in Paris he grew rich on beet sugar and bold deals. Few great ventures in the city lacked his hand by then. He sat as a deputy from 1842 and spoke on trade and money. Craft and nerve made him a power behind the throne. He helped plan the coup that made his brother emperor. Six months as interior minister followed that stroke.
britannica-1911-mortillet-louis-laurent-:
Mortillet, Louis Laurent Gabriel de, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life. Born at Meylan in Isere on the 29th of August 1821, he was French. He was schooled at a Jesuit college and at the Paris Conservatoire. In 1847 he took charge of a review called La Revue Independante.

Caught up in the revolt of 1848, he was sentenced to two years in gaol. He fled the land and lived abroad for fifteen years, chiefly in Italy. In 1858 he turned to the study of early man and Swiss lake homes. Back in Paris in 1864, he took a post at the museum at St Germain. His best known book, from 1882, deals with life before writ history.
britannica-1911-motteville-francoise-ber:
Francoise Bertaut de Motteville is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was a French writer of memoirs who lived from about 1621 to 1689. Her mother served Anne of Austria, wife of King Louis the Thirteenth. The young girl joined the queen's household at age seven.

The article tells how exile and a brief marriage took her away from court. She came back in 1642 and stayed close to the queen through the Fronde revolt. Her chief work is her memoirs, which act as a history of Anne of Austria. They give a clear and fair picture of court life at that time. The text also notes later editions and an English translation.
britannica-1911-narbonne-lara-louis-mari:
Louis Marie Jacques Amalric de Narbonne Lara is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French soldier and envoy born in Parma in seventeen fifty five. Gossip at court named a king of France as his true father. He was raised at Versailles with the royal girls of France.

The entry tells how he rose to colonel at the age of twenty five. A famed salon host won him the post of war minister in the revolt. Weak work there forced him out to join a field army in the north. He fled France in time and came home nine years later. He died on a hard envoy task in the last wars of Napoleon.
britannica-1911-nogaret-guillaume-de:
Guillaume de Nogaret, who died in 1313, was chief adviser to Philip the Fourth of France. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica puts his birth between 1260 and 1270. His father was a townsman of Toulouse. Rumour said the family had been charged with false belief in the Albigensian crusade. Guillaume taught law at Montpellier in 1291. By 1296 he sat in the king's court at Paris.

His fame rests on the clash between Philip and Pope Boniface the Eighth. In 1303 he sold the king a bold plan. The pope would be seized in Italy and hauled to France for trial. Nogaret led the plot on the ground. With help from the Colonna house, he raised a band of some 1,600 men. On the seventh of September they surprised the town of Anagni. Boniface was taken in his own birthplace, a shock that shook the church.
britannica-1911-ode:
Ode is a form of stately, high lyric verse in poetry. The 1911 Britannica entry builds the word from a Greek term for song. In its first sense an ode was a chant to be sung aloud. Strings played while the voice sang that chant in old Greece. Greek song split into two great kinds in that early age.

One kind was the lone voice of the poet in his own person. The other was the choric song of a trained band of dancers. Poets such as Alcaeus, Anacreon, and Sappho shaped the first kind. The choir song led in time to the ode in the strict sense. Alcman is thought to have first set poems in strophic form.
britannica-1911-oihenart-arnauld-de:
Arnauld de Oihenart was a Basque historian and poet of the seventeenth century. He lived from fifteen ninety two to sixteen sixty eight. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Mauleon, he studied law at Bordeaux and took his degree in sixteen twelve.

Oihenart practised law first in his home town, then at the Navarre court. He spent his free time and his wealth hunting old Basque records. He searched the stores of Bayonne, Toulouse, Pau, and other cities widely. His finds filled forty five hand written volumes sent to Colbert later. His chief work describes Gascony and Navarre and their old houses.
britannica-1911-oudenarde:
Oudenarde, a town of Belgium in East Flanders eighteen miles south of Ghent, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its count in 1904 was 6572 people. Most folk know it for the great win of Marlborough and Eugene over the French under Vendôme in 1708. The town holds much more of note than that battle.

Its town hall took ten years to build, from 1525 to 1535. Next to that of Louvain, its front is the most richly worked in Belgium. A belfry tower of five storeys with three terraces and a golden figure crowns the hall. The council room holds a fine oak door and a Gothic chimney piece from about 1530. Two old churches, St Walburga and Notre Dame, add to the stock of sights.
britannica-1911-oviedo-y-valdes-gonzalo-:
Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés (1478–1557) was a Spanish historian, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his path to the Indies. He was born at Madrid in August 1478. He was educated at the court of Ferdinand and Isabella. At thirteen he became a page to their son, the Infante Don John.

Oviedo was present at the siege of Granada as a youth. There he saw Columbus before the voyage to America. When Prince John died in 1497, Oviedo went to Italy. He served there as secretary to Gonzalo Fernandez de Cordoba. In 1514 he was made supervisor of the gold smeltings at San Domingo. On his return to Spain in 1523, he was named historiographer of the Indies. He made five more visits to America before his death in 1557.
britannica-1911-padilla-juan-lopez-de:
Juan Lopez de Padilla was the leader of a rising in Castile called the war of the communities, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his story. In that war the commons of Castile made a futile stand against the arbitrary policy of Charles the Fifth and his Flemish ministers. Padilla was the eldest son of the commendator of Castile and was born at Toledo.

The cities had first sent deputies to Avila to demand, in vain, the king's return and regard for the rights of the cortes. They also asked for thrifty rule in Spanish hands. When words failed, they resolved on force and formed the holy junta, with Padilla at its head. The junta tried to set up a national government in the name of Joanna, seized her person, and took the treasury books, archives and seals of the kingdom. But its bold claims soon alienated the nobility.
