britannica-1911-palafox-de-mendoza-juan-:
Juan de Palafox de Mendoza (1600-1659), a Spanish bishop, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Aragon, he was sent as bishop to Puebla de los Angeles in Mexico. There he won honour for his work to shield the native people from Spanish cruelty. He banned all means of winning converts other than gentle persuasion.

That stand brought him the firm enmity of the Jesuits, whom he placed under a ban in 1647. Twice he laid a formal charge against them at Rome, in 1647 and in 1649. The pope would not back his bans, though a brief did order the Jesuits to respect his rights as bishop. In 1653 they got him moved to the small see of Osma in Spain. A later push to make him a saint failed, the entry says, through Jesuit action.
britannica-1911-palafox-y-melzi-jose-de:
Palafox y Melzi, Jose de is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Spanish duke. The youngest son of an old Aragonese family, he was brought up at the Spanish court and entered the guards young. In 1808 he went with Ferdinand to Bayonne and tried in vain to arrange the king's escape. He fled to Spain and placed himself at the head of the patriot movement in Aragon.

The article centres on the two sieges of Saragossa. Proclaimed governor and captain-general in May 1808, Palafox declared war on the French though he had neither money nor regular troops. When the French took half the town, the people fought street by street until the besiegers withdrew. In the second siege the town held three months before ruin and pestilence ended resistance. Palafox, sick with the epidemic, was held at Vincennes until 1813.
britannica-1911-pareja-juan-de:
Juan de Pareja (1606–1670) was a Spanish painter, and his strange rise is told in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born a slave in the West Indies about 1606. In early life he passed into the service of Velazquez. There he ground colours and did the low work of the studio.

By day Pareja watched his master’s methods at close range. By night he practised in secret with the brushes, until he gained real skill. The story goes that he slipped a picture of his own among the works of Velazquez. The picture sat there just before a visit by King Philip the Fourth. It was found and praised by the king. Pareja then received his freedom on the spot. He chose to spend that freedom in the service of his former master.
britannica-1911-paris-francois-de: Francois de Paris, a French churchman who lived from 1690 to 1727, is the subject of a brief life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Paris, he strongly opposed the bull Unigenitus of 1713, which condemned a noted annotated Bible. He backed the Jansenists in their long fight. When he died, his grave at Saint Medard became a place of pilgrimage where crowds claimed wonders. The king had the churchyard closed in 1732.
britannica-1911-parker-sir-hyde:
Parker, Sir Hyde, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a British sea officer. Born at Tredington on the 25th of February 1714, he was a clergyman's son. He began his sea life in the merchant service as a youth. At age twenty-four he joined the royal navy as an officer.

He rose to lieutenant in 1744 and to post-captain in 1748. In the Seven Years War he served in the East Indies with skill. He helped take Pondicherry in 1761 and Manila the next year. There his two ships seized a rich Spanish plate ship at sea. In 1781 he fought a Dutch fleet near the Dogger Bank. The hard fight ended with no side the winner.
britannica-1911-parny-evariste-desire-de:
Evariste Desire de Forges de Parny is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French poet born on an isle in the Indian Ocean in seventeen fifty three. He was sent to France for school at the age of nine. A brief spell in the army gave way to a call back home.

The entry tells of a first love lost when her father barred the match. That loss fed the love poems that made his name on his return. Later work turned to mock tales of gods and of church and state. One wild poem mocked an English king in its very title page. His soft early verse still draws praise for its grace and warmth.
britannica-1911-pasquinade:
A pasquinade is a kind of libel or lampoon aimed at public men, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica admits the term is hard to pin down. In practice the line between a pasquinade and other satire was rarely kept. The chief interest of the word lies in its odd and half legendary origin. The tale was first told by Mazocchi in 1509.

In that tale, Pasquino was a schoolmaster at Rome in the fifteenth century. Other versions make him a cobbler instead. All agree that he had a biting tongue. Near the end of that century his name passed to a broken statue dug up in 1501. The statue was set up at a corner of the Piazza Navona. Sharp verses pinned to it took the name of its supposed first author.
britannica-1911-phillips-adelaide: Adelaide Phillips is the subject of a short life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Stratford-on-Avon in England in 1833, she was a singer with a deep contralto voice. Her family crossed to America in 1840, and she went on the Boston stage at ten. In 1850 her gift for song stood out, and Jenny Lind helped send her to London and Italy to train. She came home in 1855 a finished singer. For years she led her field in America.
britannica-1911-pina-ruy-de:
Ruy de Pina, a Portuguese chronicler who lived from 1440 to 1521, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Guarda, he served King John the Second as envoy to Castile and went to Rome in 1484. The king set him to write a history of his reign and paid him a pension. In 1497 King Manoel made him chronicler of the kingdom and keeper of the royal records.

By 1504 Pina had finished his chronicles of Alphonso the Fifth and John the Second. A later king charged him with a history of Manoel, which he carried down to the taking of Azamor. The entry notes a catch in his fame. Some early chronicles printed under his name seem to be work by Fernão Lopes that Pina only edited. His standing as a historian is still rated high, and his frank pen drew remark.
britannica-1911-pisan-christine-de:
Christine de Pisan, who lived from 1364 to about 1430, was a French poet born in Venice. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica brings her to Paris at the age of four. Her father served Charles the Fifth as astrologer there. At fifteen she wed a royal notary and secretary. The king's death cost her father his post, and he died soon after. Her husband's death in 1389 left her with three children and no protector.

That need drove her to write for a living. First came ballads in memory of her husband. From 1399 she read the Latin poets with care. By 1405 she had made some fifteen major works, chiefly in prose. After Agincourt she withdrew to a convent. In 1429 she broke her silence with a song for Joan of Arc.
britannica-1911-pitchblende:
Pitchblende, also called uraninite, is a mineral described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is in the main a uranium oxide, and it counts as a source of uranium and of radium. It is very heavy for a stone and breaks with a shell-like or uneven face. Its colour runs from brown to velvet black, and its shine is like that of pitch.

Crystals are rare and take the form of eight-sided or cube shapes. The stone has been known at Joachimsthal in Bohemia since 1727. It was called pitchblende for its look, but its true make was not known until 1789. In that year Klaproth broke it down and found the new element uranium in it. Tests of stone from many places show wide shifts in its mix. Thorium, cerium, yttrium, and lead oxides all show in it in small shares.
britannica-1911-poltrot-jean-de:
Jean de Poltrot, who lived from about 1537 to 1563, was a nobleman of Angoumois who murdered Francis, Duke of Guise, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells his story. He had lived some time in Spain. His knowledge of Spanish got him work as a spy in the wars against Spain.

Poltrot became a fanatical Huguenot and resolved to kill the duke. He gained entry as a deserter to the Catholic camp that was besieging Orleans. On the evening of the eighteenth of February 1563 he hid by a road the duke would pass, fired a pistol at him, and fled. He was captured the next day. After torture and a trial, he was sentenced to be drawn and quartered, and he underwent a frightful punishment that March. His shifting claims about Coligny's part in the plot appear, the entry says, to have had no foundation.
britannica-1911-pontecoulant-louis-gusta:
Louis Gustave le Doulcet, Comte de Pontécoulant, a French politician who lived from 1764 to 1853, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Caen in November 1764. He began a career in the army in 1778.

A moderate supporter of the Revolution, he was sent to the Convention for Calvados in 1792. He became commissary with the army of the North. He voted for the king to be held in prison during the war. After the peace, he voted for banishment. He then joined the party of the Gironde and was outlawed in August 1793. He had refused to defend Charlotte Corday, his fellow citizen. She wrote him a letter of reproach on her way to the scaffold. He came back to the Convention in March 1795. There he showed a rare spirit of moderation, defending old foes.
britannica-1911-pontmartin-armand-august:
Armand Pontmartin (1811–1890), comte de Pontmartin, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French critic and man of letters, born at Avignon on the 16th of July 1811. From family custom he held legitimist views. He began by attacking the followers of the encyclopaedists and the men who came after them. In the paper Assemblée nationale he put out his Causeries littéraires, a run of attacks on well known Liberals. Those pieces made a stir.

Pontmartin was a tireless journalist, and most of his papers were later put out in book form. His most famous book is Les Jeudis de Mme Charbonneau of 1862. In the shape of a novel it gave a run of sharp and witty portraits of writers of his day. He died at Avignon in March 1890.
britannica-1911-promenade: Promenade is a walk taken for exercise or for social amusement, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. Hence it is also a road, drive, or other public place laid out for that purpose. The French word was formerly pourmenade, from a verb meaning to take for a walk. Its Latin root means to drive an animal out to pasture, with a sense of driving on by cries. Promenade concerts, where the audience may walk about as they listen, were first brought from Paris to London in 1838.
britannica-1911-pulgar-hernando-de:
Hernando de Pulgar, Spanish prose writer born at Pulgar near Toledo in 1436, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was schooled at the court of John the Second. Henry the Fourth made him one of his secretaries in time. Under Isabella he rose to councillor of state and went on a mission to France.

In 1482 he was named historiographer royal for the crown. He is said to have died in 1492. His chronicle of the Catholic kings is often wrong and always fawning, the entry says. Yet it holds worth for events that fell within his own sight and hearing. His book of famed men of Castile at the court of Henry the Fourth draws praise for matter and style. Letters to men of rank and a commentary on verses round out his work.
britannica-1911-quatrefages-de-breau-jea:
Jean Louis Armand de Quatrefages de Bréau, a French naturalist who lived from 1810 to 1892, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Berthezène in the Gard in February 1810, he was the son of a Protestant farmer. He studied medicine at Strassburg and took degrees in medicine and science. His early work included a book on aerolites and a treatise on a bladder condition.

Quatrefages practised medicine briefly at Toulouse and wrote for science journals. Unable to keep up his research in the provinces, he gave up a zoology chair and settled in Paris in 1839. There Milne-Edwards became his patron. In 1852 he joined the Academy of Sciences. In 1855 he was called to the chair of anthropology at the national museum. Honours followed to the end of his career.
britannica-1911-ram-pierre-francois-xavi:
Pierre Francois Xavier de Ram was a Belgian churchman and writer of history, born at Louvain. He took orders young, and was made a teacher of verse at a priests school and keeper of the records of his diocese. The head note of his dates in the piece bears a misprint, but his life ran in the eighteen hundreds.

In the years just before the Belgian revolt, Ram worked to join men of free views and men of his church in one front. He sought to give a broad cast to the line of his church in the new land. He would not stand for the new state assembly, the 1911 Britannica entry says. He gave his life to teaching and to books of the past. He helped found a Catholic college, moved to his home town, and led it as rector till his death.
britannica-1911-rambouillet-catherine-de:
Catherine de Vivonne, marquise de Rambouillet, lived from 1588 to 1665. The 1911 Britannica life hails her place in the letters of France. She was the daughter and heir of Jean de Vivonne, marquis of Pisani. Her mother came of the noble Roman house of Savelli in Italy. At age twelve she wed Charles d'Angennes, later marquis de Rambouillet.

The young bride found court life coarse and full of plots. It held no charm for her keen and refined taste at all. After her first child's birth in 1607, she drew a circle round her. She set up at the Hotel de Rambouillet in Paris in state. She planned suites of small rooms where guests could move with ease.
britannica-1911-rapin-paul-de:
Rapin, Paul de is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French writer of history. Paul de Rapin, sieur of Thoyras, was born at Castres on the twenty-fifth of March 1661 and died in 1725. He was the son of a lawyer there. He was schooled at Saumur and became a lawyer in 1679, but soon joined the army.

The wiping out of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, and his father's death, drove him to England. Finding no work, he crossed to Holland and joined a band of French volunteers under his cousin Daniel de Rapin. He came back to England with the prince of Orange in 1688. In the Irish campaign he fought at Carrickfergus and the Boyne and was hurt at Limerick. He later gave up his captain's post to tutor the earl of Portland's son, then settled in Holland.
britannica-1911-recamier-jeanne-francois:
Recamier, Jeanne, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a famed French hostess. Born at Lyons on the 4th of December 1777, her maiden name was Bernard. At age fifteen she wed a banker old enough to be her father. Beauty, skill, and a true love of letters marked her out.

From the consulate days her Paris salon drew the cream of society. Men of letters and state life made her house a chief resort. Old royalists mixed there with men ill at ease with the regime. Her refusal to serve the Empress Josephine drew Napoleon's distrust. Her close bond with Madame de Stael added to that distrust of her. In the end Napoleon exiled her from Paris by his order.
britannica-1911-regicide:
Regicide, the killing of a king, is the head word of a history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In English use, the Regicides are the men held to blame for the death of Charles the First. When Charles the Second came back in 1660, his pledge at Breda spared all but those Parliament chose to leave out.

Parliament moved fast. The Commons told officers to seize all who had sat in judgment on the late king. The count of such men came to more than eighty, from judges at the sittings to court staff and the two men who carried out the death. Some were caught and some gave themselves up. The Commons first named twelve to lose their lives, while the Lords pressed for far more. In the end the law of August 1660 split the regicides into six groups for their pains.
britannica-1911-regnier-henri-francois-j:
Henri Francois Joseph de Regnier was born in 1864 and is a French poet. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Honfleur in Calvados, his birth town. He was born there on the twenty eighth of December 1864. He was schooled in Paris for the law as a young man. In 1885 he began to place verse in the Paris reviews.

His poems ran in most French and Belgian journals of the symbolist kind. Yet he kept the classical line of the Parnassians he first followed. New turns from Moreas and Kahn entered his work as well. His rich, vague style shows the mark of Mallarme, his master. A first book of poems, Lendemains, came out in that same year 1885.
britannica-1911-remusat-charles-francois:
Charles François Marie, Comte de Rémusat (1797-1875), was a French statesman and man of letters, born in Paris, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. His father had been chamberlain to Napoleon and later a prefect under the restored kings. His mother, a lady of the court of Josephine, was famed for her mind and grace, and her memoirs later threw much light on Napoleon's court.

Charles held more liberal views than his parents, trained for the bar, and issued a pamphlet on trial by jury in 1820. He was an active journalist, signed the protest against the Ordinances of July 1830, and was elected a deputy that October. He ranked himself with the doctrinaires and backed many of the curbs on popular liberty that made the July monarchy disliked by French radicals.
britannica-1911-renneville-rene-auguste-:
Rene Auguste Constantin de Renneville was a French writer of the Bastille. He lived from sixteen fifty to seventeen twenty three. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Caen, he left France for Holland in sixteen ninety nine. His Protestant faith drove that flight from his home land then.

On his return three years later, Renneville was named a spy by foes. He was locked in the Bastille from that time until seventeen thirteen. In prison he wrote poems in the margins of a book copy. Queen Anne plea won his freedom, and he fled to England next. There he issued his History of the Bastille in seven parts.
britannica-1911-resende-andre-de:
Andre de Resende, who lived from 1498 to 1573, is called the father of archaeology in Portugal in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He began life as a Dominican friar, but about 1540 he passed to the ranks of the secular clergy. He spent many years in travel in Spain, France, and Belgium. There he wrote to Erasmus and to other men of learning.

He was close to King John the Third and to his sons, and he served as tutor to the Infante Duarte. In his own day his fame was great. Later writers have shown, the article warns, that he was not exact and not strict in his use of sources. His Portuguese works include a history of the antiquity of Evora and a life of the Infante Duarte. His chief Latin work deals with the antiquities of Lusitania, the old Roman name for his land.
britannica-1911-resende-garcia-de:
Garcia de Resende, a Portuguese poet and editor, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He was born at Evora in 1470. At the age of ten he became a page to King John the Second. By 1491 he was the king's private secretary. He was present at the king's death in 1495. He kept royal favour under King Manoel as well.

Manoel made him a knight of the Order of Christ. In 1514 he went to Rome with a famed embassy. He served it as secretary and treasurer. In 1516 he gained rank in the royal household. Resende wrote verse at the court of John from his youth. The king once made him recite poems from memory at night. He also drew and made music with skill. His great work was an album of court verse. That songbook holds pieces by some three hundred nobles.
britannica-1911-reszke-jean-de:
Jean de Reszke, an opera singer born in 1850, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Warsaw, the son of a state official and of a mother who sang well at home. Their house was a known centre of music. The boy sang in the cathedral choir and then read law at the university there.

He soon gave up law and went to Italy to train his voice. He first sang in public as a baritone at Venice in 1874, then in London and Paris, with no great success. He rested and trained more, and his voice gained in its top range. In 1879 he came back at Madrid as a tenor, and his great fame dates from then. He sang year by year in Paris and London, went to America in 1891, and was a star at the New York opera house through the nineties.
britannica-1911-retz-jean-francois-paul-:
Jean Francois Paul de Gondi, Cardinal de Retz, was a French churchman and stirrer of strife in the sixteen hundreds. Born at Montmirail, he came of a house brought into France by a famed queen and grown rich in land and rank. He was the third son, short, near sighted, and clumsy in form, with no look of a soldier.

The 1911 Britannica entry shows a youth pushed toward the church by his kin, though he had little bent for that life. He threw himself into the debates of the Sorbonne with force. While still in his teens he wrote a short work of history that made his name. Readers get a sharp early sketch of a man set to mix faith, plots, and power.
britannica-1911-rezanov-nicolai-petrovic:
Nicolai Petrovich de Rezánov, a Russian nobleman and administrator who lived from 1764 to 1807, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He served under Catherine the Second, Paul the First, and Alexander the First. He was one of the ten barons of Russia and held the court title of chamberlain. In 1803 he was made a privy councillor and given the order of St Ann.

Rezánov wrote a lexicon of the Japanese language and was a member of the St Petersburg Academy. He was the first Russian ambassador to Japan, in 1804, and prompted Russia's first attempt to sail around the globe. His lasting monument, though, was the Russian American Fur Company. In 1788 he met the fur merchant Shelikov, became a partner in his project, and grew into a keen man of business.
britannica-1911-rivarol-antoine-de:
Antoine de Rivarol (1753-1801) was a French writer famed for his sharp sayings. He was born at Bagnols in Languedoc on 26 June 1753 and died at Berlin on 11 April 1801. His father is said to have been an innkeeper with a love of good letters. The son took the title of count and claimed a tie to a noble Italian house. His foes said his true name was Riverot and that the family was not noble.

Rivarol came to Paris in 1777 and won school prizes there. In 1784 he made his name with a treatise on why French is spoken so widely, and with a rendering of Dante's Inferno. Just before the Revolution he joined in a cruel lampoon of the great men of the day. That book mocked men of real gifts and a crowd of nobodies with no mercy at all.
britannica-1911-riverside:
Riverside is the subject of a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Riverside is a city in southern California and the seat of Riverside County. It stands on the Santa Ana river in the San Bernardino valley. By 1910 its people numbered just over fifteen thousand. The city sits on a slope and was known as a winter health resort.

The article notes broad avenues lined with pepper trees and parks. It names a large boarding school for Native pupils, opened in 1903. The city lives by growing oranges, lemons, and other warm climate fruits. Navel oranges were first brought to the country at Riverside in 1873. The two first trees still stood in 1909, guarded by a rail. A state fruit test farm also works near the city.
britannica-1911-roberval-gilles-personne:
Gilles Personne de Roberval was a French worker in maths, born in a village near Beauvais that gave him his known name. Like a famed peer of his age, he was at a great siege in his youth. That same year he went to Paris to make his way in the world of learning.

He won a chair of thought at one college, then the chair of maths at the royal college of France. A hard term hung on that chair, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Its holder had to pose maths tasks for men to solve, and had to yield his post to any man who solved them with more skill than he. In spite of that rule, Roberval kept the chair till his death in Paris. He stands among the men who paved the way to a new maths of the small.
britannica-1911-rodomontade: Rodomontade, a term for boastful and inflated speech, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It can also be spelled Rhodomontade. The word refers to Rodomonte, the brave but boastful Saracen leader in Ariosto's poem Orlando Furioso. The name appears earlier, as Rodamante, in Boiardo's Orlando Innamorato. It is thought to join words for to roll and a mountain.
britannica-1911-rohan-henri-duc-de:
Henri, Duc de Rohan, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rohan was a French soldier, writer, and leader of the Huguenots. He was born in 1579 at the chateau of Blain in Brittany. His family ranked among the oldest and greatest in France.

His mother, a woman of rare learning and force, saw to his education. He was the second son, but his elder brother's early death made him heir. At sixteen he appeared at court and in the army. King Henry the Fourth held him in special favour. After Condé, Rohan stood as the natural chief of the French Protestants. He served until the peace of Vervins, then travelled widely in Europe. Visits to England and Scotland form part of that tour. The entry sets up the making of a Protestant leader in a Catholic kingdom.
britannica-1911-rohan-louis-rene-edouard:
Louis René Édouard de Rohan, cardinal and archbishop of Strassburg, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He was born in Paris in 1734 into the great Rohan family. His kin had held the see of Strassburg since 1704. That post made its holder a prince of the empire. Rohan was marked for it from birth. He took orders in 1760 and became coadjutor to his uncle.

The article shows a churchman who liked Paris life more than duty. He joined the party set against the Austrian alliance. In 1771 he was sent on a special embassy to Vienna. His task was to learn what was planned for the partition of Poland. His lavish feasts made a stir there. But the empress Maria Theresa was firmly against him. On the death of Louis the Fifteenth he was recalled.
britannica-1911-ronsard-pierre-de:
Pierre de Ronsard, a French poet born in fifteen twenty four, was called prince of poets by his own age in France. He was born at a chateau near Couture in the Vendomois. His family were said to come from Slav lands south of the Danube. They reached France in the first half of the fourteenth century. His father served the king as head of his household.

Pierre was the youngest son and was schooled at home for some years. At nine he was sent to the College de Navarre at Paris. The rough life of a medieval school did not suit him, the entry says. He had little of it, since he soon became a page. He served first the king's eldest son, then the duke of Orleans. When Madeleine of France wed James the Fifth of Scotland, Ronsard joined her train.
britannica-1911-roskilde:
Roskilde is a town in Denmark, west of the chief town by rail, on a wide lake like mouth of the sea. Its count of folk in nineteen one was past eight thousand. It has a small port and is a chief rail hub for the isle. Its true draw, though, is its past.

It was chief town of the realm till fourteen forty-three and home of the bishops till the great change of faith. Its great church stands as the tomb house of the kings of Denmark, much as a famed abbey does for England. Chapels, carved stalls, and a rich altar fill that church.
britannica-1911-rossi-luigi-de:
Luigi de Rossi is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an Italian writer of music in the 1600s, said to have been born at Naples late in the 1500s. Of his life, the text says, next to nothing is known.

The article rests instead on his works and his fame. His opera The Enchanted Palace was staged at Rome in 1642. In 1646 Cardinal Mazarin called him to Paris. There his opera on Orpheus and Eurydice was staged in 1647. It was the first Italian opera heard in Paris. A set of his songs came out in 1646. One later writer ranks him with Carissimi and Cesti as a great light of the craft. His chamber songs hold the highest place in his output.
britannica-1911-rozas-juan-martinez-de:
Juan Martinez de Rozas (1759-1813) was the earliest leader in Chile's fight for freedom from Spain, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells his story. He was born at Mendoza and first taught law, theology, and philosophy at Santiago. He served for a time as acting governor of Concepcion and as a colonel in a militia regiment. In 1808 he became secretary to the last Spanish governor, Carrasco.

Rozas used that post to prepare the nationalist movement that broke out in 1809. He helped force the governor's resignation and the forming of a national junta in September 1810, and he was its real leader. Under him came free trade, an army, and a national congress in 1811. But his followers split with the men of Santiago, and his rival Carrera had him banished in 1812. He died at Mendoza in March 1813.
britannica-1911-ruvigny-henri-de-massue-:
Henri de Massue, Marquis de Ruvigny, afterwards Earl of Galway, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He lived from 1648 to 1720 and was born at Paris in April 1648. His father was a noted French diplomatist. Ruvigny saw service under Turenne, who thought very highly of him. His English connexions led Louis the Fourteenth to choose him in 1678 for secret talks.

Those talks aimed at a compact with Charles the Second, and Ruvigny handled them with great skill. He succeeded his father as general of the Huguenots. When the Edict of Nantes was revoked, he refused the king's offer to keep that office. In 1690 he went into exile and entered the service of William the Third. He stood out at the battle of Aughrim in 1691. He was later made Viscount Galway and given large estates in Ireland.
britannica-1911-sa-de-miranda-francisco-:
Francisco de Sá de Miranda (1485-1558) was a Portuguese poet from a noble family of Coimbra. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica shows him at court and at Lisbon University from 1505. He took a degree in law and won the friendship of Prince John. Verse and court life filled much of his early time.

He gave up law after his father died and turned to moral thought and poetry. Travel abroad shaped his aim to bring new forms of art to Portugal. He felt his land had great deeds but weak verse to match them. His early poems had appeared in a court songbook that showed that lack plainly.
britannica-1911-saavedra-angel-de:
Angel de Saavedra, duke of Rivas (1791–1865), was a Spanish poet and man of state. He was born at Cordova on 19 March 1791. He fought in the war of independence and was a marked man of the advanced Liberal party from 1820 to 1823. In that last year he was sentenced to death. He got away to London and lived in Italy, Malta, and France in turn. He came back to Spain on the pardon of 1834 and soon took his brother's title as duke.

In 1835 Saavedra became minister of the interior, but he had to leave the land once more with his chief. Back in 1837, he joined the moderate party and became prime minister. He was later an envoy at Paris and at Naples, and he died on 22 June 1865.
britannica-1911-saavedra-fajardo-diego-d:
Diego de Saavedra Fajardo is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born of a noble family at Algezares on the sixth of May 1584, he was a Spanish envoy and man of letters. He was schooled for the church at Salamanca and took orders.

The article follows his service to the Spanish crown abroad. In 1606 he became secretary to the Spanish envoy at Rome. In time he rose to speak for Spain at Regensburg and at Munster. He came home in 1646 to a seat on the council of the Indies. His famed book of 1640 holds a hundred short essays on the schooling of a prince. It was written for the son of Philip the Fourth. Its crisp, pointed style is still praised in Spain, the text says.
britannica-1911-sable-madeleine-de-souvr:
Madeleine de Souvre, marquise de Sable, a French writer who lived from 1599 to 1678, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Gilles de Souvre, tutor of Louis the Thirteenth and a marshal of France. In 1614 she wed the marquis de Sable, who died in 1640 and left her in narrow means.

With a friend she took rooms in the Place Royale in Paris and set up a salon for men and women of letters. From that circle came a new class of writing, the short maxims of which La Rochefoucauld is the famed case. Her own maxims were in fact written before his, though printed only after her death. In 1655 she withdrew to the convent of Port Royal des Champs. She moved as houses closed, and died at the Port Royal convent in Paris in 1678.
britannica-1911-saint-albin-alexander-ch:
Alexander Rousselin de Saint Albin was a French leader in public life, born in Paris of a noble house. Schooled at a famed college, he took up the new ideas of the revolt with zeal. Sent as a state envoy to a town, he was charged by some with harsh rule and by the revolt court with softness.

The 1911 Britannica entry notes a short spell in jail, then posts at the heart of the state under the Directory. Tied to a famed general, he fell under the watch of the emperors police and spent the late empire years in quiet exile in the south. He served in a brief return of rule, then backed free views in a paper he founded. Though a past king was his friend, he took no post from him.
britannica-1911-saint-amant-marc-antoine:
Marc Antoine de Saint-Amant was a French poet born near Rouen in the late fifteen hundreds. His father was a merchant who, by his sons tale, had sailed at sea and led a fleet for a great queen. That tale lacks proof from other hands, the 1911 Britannica entry warns.

The son won a grant of noble rank and tied himself to great lords of the court in turn. He saw war service and lived at times in Italy, in England, in Poland on a court post, and in other lands. His stay in England drew from him a fierce verse attack on that land. His late years were spent in France, and he died in Paris. He left a fair body of verse, and set a vogue for the comic mock poem.
britannica-1911-saint-andre-jacques-d-al:
Jacques d'Albon, seigneur de Saint Andre (about 1505-1562), a French soldier and a favourite of King Henry the Second, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was made a marshal of France, governor of the Lyonnais, and an envoy to England. He served with great bravery against the emperor Charles the Fifth in 1552.

The article traces the close of his career. He was taken prisoner at the battle of Saint Quentin in 1557 but freed the next year. He then helped make the peace of Cateau-Cambresis. After the death of Francis the Second, he joined with Montmorency and the duke of Guise in a league of three against the Protestants and the queen mother. He died at the battle of Dreux, killed by a private foe.
britannica-1911-saint-arnaud-jacques-ler:
Jacques Leroy de Saint Arnaud, a marshal of France born in eighteen hundred and one, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Paris, he joined the army in eighteen seventeen. After ten years of quiet post duty he still held the lowest officer rank. He then quit the ranks.

He led a roving life in more than one land. At age thirty he came back at the lowest grade. He helped crush a rising in the west of France and served a famed general. Debt and scandal then drove him to Algeria as a captain in the Foreign Legion. There he stood out time and time again. In twelve years he rose to high field rank. The life is a sharp tale of fall and rise.
britannica-1911-saint-simon-louis-de-rou:
Louis de Rouvroy, duke of Saint-Simon, a French soldier and memoir writer, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He lived from 1675 to 1755 and was born at Versailles on January 16, 1675. The peerage granted to his father is called the central fact of his life. The piece spends much space on what a French peer was.

A peer was not the same as a man made noble, the text shows. The rank clung to set lands, not to the man himself. Peers formed a sort of standing group for the whole body of nobles. Saint-Simon spent his life in a bid to turn them into a great council of the nation. His mother came from a family long in public service.
britannica-1911-salade:
Salade, a light helm of the fifteenth century, gets a short arms entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry says it took the place of the heavy helmet of earlier war. Its key marks are a smooth round face, like a bowl turned upside down. A long neck guard juts out at the back to shield the neck.

There was most often no vizor that could be raised or lowered. The fixed front still hid most of the wearer face from view. One slit was left in that front plate for the eyes alone. The name came by French from words for an engraved helm.
britannica-1911-sancy-nicolas-de-harlay-:
Nicolas de Harlay, Seigneur de Sancy, who lived from 1546 to 1629, is profiled in a life from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born to the Protestant branch of the Harlay family in France, he turned Catholic in 1572, in the year of the massacres of the Huguenots. He worked as both a soldier and a diplomat.

The life tells how he raised cash in Geneva and Berne in 1589 to hire troops for Henry the Third, in part by selling jewels such as the famed Sancy diamond. Henry the Fourth made him head of his finances in 1594, but Sully took his place five years later. His sway at court then faded, and he left public life in 1605. A short second part covers his son Achille, a bishop who built a fine store of eastern books.
britannica-1911-saumarez-james-saumarez-:
James Saumarez, Baron de Saumarez (1757–1836), was an English admiral, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his rise at sea. He was born at St Peter Port, Guernsey, on the eleventh of March 1757. Many men of his old family had served in the navy before him. He entered the service as a midshipman at the age of thirteen.

Saumarez won a lieutenancy for bravery at the attack on Charleston in 1776, aboard the Bristol. He was made commander for gallant service off the Dogger Bank in 1781, where he was wounded. In command of the Russell, he shared in Rodney’s victory over De Grasse in 1782. He was knighted in 1793 for taking the French frigate La Réunion. The entry follows a career built on bold action in close fights.
britannica-1911-semonville-charles-louis:
Charles Louis Huguet, marquis de Sémonville (1759-1839), was a French diplomat, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his eventful missions. He was born in Paris, the son of a royal secretary. As envoy to Genoa in 1790 and 1791 he did his first work abroad. Sent toward Turin to pull Sardinia away from the Austrian alliance, he was not even let across the border.

In 1793, travelling into Italy with a fellow envoy, he was seized on Austrian orders and held in a Tyrolean prison. He was freed in December 1795 in an exchange tied to the release of the daughter of Louis the Sixteenth. Bonaparte, who had helped gain his freedom, sent him to The Hague in 1799 to firm up the bond with the Batavian Republic. The entry credits him with full success there and with a hand in the plan for the Austrian marriage.
britannica-1911-sevigne-marie-de-rabutin:
Marie de Rabutin-Chantal, Marquise de Sevigne (1626-1696), a French letter writer, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was born at Paris in February 1626. Her family was old and of high standing in Burgundy, traced in records to the twelfth century. For the most part they were men of the sword.

The article traces a childhood marked by loss. Her father, a great duellist, was killed in 1627 during an English attack on an island off France. Her mother did not long survive him, and Marie was left an orphan at the age of seven. She passed into the care of her mother's parents, both of them aged. Her grandmother on her father's side was the famed friend of Saint Francis of Sales. The entry builds the family ground from which the great letters later grew.
britannica-1911-side:
Side, a dead city of the Pamphylian coast, gets a site entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The place stands east of the mouth of the Eurymedon River. Its good harbour made it the chief town of Pamphylia in old times. Alexander the Great came there and held the city. Later a Rhodian fleet beat the fleet of Antiochus there. In time sea pirates made Side their main seat on that coast.

The ruins rank among the finest in Asia Minor. A wall and ditch fence the point from the mainland. The great theatre rises on arches, for no hill fit the Greek style. Temples, a water channel, and a fountain house also stand in the maze.
britannica-1911-solis-antonio-de:
Antonio de Solis, a Spanish playwright and historian, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in sixteen ten, he studied law at Salamanca. While there he wrote a comedy that was staged while he was still a student. He later became secretary to the count of Oropesa.

In sixteen fifty four he was made secretary of state and private secretary to Philip the Fourth. Later he gained the well paid post of chronicler of the Indies. On taking orders in sixteen sixty seven he cut his ties to the stage. The entry notes that ten of his plays survive, with two holding a place in drama history.
britannica-1911-soto-ferdinando-de:
Ferdinando de Soto, a Spanish captain and explorer who died in 1542, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born in Estremadura, of a poor family of good rank. A patron's favor paid for his studies. In 1519 he sailed with that patron on a second trip to Darien.

De Soto roamed the coasts of Guatemala and Yucatan in 1528. In 1532 he led three hundred men to aid Pizarro in Peru and shared in the fall of the Inca realm. He came home rich and wed his patron's daughter. Lured by tales of gold in Florida, he sold much of his wealth, raised a force, and won a royal post. For near four years he led his men on a fruitless hunt for gold.
britannica-1911-soubise-benjamin-de-roha:
Benjamin de Rohan, duc de Soubise, a Huguenot leader born at about 1589, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the younger brother of Henri de Rohan. His title came to him through his mother, Catherine de Parthenay. He learned war as a soldier under Prince Maurice of Orange-Nassau in the Low Countries.

In the wars of religion from 1621 his elder brother led on land in the south. Soubise took the west and the sea coast as his sphere. His chief feat was a bold attack in 1625 on the Royalist fleet in the river Blavet. His men cut a boom in the face of greater force and seized Oléron. He held command at Rochelle in the famed siege that followed. His brother tells his deeds with warmth and sharp eyes for war.
britannica-1911-sousa-luiz-de:
Luiz de Sousa, born Manoel de Sousa Coutinho (1555-1632), was a Portuguese monk and prose writer, and his life is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Santarem of a noble family, he left his studies at Coimbra in 1576 to join the order of Malta. Soon after, Moorish pirates captured him at sea.

The entry tells how he spent a year as a prisoner in Algiers, where he met Cervantes, before ransom set him free. Back in Portugal he saw his country lose its freedom to Spain, a loss that fed his dislike of foreign rule. He married in the mid 1580s, settled at Almada on the Tagus, and split his time between home, study, and army duty.
britannica-1911-souvre-gilles-de:
Gilles de Souvre, marquis de Courtanvaux, was a marshal of France in early times. He lived from about fifteen forty to sixteen twenty six. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came of an old family of the Perche region in France.

Souvre went with the duke of Anjou to Poland in fifteen seventy three. When Anjou became Henry the Third, Souvre gained high court posts fast. He fought at Coutras and held Tours against the Leaguers in war. In fifteen eighty five he was made governor of Touraine province. He was among the first to back Henry the Fourth in fifteen eighty nine. That king gave him charge of the dauphin schooling in court.
britannica-1911-spens-thomas-de:
Thomas de Spens is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Spens was a Scottish statesman and churchman who lived from about 1415 to 1480. He was schooled at Edinburgh. His rare abilities drew the notice of the advisers of King James the Second of Scotland. The king sent him on errands to England and to France. Near 1450 he became bishop of Galloway.

The article tells how he was made keeper of the privy seal and then bishop of Aberdeen in 1459. Much of his time passed in journeys to France and England on state business. In 1464 English sailors captured him at sea with a royal duke. King Edward the Fourth set him free, since Spens had once revealed a murder plot to him. He helped bring about peace treaties between England and Scotland. He gave generously to adorn his cathedral at Aberdeen.
britannica-1911-stade:
Stade, a town of Germany in the province of Hanover, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the river Schwinge, not far from where that stream joins the Elbe. In 1905 it held just under eleven thousand people. Its trade by ship runs chiefly to Hamburg, though the rise of Harburg has cut its old rank as a port.

Legend makes Stade the oldest town of the Saxons, founded in 321 before Christ. The record in fact reaches back only to the tenth century. It was once the seat of a line of counts and later joined the Hanseatic League. Sweden held it from 1648, then ceded it to Hanover in 1719. Prussian troops took it with no fight in 1866.
britannica-1911-stael-madame-de:
Madame de Stael was born Anne Louise Germaine Necker at Paris on 22 April 1766. She grew into a French novelist and a writer on many themes. Her father was Necker, the famed finance minister. Her mother, Suzanne Curchod, had been loved by Gibbon in her youth. She kept one of the most sought salons of Paris. Yet mother and daughter felt little warmth for each other.

Mme Necker was strict in her ways and set on a hard course of training for her child. The young Germaine was from her first years wild, flirtatious, and keen for note and praise. A kind of contest seems to have grown between mother and daughter. Each sought the first place in Necker's love. The article doubts that the daughter's love for her mother grew with time.
britannica-1911-stratford-john-de:
John de Stratford, archbishop of Canterbury who died in 1348, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Stratford on Avon and schooled at Merton College in Oxford. He then entered the service of Edward the Second. Posts as archdeacon, canon, and dean came to him in turn.

In 1323 he became bishop of Winchester while on a visit to the pope at Avignon. Edward the Second much disliked that choice at the time. In 1327 Stratford joined the party of Queen Isabella against the king. He drew up six charges against Edward and urged him at Kenilworth to give up the crown to his son. Under Edward the Third he rose to the royal council. From 1330, as chancellor, he stood for ten years as the king chief adviser in public work.
britannica-1911-strathclyde:
Strathclyde is the subject of a kingdom article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name was given in the ninth and tenth centuries to a British kingdom in the west of Scotland. From the seventh century it was likely confined to the basin of the Clyde and nearby coast districts. Its capital was Dumbarton, called the fortress of the Britons. The kingdom is also sometimes called Cumbria.

The article says no information survives on the origin of this kingdom of the north Britons. They seem to have been the ruling people in southern Scotland before the Roman invasion. After the Romans withdrew in the fifth century, they held their independence with more resolve than the southern kingdoms. Welsh tradition links northern princes to later Welsh royal lines. One prince, Rhydderch Hen, won supremacy after a great battle near the year 573. His death seems to have taken place in 603.
britannica-1911-suffren-saint-tropez-pie:
Suffren Saint Tropez, Pierre André de is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a French admiral. Suffren was the third son of the marquis de Saint Tropez. The French navy and the Order of Malta were the usual careers for younger sons of such families who did not enter the Church. Suffren was destined for both, and entered the corps of naval officers as a cadet in October 1743.

The article follows his early service at sea. He fought off Toulon in 1744, cruised in the West Indies, and endured the Cape Breton expedition of 1746. In 1747 Hawke took him prisoner in the Bay of Biscay. After the peace he did the cruises with the galleys of Malta called caravans.
britannica-1911-surville-clotilde-de:
"Clotilde de Surville" is the supposed maker of the Poésies de Clotilde. Tale gives her a full life. Born Marguerite Éléonore Clotilde de Vallon Challis at Vallon early in the 1400s, she wed Bérenger de Surville in 1421. War took him, and Orleans' siege killed him in 1428. His absence fed heroic verse and his death fed laments.

Some forty poems on love and war saw print in 1803, put out by Charles Vanderbourg. The tale of the found manuscript was a fable on its face. Wrong-age marks and modern verse rules led most judges to cry forgery. In 1863 Antonin Macé dug up letters to the marquis de Surville's widow. Those letters clear Vanderbourg of the fraud. Touching-up by Surville, an émigré shot for revolt work, explains the flaws. Local diggers then traced the case past that point.
britannica-1911-szigligeti-ede:
Ede Szigligeti (1814–1878) was a Hungarian dramatist, and his hard start in the theatre opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Nagyvárad Olaszi on the eighth of March 1814. His birth name was József Szathmáry. His parents wished to make him a priest, while he dreamed of being a doctor.

He entered an engineer office, but his heart was set on the stage. On the fifteenth of August 1834 he acted at Budapest, against his father’s express ban. His father then forbade him to bear the family name. The young man took the name Szigligeti instead. He drew it from a hero in a romance by Sándor Kisfaludy. For years after, he kept himself alive on very small earnings from the stage.
britannica-1911-talleyrand-perigord-char:
Charles Maurice de Talleyrand was a French envoy and statesman born in Paris of old and strong houses. His parents, in near constant wait at the court of the king, left the child to the care of others, as was the way of their class. As a small boy in the care of a nurse he fell and hurt his foot for life.

That hurt changed his whole path, the 1911 Britannica entry says. By rights, on his elder brothers death, he should have stood for the house and joined the army. The lame foot barred him from arms and cost him his birth rights. Sent to his grandmothers house in the south, he found there the sole kind care of his early years.
britannica-1911-tchihatcheff-pierre-alex:
Pierre de Tchihatcheff, a Russian man of science, is noted in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Gatchina near St Petersburg in 1812, he joined the state service. From 1842 he served at the mission in Constantinople for two years. From there he roamed Asia Minor, Syria, and Egypt on his own. In 1844 the state sent him to study the Altai mountains.

His books map the lands he crossed in close detail. His Altai trip came out in 1845 with a full atlas. His great work on Asia Minor ran to four books and three atlases. It was built up across the years from 1853 to 1869. Later books treat the Bosphorus, sea isles, Spain, and Tunis. He died at Florence in October of the year 1890.
britannica-1911-teligny-charles-de:
Teligny, Charles de, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a French soldier. Born about 1535, he came of a held-in-honour Huguenot house of Rouergue. He was trained in letters and arms at the house of Coligny. Peace work was his first field of service for his faith.

He spoke for the Protestant side before the king on missions. In 1567 Conde trusted him to lay terms before the queen-mother. The next year he helped sign the peace of Longjumeau at Chalons. When war broke out again he fought at the siege of Poitiers. He also led a failed attack on the town of Nantes. In 1571 he wed Louise de Coligny at La Rochelle. He was among the first slain in the St Bartholomew massacre of 1572.
britannica-1911-tencin-claudine-alexandr:
Claudine de Tencin is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. She was a French hostess and writer from 1681 to 1749. She was born at Grenoble in France. Her father led the law court of that town. She was raised in a convent near her home town. At her parents wish she took the veil as a nun. She broke those vows and won leave to quit in 1714.

She then joined her sister in Paris life. There she set up a salon for wits and rakes. A lover killed himself in her house in time. She was held in jail on that count for a spell. A high court cleared her of blame in the case. Her later salon drew famed minds of France and abroad. Her own tales won praise for ease and charm.
britannica-1911-tillemont-sebastien-le-n:
Sebastien le Nain de Tillemont is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French church historian. He lived from 1637 to 1698. He was born in Paris on the last day of November 1637. His father was a rich man of the legal class. That father was a devoted Jansenist in faith. The boy was raised in the little schools of Port Royal. There his bent toward history was warmly encouraged.

In 1660 he became a tutor at the seminary of Buzenval. Ten years later he came back to Paris. In 1676 he was persuaded to enter the priesthood. He became a chaplain at Port Royal at that time. In 1679 persecution drove him from that refuge. He settled on his family estate of Tillemont. There he spent the rest of his life in study. He died there in January 1698.
britannica-1911-torquemada-juan-de:
Juan de Torquemada is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Valladolid in Spain in 1388, he was a churchman who joined the Dominican order while still young. He soon stood out for his learning and his strict life.

The article follows his rise in church service. He went to the Council of Constance in 1415 and took his doctor's degree at Paris in 1423. After teaching in Paris he led Dominican houses at Valladolid and Toledo. Pope Eugenius the Fourth called him to Rome in 1431. He backed the Roman court at the Council of Basel and won a cardinal's hat in 1439. His chief works are then listed.
britannica-1911-torres-naharro-bartolome:
Bartolome de Torres Naharro (1480-1530) was a Spanish playwright born at Torres, near Badajoz. He spent some years as a soldier and as a captive in Algiers. He then took holy orders and settled in Rome about 1511. There he gave most of his time to writing plays. About 1517 his works were printed at Naples under the title Propaladia. He is thought to have gone home and died there soon after 1529.

Torres Naharro sorts his plays into two kinds. One kind draws on things he lived through himself, as in Soldatesca and Tinellaria. The other kind deals in made-up scenes, as in Serafina, Himenea, Calamita, and Aquilana. His first play copies Encina in a clear but unowned way. His later plays show a far larger grasp of what drama can do.
britannica-1911-torres-y-villaroel-diego:
Diego de Torres y Villaroel, a Spanish rogue of letters, is drawn in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Salamanca in 1696, he was a bookseller's son there. In his teens he fled to Portugal and served under a false name. Next he hawked goods in Madrid and lived from hand to mouth. Ordained in 1717, he went back to his books at Salamanca.

In 1726 Torres won the chair of mathematics at that school. Men called the pick a scandal, for his sums were slight. Yet he learned fast and showed his store with cool nerve. When a friend stabbed a priest, doubt fell on Torres too. He fled again till his clear name was proved in full. Of his fourteen books, his own life tale alone still lives.
britannica-1911-tourville-anne-hilarion-:
Anne-Hilarion de Cotentin, comte de Tourville (1642-1701), was a French admiral and marshal of France, and this 1911 Britannica entry covers his early life and training. He was the son of an officer in the king's household and was baptised in Paris in November 1642. His family meant him for the Order of Malta. From fourteen to twenty-five he served with the Order's galleys, which fought the Barbary pirates.

Little is known of those years, and the entry warns that the memoirs under his name are really a made-up romance from a later century. In 1667 he came back to France and joined the officer corps of the royal navy, which Louis the Fourteenth was then rebuilding. In 1689 he married a rich widow and was made count of Tourville.
britannica-1911-tracy-antoine-louis-clau:
Antoine Destutt de Tracy, who lived from 1754 to 1836, was a French philosopher of noble birth. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from home schooling and study at Strassburg to army life. He sat in the states general beside his friend La Fayette at the start of the Revolution. In 1792 he held a cavalry command in the army of the north.

As radicals gained power he withdrew to Auteuil and turned to study with close friends. The Terror jailed him for near a year, and in prison he read Condillac and Locke. That reading turned him from natural science to philosophy for good. He then won a seat in the Institute for moral and political science.
britannica-1911-travemunde:
Travemünde is a seaport of Germany in the free state of Lübeck. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on the Baltic, at the Trave mouth. Its people numbered just over two thousand in 1905 by count. A church from the late fifteenth century serves its faithful there still.

Bathers crowd it as a watering place in the warm season each year. Herring fisheries run on a large scale from its shore in trade. Henry the Lion first raised a stronghold there in the twelfth century. Danes later strengthened that post at the river mouth for war. Town rights came in 1317; Lübeck has held it since 1329.
britannica-1911-turenne-henri-de-la-tour:
Henri de la Tour d’Auvergne, Vicomte de Turenne (1611–1675), was a marshal of France, and his early life fills the opening of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He was born at Sedan on the eleventh of September 1611. His father was Henri, duke of Bouillon and prince of Sedan. His mother was Elizabeth, a daughter of William the Silent, prince of Orange.

Turenne was raised in the Reformed faith and trained as a young noble of his time. A speech impediment and weak health slowed his early progress. He loved history and geography, and he admired Alexander the Great and Caesar. After his father died in 1623, he built up his strength by hard exercise. At fourteen he went to learn war in the camp of his uncle, Maurice of Nassau.
britannica-1911-valenzuela-fernando-de:
Fernando de Valenzuela (1630–1692) was a Spanish royal favourite and minister. He was born at Naples on 19 January 1630. His father, a man of Ronda, had fled Spain after a brawl and served as a soldier in Naples. When his father died young, the boy was placed as a page in the house of the duke of Infantado. He lost that place when the duke cut his house staff, and he lived in shade for years.

By good luck, Valenzuela won the hand of Maria de Uceda, a lady-in-waiting to Mariana, second wife of Philip IV. By her help he gained a foot in the palace. In 1671 he was made the man who brought envoys before the queen. It was soon known that any man with a plea or a post to seek must go through him. The people called him the duende, the fairy of the palace.
britannica-1911-vendome-louis-joseph-duc:
Louis Joseph, duc de Vendôme, who lived from 1654 to 1712, was a marshal of France. The 1911 Britannica article says he was the great-grandson of Henry the Fourth. He entered the army at eighteen and soon stood out for drive and nerve in the Dutch wars. By 1688 he was a lieutenant-general. He served with credit under Luxemburg and Catinat, and in 1695 took command in Catalonia, where he seized Barcelona.

As marshal, Vendôme led the Franco-Spanish army in Italy from 1702. For three campaigns he matched Prince Eugene blow for blow. At Cassano he turned a loss by his brother into a fine win. Sent to Flanders after Ramillies, he could not stop the defeat at Oudenarde and left in disgust. Recalled to Spain, he won his last triumphs there. He died at Vinaros in June 1712.
britannica-1911-venette-jean-de:
Jean de Venette, a French chronicler who lived from about 1307 to about 1370, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Venette near Compiègne, he rose to lead the Carmelite house in Paris in 1339 and ran the order in France for more than two decades. His Latin chronicle covers the years from 1340 to 1368.

The chronicle was printed with the works of William of Nangis, but the entry is clear that it stands on its own. Parts were written as events took place, and the rest was revised later. Venette came from plain folk and his heart stayed with the peasants, a stance that sets him apart from Froissart. He backed Étienne Marcel, stayed sharp in his views of kings, and also wrote a long French poem on the three Marys. For readers of the Hundred Years War years, his is a rare voice from below.
britannica-1911-villehardouin-geoffroy-d:
Geoffroy de Villehardouin, first writer of history in a modern tongue in France with true merit, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at about 1160 at the château that gave him his name, near Troyes in Champagne. Nearly all that is known of him comes from his own chronicle. That work tells of the fourth crusade and the conquest of Constantinople.

He held the post of marshal of Champagne, as his forebears may have done. In Advent 1199 he took the cross at a tournament at Escry-sur-Aisne with his count Thibault. The next year he was one of six deputies sent to Venice. Their task was to bargain for ships and food for the host. When Thibault sickened and died, the plan faltered. Villehardouin made more trips to Italy to hold the deal with Venice together.
britannica-1911-villoison-jean-baptiste-:
Jean Baptiste Gaspard d'Ansse de Villoison lived from 1750 to 1805. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica presents him as a French scholar of Greek and Latin. He was born at Corbeil on the Seine to a noble house of Spanish roots. In 1773 he issued a Homeric word book from an abbey manuscript. In 1781 the French state sent him to Venice for three years.

There he found a tenth century copy of the Iliad. Its margins held old notes that flagged false or moved lines. A trip east to Greece and Mount Athos yielded less than he hoped. In 1788 he brought out that Venice Homer to great acclaim. The revolution drove him from Paris to quiet years at Orléans. On his return he took a chair of modern Greek. He held it until it passed to the Collège de France.
britannica-1911-voltaire-francois-marie-:
Voltaire, born Francois Marie Arouet, was a French thinker, historian, and playwright. He lived from sixteen ninety four to seventeen seventy eight. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Paris on the twenty first of November sixteen ninety four.

Voltaire father was a notary, and his mother died when he was seven. Both parents came from Poitevin stock long settled in Paris trade. The abbe de Chateauneuf taught the boy letters and deist thought early. He showed as a child a rare gift for quick and clear writing. His elder brother Armand, a stern Jansenist, shared no bond with him.
britannica-1911-wailly-noel-francois-de:
Noel Francois de Wailly was a French man of words who lived from seventeen twenty-four to eighteen one. He was born at Amiens and spent his life in Paris. There he ran a school that drew crowds of guests from abroad who wished to learn French. His book of rules for the tongue came out in seventeen fifty-four.

That book changed how the tongue was taught all through France. The chief school of Paris took it as its text, and a short form served young pupils. He also pled for spelling as words sound. He helped make the great word book of the French school.
britannica-1911-walther-von-der-vogelwei:
Walther von der Vogelweide was the most famed song poet of the German old age, who lived from about eleven seventy to about twelve thirty. For all his fame, few records of his day name him. One bishops bill notes a gift of coin to buy him a fur coat. His own songs are the chief source for his life.

He was of noble birth, but of the low rank that served great lords. He learned his craft at Vienna under a famed master. When his duke died, he became a wanderer from court to court. He sang for bed and board and spoke with a sharp tongue.
britannica-1911-wernigerode:
Wernigerode, a town of Germany in Prussian Saxony, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It lies on the Holzemme, on the north slopes of the Harz Mountains. Its count in 1905 was 13,137 people. The town holds fine Gothic buildings, with a town hall of wood front from 1498.

Old houses that escaped the town's many fires bear rich wood carving. Trades list brandy, cigars, and dye stuffs. Above the town rises the castle of the prince of Stolberg-Wernigerode. Its park house holds a library of 117,000 books, famed for more than three thousand Bibles. The county counts back to the early 1100s and passed to the Stolberg line in 1429.
britannica-1911-whitelocke-bulstrode:
Bulstrode Whitelocke was an English lawyer and man of the Commons, eldest son of a judge knight. Schooled at a great London school and at Oxford, he left college with no degree for the bar. He was called to the bar in his early twenties and rose to a high post in his inn of court two years on.

He loved field sports and music, the 1911 Britannica entry says. He had charge of the music in a grand mask shown by the inns of court before the king and queen. He sat in the Commons for a borough while still young, and held the post of town clerk for two towns. In the Long Parliament he took a lead part in the case against a doomed earl, as chair of the team that ran it. He drew a key bill on the life of parliaments as well.
britannica-1911-wimpffen-emmanuel-felix-:
Emmanuel Felix de Wimpffen, a French soldier born in eighteen eleven, came out of the school of Saint Cyr. He saw much active service in Algeria in his early career. He became captain in eighteen forty and battalion chief in eighteen forty seven. In the Crimean War he won marked fame as colonel of a Turco regiment. His conduct at the storm of the Mamelon won him a general's grade.

In the campaign of eighteen fifty nine Wimpffen served at Magenta with MacMahon. He led a brigade of Guard infantry and won promotion on the field. Between that campaign and that of eighteen seventy he served mainly in Algeria. At the war's start he got no command in the Army of the Rhine. When a corps commander failed, he was ordered to take that corps over. He reached the front in time to rally its beaten men at Sedan.
by-the-roadside:
Katherine M. Yates wrote a tale for the young, printed at Boston in 1908. The Harmony Shop put out the book. Her past tales line the title page: Up the Sunbeams, What the Pine Tree Heard, and At the Door among them. A small brown Dream opens the tale.

Marjorie, the girl of the book, will not rise. Work time, the Dream says, and she turns cross in her bed. He sits on the foot-board and swings his feet, still. Half an hour of turns and cross words pass. Talk, not force, moves the scene. Dream folk and day work form the stock of Yates's line, as her titles show: sunbeams, pine trees, and hill tops all teach in her books. Soft voice and slow dawn mark the road this tale walks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adelaide:
Adelaide is the archdiocese centred on South Australia's capital city. It covers all South Australia south of Victoria and Burra counties to Northwest Bend. The River Murray then forms the boundary to New South Wales. Flinders, Musgrave, and Jervois counties form its western portion, with adjacent islands. Its area is 40,320 square miles.

A chartered company founded South Australia in 1836 as a free, non-convict, Protestant colony. Papists and pagans were meant to be excluded, yet a few Catholics came among the first immigrants. Dr. Ullathorne visited Adelaide in June 1840. Governor Gawler refused the government school for Mass, so a generous Protestant lent a store where the first Mass drew about fifty. Adelaide became a see in 1843, with Francis Murphy its first bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-of-sta:
Albert of Stade chronicled the thirteenth century, having been born in the late 1100s. In 1232 he took charge as abbot of Stade's Benedictine house near Hamburg. In 1236 he tried to replace his abbey's Benedictine rule with the Cistercian rule, and resigned when he failed. In 1240 he joined the Franciscans and began his chronicle the same year.

His chronicle runs from the creation of the world down to 1256, with possible continuations to 1265. Its early parts draw on Bede's book on the six ages of the world and Ekkehard's chronicle. The entry notes that Albert grows fuller and more reliable as he nears his own times. The first complete edition appeared at Helmstadt in 1587, and he is also credited with Troilus, a Latin poem on Troy running to 5,320 lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-side:
The altar side is the part facing the congregation, as opposed to the side where the priest formerly stood facing the people. Ceremonials often mention the altar's right and left sides. Before 1488, right meant the epistle side and left the gospel side.

In that year Augustine Patrizi, Bishop of Pienza, issued a ceremonial that named the epistle side left and the gospel side right. The denomination came from the cross's facing alone, not the priest's or the laity's. St. Pius V accepted the change and put it into the rubrics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-averbode:
Averbode is a Premonstratensian abbey in the circary of Brabant, near Diest in the Archdiocese of Malines. Count Arnold of Losen founded it about 1132, and it ran without break until the general suppression of Belgian monasteries in 1796. The abbey was restored in 1834. At present it counts 82 priests, 20 clerics and novices, and 36 lay brothers.

Of those members, 27 priests and 21 lay brothers labor among the Indians in Brazil. At Leo XIII's request they set up a missionary monastery at Pirapora in the Diocese of Sao Paulo in 1896. They added a college at Jaguarao in the Diocese of Sao Pedro do Rio Grande do Sul in 1901. More recently two priests and three lay brothers from Averbode opened a mission house at Veile in Denmark. The entry cites Hugo's annals of the order and its general catalogue for the house's story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bede:
Bede is the old English word for a prayer, from Anglo-Saxon bed, though gebed was the commoner form. In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, little perforated globes of bone, wood, or amber, strung to count prayers, took the name bedes. Our modern bead, for small glass or coral globes, derives from nothing else. In middle English, bedes meant both prayer and rosary, as Shakespeare's plays and Chaucer's Prioress show.

The gauds were larger beads dividing the decades, and a pair of beads still means the five-decade chaplet, not the full rosary. To bid beads first meant simply to say prayers, though bidding the beads later attached to certain public devotions. Bede-roll meant the roll of those to be prayed for, kept by early English guilds for departed members. The word survives provincially and in Welsh place-names like Bettws y Coed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bull-of-the-c:
The Bull of the Crusade granted indulgences to fighters in wars against the infidels, above all in Spain's reconquest. Such grants reached back to the eleventh century, when the Spanish Mark's faithful earned them by building churches or giving alms. The first Spanish crusade bulls came from Urban II in 1089 for Barcelona's counts at Tarragona's reconquest and from Gelasius II in 1118 for Alfonso I of Aragon at Saragossa.

Clement IV extended a bull to all Spain in 1265 for the Murcia expedition, and grants multiplied under the Catholic kings in 1478 through 1505 and beyond. Alms first funded war alone, then church building and pious works, and at times state expenses, despite Cortes protests in 1523 and 1592 and Philip III's rules. After 1847 the funds endowed churches and clergy by law in 1849 and the Concordat of 1851. The faithful, confessed and communicated, gained a plenary indulgence, double absolution from reserved sins, and commutation of hard vows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-certitude:
Certitude names a state of mind on the one hand and a quality of a proposition on the other, whether the phrase is I am certain or It is certain. Philosophy marks the distinction as subjective certitude and objective certitude. Newman reserves certitude for the state of mind and uses certainty for the condition of a proposition's evidence.

Certitude is correlative to truth, since truth is the intellect's object. We commonly call a proposition certain when its truth is so evident as rightly to produce certitude. Certitude stands against ignorance, doubt, and opinion, the last meaning in the strict sense the holding of a proposition as probable. Certitude itself is assent to a proposition's truth that excludes all real doubt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-judde:
Claude Judde, a French preacher and spiritual father, was born at Rouen about 20 December 1661 and died at Paris on 11 March 1735. He joined the Society of Jesus on 18 September 1677, taking final vows on 2 February 1695. At first he preached with success in the provinces and the capital, and his oratorical gifts were judged equal to Bourdaloue's. Bourdaloue even wished him as successor and spoke of bequeathing his papers.

Judde's superiors instead asked him to give up pulpit success for training his brethren in religious virtues. From 1704 to 1721 he instructed the third probation at Rouen and served as rector of the Paris novitiate. Hearers of his retreats and exhortations, charmed by solid eloquence at once vigorous and pathetic, preserved his words in writing. He published nothing himself, but after his death collections appeared from transcripts. They include a spiritual retreat of 1746, Christian reflections of 1748, exhortations of 1772, and complete spiritual works of 1781 to 1782.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claudio-monte:
Claudio Monteverde, a distinguished musician, was born at Cremona in May 1567 and died at Venice on 29 November 1643. He studied under Ingegneri and published a book of canzonets at sixteen, followed by four volumes of madrigals. One madrigal of 1592 already shows his inventive turn, with suspensions of the dominant seventh and suspended ninths. He became the Duke of Mantua's Maestro di Cappella in 1602 and at Venice in 1613. His Venice salary rose to five hundred ducats in 1616.

Until his death he produced choral works, operas, cantatas, and ballets, most now untraced. The score of Orfeo, printed in 1609, survives and shows a musician breaking from the older school to create his own. His novelties include new instrumental effects and combinations, an instrumental tremolo in a festival interlude, and trombones accompanying a Mass's Gloria and Credo in 1631. His fame rests on unprepared discords, improved recitative, and a revolution in orchestration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colonnade:
Thomas Poole's entry defines a colonnade as a set of columns arranged in one or more rows, set in symmetry. A single row makes it monostyle, while many rows make it polystyle. When it rings a building or court, it is called a peristyle. When it juts past the building line, it is a portico. Sometimes it bears a building. Sometimes it bears only a roof. The terms sort a common sight of classical building into clear kinds.

For church building, the most famous example stands at Saint Peter's in Rome. Bernini raised it in 1665 to 1667, with 284 columns. Above its balustrades stand 162 statues of saints. Poole points readers to the Bernini entry for more. Short as it is, the entry gives a builder or visitor the words to name each form of columned walk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Sister St. Beatrice's entry follows the Sisters of Misericorde, a women's congregation founded on 16 January 1848 to give spiritual and corporal help to poor mothers and unfortunate girls. Foundress Rosalie Jette, in religion Mother Mary of the Nativity, declined the superior's office, so Sister Saint Jane de Chantal held it. Pius IX approved the institute on 7 June 1867. Constitutions revised under Rome's latest rules won Pius X's approbation on 21 March 1905.

A superior general governs, assisted by four councillors, a secretary, and a bursar, all resident at Montreal's mother-house in Canada. Branch houses answer to general administration, each under a local superior, two assistants forming her council, and a bursar for temporal matters controlled by that council. Present numbers count 189 professed sisters, 23 novices, and 10 candidates. American houses include Milwaukee, Oak Park in Illinois founded in 1905 with fifteen sisters and 712 patients, and a Wisconsin house from 1900 serving 450 patients and children yearly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-cor:
John Peter Van Kasteren's entry treats Cornelius Cornelii a Lapide, Cornelis Cornelissen van den Steen, Flemish Jesuit and exegete. Born at Bocholt in Flemish Limburg in 1567, he died at Rome in 1637. He studied humanities and philosophy at Maestricht and Cologne, theology first for half a year at Douai, then for four years at Louvain. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1592, and, after two years' noviciate and another theology year, was ordained priest in 1595.

After teaching philosophy for half a year, he became Louvain's professor of Scripture in 1596, and of Hebrew the next year. In 1616 Rome called him in the same capacity, where on 3 November he assumed an office he filled with renown for years. His later years seem devoted to finishing his commentaries. Cornelius a Lapide wrote ample commentaries on all Catholic Canon books except Job and the Psalms. Their numerous editions show how highly Catholics estimate the works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ag:
The Council of Agde met in 506 at Agde in Languedoc, under St Caesarius of Arles, with thirty-five bishops in attendance. Its forty-seven genuine canons govern church discipline in southern France at the moment the Graeco-Roman order gave way to barbarian conquerors. They also matter for the study of certain early church institutions.
